There is periorbital and scrotal edema and mild ascites. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 6.5 g/g. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL, cholesterol 380 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.3 mg/dL. C3 is normal. He weighs 17 kg (body surface area 0.7 m²).
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Intravenous rituximab", "Kidney biopsy before starting any treatment", "Intravenous albumin and furosemide without glucocorticoids", "Oral prednisone 60 mg/m² per day, then alternate-day dosing for a total course of 8 to 12 weeks", "Oral cyclophosphamide"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "childhood idiopathic nephrotic syndrome initial therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Typical pediatric nephrotic syndrome: empiric prednisone 60 mg/m²/day (max 60 mg) then alternate-day, 8-12 weeks total; biopsy only if atypical or steroid-resistant.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral prednisone 60 mg/m² per day, then alternate-day dosing for a total course of 8 to 12 weeks
before.explanation: Oral prednisone 60 mg/m² per day (or 2 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg) followed by alternate-day dosing is correct: a young child with nephrotic syndrome, no hematuria, normal blood pressure, kidney function, and complement most likely has minimal change disease, and KDIGO 2025 recommends 8 weeks (4 daily plus 4 alternate-day) or 12 weeks (6 plus 6) of oral glucocorticoids. Kidney biopsy before treatment is incorrect because typical children are treated empirically; biopsy is reserved for steroid resistance or atypical features. Oral cyclophosphamide is incorrect because it is a steroid-sparing agent for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease. Rituximab is likewise a second-line agent. IV albumin and furosemide alone is incorrect because it treats refractory edema but does not induce remission. Takeaway: typical childhood nephrotic syndrome, treat with prednisone without biopsy; steroid responsiveness predicts minimal change disease.

references.label: KDIGO 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in Children
KDIGO 2025 Nephrotic Syndrome in Children Guideline Executive Summary

before.scenario: A 24-year-old man reports 4 days of gradually worsening right scrotal pain and dysuria. He has had two new female partners in the past 2 months and uses condoms inconsistently. He does not practice insertive anal sex. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). The right epididymis is swollen and tender; the testis lies normally and the cremasteric reflex is present. Pain decreases with scrotal elevation. Urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase, and urethral Gram stain shows white cells. Nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia is pending. Doppler ultrasound shows increased epididymal blood flow.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once alone", "Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 14 days", "Levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days", "Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days", "Azithromycin 1 g orally once"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "acute epididymitis treatment", "keyTakeaway": "Epididymitis with STI risk: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100 mg BID x10 days; add levofloxacin instead of doxycycline for insertive anal sex.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days
before.explanation: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days is correct: in men younger than 35 or with STI risk, acute epididymitis is most often caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae, and CDC 2021 recommends this regimen empirically after specimens are collected, with scrotal elevation and analgesia. Levofloxacin alone is incorrect because CDC reserves levofloxacin for enteric organisms, as with insertive anal sex (combined with ceftriaxone) or men with low STI risk, and fluoroquinolones do not reliably treat gonorrhea. Azithromycin 1 g once is incorrect because it is not a recommended epididymitis regimen and does not cover gonorrhea. Ceftriaxone alone is incorrect because it does not treat chlamydia. TMP-SMX is incorrect because it does not cover the sexually transmitted causes. Takeaway: sexually active man with epididymitis, ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline for 10 days; treat partners and retest.

references.label: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021: Epididymitis
Workowski KA et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021

before.scenario: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a painful erection that began 6 hours ago and has not subsided. He denies trauma and takes no erectile medications. The penile shaft is rigid and tender, while the glans is soft. Blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg and pulse 96/min. Corporal blood aspirated for gas analysis is dark, with pH 7.10, PO2 20 mm Hg, and PCO2 70 mm Hg. Oral hydration and analgesia have been started.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Ice packs and observation for 6 more hours", "Oral pseudoephedrine and observation", "Selective penile arterial embolization", "Corporal aspiration with intracavernosal phenylephrine injection", "Exchange transfusion alone and observation"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "acute ischemic priapism", "keyTakeaway": "Ischemic priapism (pH <7.25, PO2 <30, PCO2 >60): aspiration ± irrigation + intracavernosal phenylephrine; sickle cell care must not delay it; embolization is for high-flow.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Corporal aspiration with intracavernosal phenylephrine injection
before.explanation: Corporal aspiration with intracavernosal phenylephrine is correct: a painful, rigid shaft with a soft glans and hypoxic, acidotic corporal blood indicates ischemic (low-flow) priapism, a compartment syndrome; the AUA guideline recommends aspiration with or without irrigation plus intracavernosal phenylephrine as first-line therapy, with blood pressure and heart rate monitored. Exchange transfusion alone is incorrect because sickle cell measures must not delay or replace intracavernosal therapy. Embolization is incorrect because it treats nonischemic (high-flow) priapism with bright red, well-oxygenated blood, typically after perineal trauma. Oral pseudoephedrine is incorrect because oral agents have little evidence and waste time. Ice packs with observation are incorrect because ischemic time beyond about 4 hours raises the risk of fibrosis and permanent ED. Takeaway: dark, acidotic corporal blood means ischemic priapism, so aspirate and inject phenylephrine now.

references.label: AUA/SMSNA Guideline: Acute Ischemic Priapism
Bivalacqua TJ et al. Acute Ischemic Priapism: An AUA/SMSNA Guideline. J Urol 2021

before.scenario: A screening test for a disease has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 95%. In a specialty clinic where the disease prevalence is 30%, the positive predictive value is about 89%. The same test is then offered to an asymptomatic general population in which the prevalence is 1%.
before.question: Which of the following best describes the test's performance in the general population compared with the specialty clinic?
before.options: {"options": ["Negative predictive value falls substantially", "Positive predictive value rises", "Sensitivity and specificity both fall", "Positive predictive value falls substantially while sensitivity and specificity are unchanged", "Specificity rises while sensitivity falls"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "effect of prevalence on predictive value", "keyTakeaway": "Prevalence changes predictive values, not sensitivity/specificity: low prevalence leads to low PPV and high NPV.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Positive predictive value falls substantially while sensitivity and specificity are unchanged
before.explanation: PPV falls substantially while sensitivity and specificity are unchanged is correct: sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test that do not depend on prevalence, whereas predictive values do. At 1% prevalence, in 10,000 people there are 95 true positives and 495 false positives (5% of 9,900), so PPV is 95/590, about 16%. Sensitivity and specificity falling is incorrect because they are intrinsic test characteristics (aside from spectrum effects). PPV rising is incorrect because a lower pretest probability lowers the probability that a positive result is true. NPV falling is incorrect because NPV rises as prevalence falls (here about 99.9%). Specificity rising while sensitivity falls is incorrect because that trade-off occurs only when the positivity cutoff is changed. Takeaway: lower prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV; that is why screening low-risk populations produces many false positives.

references.label: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy

before.scenario: A 16-year-old girl comes alone to an urgent care clinic with 4 days of vaginal discharge and dysuria. She is sexually active with one male partner and asks that her parents not be told about the visit. She is articulate and understands her options. Nucleic acid amplification testing is collected, and the physician assistant plans to treat her empirically for cervicitis. Her mother is listed as the guarantor on her insurance.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
before.options: {"options": ["Refuse treatment and refer her to her pediatrician", "Evaluate and treat her with her own consent and maintain confidentiality within the limits of state law", "Obtain parental consent before testing or treatment", "Call her parents after the visit because she is a minor", "Treat her only if she agrees to involve her partner's parents"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "minor consent for confidential STI care", "keyTakeaway": "All U.S. states allow minors to consent to STI care; keep it confidential, encourage (not require) parental involvement, and warn about EOB disclosures.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Evaluate and treat her with her own consent and maintain confidentiality within the limits of state law
before.explanation: Evaluating and treating with her own consent while maintaining confidentiality is correct: all 50 states and the District of Columbia explicitly allow minors to consent to STI diagnosis and treatment without parental consent, and CDC STI guidelines emphasize confidential care for adolescents because fear of disclosure deters care. The AMA Code advises respecting the confidentiality of minors when they can consent to services, while encouraging, not requiring, parental involvement. Warn her that insurance statements may reveal the visit. Obtaining parental consent is incorrect because state law allows her to consent. Calling her parents is incorrect because doing so breaches confidentiality without a safety exception. Refusing treatment is incorrect because it denies needed care. Involving her partner's parents has no basis. Takeaway: minors may consent to confidential STI care; know your state's specific rules on notification.

references.label: Guttmacher Institute: Minors' Access to STI Services
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021: Adolescents
AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 2.2.1: Pediatric Decision Making

before.scenario: A 70-year-old man hospitalized with pneumonia received a dose of intravenous ceftriaxone despite a documented severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy listed in his chart. He developed hives and wheezing that resolved with epinephrine and antihistamines and is now stable. The physician assistant who wrote the order realizes the allergy alert was overridden in error. The patient asks what happened.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
before.options: {"options": ["Disclose only if the patient's family asks for details", "Promptly explain what happened, take responsibility, apologize, and describe steps to prevent recurrence", "Document the event in the chart without informing the patient", "Tell the patient he had an unpredictable reaction to an antibiotic", "Wait to discuss the event until risk management completes its review"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "disclosure of a medical error", "keyTakeaway": "Harmful error: prompt, honest disclosure, apology, explanation, prevention plan (AMA; AHRQ CANDOR); also report the event to the safety system.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Promptly explain what happened, take responsibility, apologize, and describe steps to prevent recurrence
before.explanation: Promptly explaining, taking responsibility, apologizing, and describing prevention steps is correct: the AMA Code states that patients have a right to know when an error has caused harm, and that clinicians should disclose the facts, express regret, explain consequences, and describe what will be done to prevent recurrence. AHRQ's CANDOR toolkit promotes early, honest communication, an apology, and support for both patients and clinicians. Calling it unpredictable is incorrect because it is a deceptive account. Waiting for risk management is incorrect because disclosure should be timely; risk management supports rather than delays the conversation. Disclosing only if the family asks is incorrect because the duty is proactive and owed to the patient. Documenting without informing him violates honesty. Takeaway: disclose harmful errors to the patient promptly and honestly, apologize, and report the event for systems improvement.

references.label: AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 8.6: Promoting Patient Safety
AHRQ Communication and Optimal Resolution (CANDOR) Toolkit

before.scenario: A physician assistant on a busy medical floor is about to draw blood for a type and crossmatch from a patient in room 412. The patient is alert. The PA has the labeled tubes and the patient's armband is visible. The patient in room 414 has a similar last name.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate method to confirm patient identity before drawing the specimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Check the bed assignment on the electronic census", "Ask the nurse which patient is in the bed", "Address the patient by last name and wait for a response", "Ask the patient to state full name and date of birth and match them with the armband and labels", "Confirm the room number on the door"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "two patient identifiers", "keyTakeaway": "Two identifiers (e.g., name + DOB) for every specimen, medication, or blood product; never room/bed number; label at the bedside.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ask the patient to state full name and date of birth and match them with the armband and labels
before.explanation: Asking the patient to state full name and date of birth and matching them to the armband and labels is correct: the Joint Commission requires at least two patient identifiers, such as name and date of birth, when providing care, treatment, or services, including collecting blood samples, administering medications, or giving blood products, and labeling specimens in the patient's presence. Room number is incorrect because location is never an acceptable identifier; patients move and rooms are reassigned. Saying the last name and waiting for a response is incorrect because confused or hard-of-hearing patients may answer to a similar name. The census also relies on location. Asking the nurse is incorrect because it is secondhand and does not use two identifiers tied to the patient. Takeaway: use two person-specific identifiers, never room or bed number, and have the patient state them.

references.label: The Joint Commission National Performance Goals: Right Patient, Right Care

before.scenario: A physician assistant who passed the PANCE 3 years ago is mentoring a new graduate. The graduate asks what is required to keep NCCPA board certification active over the 10-year certification maintenance process.
before.question: Which of the following best describes NCCPA certification maintenance requirements?
before.options: {"options": ["Earn and log 100 CME credits every 2 years, including at least 50 Category 1, and pass PANRE or PANRE-LA by the end of the 10th year", "Earn 100 CME credits every 10 years with no recertification examination", "Earn 50 CME credits every year and retake PANCE every 6 years", "Complete a supervised clinical rotation every 5 years", "Pass PANRE every 2 years with no CME requirement"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "NCCPA certification maintenance", "keyTakeaway": "NCCPA: five 2-year cycles; 100 CME per cycle (>=50 Category 1) + fee; pass PANRE or PANRE-LA by end of year 10.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Earn and log 100 CME credits every 2 years, including at least 50 Category 1, and pass PANRE or PANRE-LA by the end of the 10th year
before.explanation: Earning and logging 100 CME credits every 2 years, at least 50 of them Category 1, and passing PANRE or PANRE-LA by the end of the 10th year is correct: NCCPA's 10-year certification maintenance process consists of five 2-year cycles; each requires logged CME and a fee, and the recertification exam (PANRE or longitudinal PANRE-LA) is due by the end of year 10. Earning 50 credits yearly and retaking PANCE every 6 years is incorrect because it describes an outdated 6-year cycle and PANCE is the initial exam. 100 credits per 10 years without an exam is incorrect because CME is required every 2-year cycle and an exam is required. A supervised rotation is not required. PANRE every 2 years is incorrect because the exam is taken once per 10-year process. Takeaway: NCCPA maintenance means 100 CME (50 Category 1) every 2 years and PANRE or PANRE-LA by year 10.

references.label: NCCPA: Maintain Certification
NCCPA: Continuing Medical Education (CME)

before.scenario: A 30-year-old nurse sustains a deep percutaneous injury with a hollow-bore needle used to draw blood from a patient with known HIV infection whose most recent viral load is unknown. The injury occurred 1 hour ago; the wound was washed with soap and water. The nurse has no known kidney disease and a negative pregnancy test. Baseline HIV testing of the nurse has been drawn. The source patient's current viral load result will take 2 days.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Wait for the source patient's viral load before deciding on prophylaxis", "Start a 28-day post-exposure prophylaxis regimen immediately, such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide", "Start zidovudine monotherapy for 4 weeks", "Start prophylaxis only if the nurse's 6-week HIV test is positive", "Squeeze the wound and apply bleach, then observe"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "occupational HIV post-exposure prophylaxis", "keyTakeaway": "Occupational HIV PEP (2025 USPHS): start ASAP (<=72 h), 28 days, preferred BIC/FTC/TAF or DTG + tenofovir/FTC; don't delay for source testing.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Start a 28-day post-exposure prophylaxis regimen immediately, such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide
before.explanation: Starting a 28-day PEP regimen immediately is correct: the 2025 US Public Health Service guideline advises initiating PEP as soon as possible, up to 72 hours after occupational exposure, prescribing it for 28 days, and not delaying PEP while awaiting information about the source; preferred regimens include the single-tablet bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide or dolutegravir with a tenofovir-based backbone. Waiting for the viral load is incorrect because the guideline states PEP should not be delayed for source information. Zidovudine monotherapy is incorrect because modern guidance uses 3-drug, well-tolerated regimens. Starting only after a positive test is incorrect because that would treat established infection rather than prevent it. Squeezing or applying bleach is not recommended; soap and water is. Takeaway: occupational HIV exposure, start 3-drug PEP within hours and continue for 28 days; don't wait for source results.

before.scenario: A 23-year-old woman with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of severe low back and bilateral thigh pain typical of her prior pain crises. She rates the pain 9/10. Temperature is 37.2 C (99.0 F), pulse 108/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. Lungs are clear. She has an individualized pain plan on file. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, near her baseline.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral acetaminophen and reassessment in 4 hours", "Intravenous methylprednisolone", "Simple transfusion of 2 units of packed red cells", "Wait for a chest radiograph and urinalysis before giving analgesia", "Parenteral opioid administered within 1 hour of arrival, dosed per her individualized plan, with reassessment every 30-60 minutes"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain in the emergency department", "keyTakeaway": "ASH 2020 SCD pain: rapid analgesia within 60 minutes of arrival, individualized opioid plan, reassess every 30-60 minutes; NSAID adjunct; no steroids.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Parenteral opioid administered within 1 hour of arrival, dosed per her individualized plan, with reassessment every 30-60 minutes
before.explanation: A parenteral opioid within 1 hour, dosed per the individualized plan, with reassessment every 30-60 minutes is correct: the ASH 2020 sickle cell pain guideline recommends rapid assessment and analgesia (within 1 hour of ED arrival), individualized opioid dosing, and frequent reassessment, and suggests a short course of NSAIDs as an adjunct in the absence of contraindications. Oral acetaminophen alone with delayed reassessment undertreats severe vaso-occlusive pain. Transfusion is not indicated for an uncomplicated pain episode with hemoglobin at baseline; it is reserved for indications such as acute chest syndrome or symptomatic anemia. Corticosteroids are not recommended for acute pain in sickle cell disease and are associated with rebound pain. Analgesia should not be delayed while diagnostic tests are pending. Takeaway: in a sickle cell pain crisis, give analgesia within 1 hour and reassess every 30-60 minutes.

references.label: Brandow AM et al. American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for sickle cell disease: management of acute and chronic pain. Blood Adv 2020

before.scenario: A 31-year-old woman notices petechiae on her legs and gum bleeding after brushing for 4 days. She has no other symptoms and takes no medications. Examination shows scattered lower-extremity petechiae and no splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Platelet count is 18,000/mm3; hemoglobin and WBC count are normal. The smear shows large platelets without schistocytes. HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Platelet transfusion", "Corticosteroid therapy such as a prednisone course of no more than 6 weeks", "Splenectomy", "Observation with repeat platelet count in 1 month", "Rituximab as first-line monotherapy"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia in adults", "keyTakeaway": "ASH 2019 adult ITP: platelets <30,000 → corticosteroids (prednisone ≤6 weeks or dexamethasone 40 mg x 4 days); IVIG for rapid rise; splenectomy/rituximab/TPO-RA are second line.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Corticosteroid therapy such as a prednisone course of no more than 6 weeks
before.explanation: A corticosteroid course of no more than 6 weeks is correct: the ASH 2019 ITP guideline suggests corticosteroids rather than observation for newly diagnosed adults with a platelet count below 30,000/mm3, and recommends against prolonged prednisone courses longer than 6 weeks (including taper); either prednisone (0.5-2 mg/kg/day) or dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days is acceptable, with IVIG added when a rapid rise is needed. Observation is incorrect because the platelet count is below 30,000/mm3 with mucosal bleeding. Splenectomy is incorrect because it is a second-line option, generally deferred for at least 12 months from diagnosis. Rituximab is incorrect because it is a second-line therapy. Platelet transfusion is incorrect because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed and are reserved for life-threatening bleeding. Takeaway: adult ITP with platelets <30,000 = short corticosteroid course (≤6 weeks).

references.label: Neunert C et al. American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv 2019

before.scenario: A 52-year-old woman receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer presents 9 days after her last cycle with a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). She feels mildly fatigued but is otherwise well, is eating and drinking, and lives 15 minutes from the cancer center with her husband. Pulse is 92/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination shows no focal source. ANC is 300/µL. Lactate and creatinine are normal; MASCC score is 23. She has no penicillin allergy and has not received fluoroquinolone prophylaxis.
before.question: After obtaining blood cultures, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Admission for IV vancomycin plus cefepime", "Oral levofloxacin alone discharged without observation", "Oral fluconazole plus acyclovir", "Observation without antibiotics until culture results return", "Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate with outpatient follow-up after a period of observation"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "low-risk febrile neutropenia outpatient therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Febrile neutropenia: cultures + empiric antibiotics within 1 h; MASCC ≥21 low risk → oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin-clavulanate outpatient; high risk → IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., cefepime).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate with outpatient follow-up after a period of observation
before.explanation: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate is correct: the ASCO/IDSA 2018 guideline on outpatient management of febrile neutropenia recommends that patients judged low risk (e.g., MASCC ≥21, no high-risk features, able to take oral medication, with caregiver and ready access) receive empiric oral therapy with a fluoroquinolone plus amoxicillin-clavulanate after initial assessment and a period of observation, with close follow-up. Vancomycin is not routine empiric therapy without specific indications such as hemodynamic instability, skin/catheter infection, or pneumonia, and this patient is low risk. Discharge without observation is not advised. Withholding antibiotics in neutropenic fever is dangerous because infection can progress rapidly. Antifungal and antiviral therapy are not initial empiric treatment. Takeaway: neutropenic fever is an emergency; low-risk patients can receive oral fluoroquinolone plus amoxicillin-clavulanate as outpatients.

references.label: Taplitz RA et al. Outpatient management of fever and neutropenia in adults treated for malignancy: ASCO/IDSA guideline update. J Clin Oncol 2018

before.scenario: A 16-year-old boy has had acne for 1 year that has not improved with over-the-counter salicylic acid cleanser. Examination shows numerous open and closed comedones and about 15 inflammatory papules and pustules on the forehead, cheeks, and chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring. He prefers to avoid oral medications if possible.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial regimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral doxycycline as monotherapy for 6 months", "Oral isotretinoin", "Topical adapalene plus benzoyl peroxide, with or without topical clindamycin", "Oral prednisone for 2 weeks", "Topical clindamycin as monotherapy"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "moderate inflammatory acne initial therapy", "keyTakeaway": "AAD 2024 acne: topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide (± topical clindamycin) first line; oral doxycycline with topicals for moderate-severe; isotretinoin for severe/scarring.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Topical adapalene plus benzoyl peroxide, with or without topical clindamycin
before.explanation: Topical adapalene plus benzoyl peroxide, with or without topical clindamycin, is correct: the AAD 2024 acne guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide and recommends fixed-dose combination topicals; topical antibiotics should be paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit Cutibacterium acnes resistance. Topical clindamycin alone promotes resistance and is discouraged. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodular, scarring, or treatment-resistant acne. Oral doxycycline is appropriate for moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne but should be combined with topical therapy and limited in duration, ideally about 3 months, not used as monotherapy. Systemic corticosteroids are only considered short-term in severe inflammatory acne (e.g., when starting isotretinoin). Takeaway: comedonal and inflammatory acne = topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide ± topical antibiotic; never antibiotic monotherapy.

references.label: Reynolds RV et al. Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris. J Am Acad Dermatol 2024

before.scenario: A 6-year-old boy weighing 24 kg (53 lb) has had a patch of scaling hair loss on his scalp for 6 weeks. Examination shows a 4-cm round patch with broken hairs at the scalp surface ('black dots') and mild scale; there is occipital lymphadenopathy. A KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows spores within the hair shafts. Fungal culture is pending.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Topical hydrocortisone 1% cream", "Oral nystatin", "Topical clotrimazole cream for 4 weeks", "Oral terbinafine", "Ketoconazole 2% shampoo alone"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "tinea capitis treatment", "keyTakeaway": "Tinea capitis: always oral therapy; terbinafine (Trichophyton, weight-based 2-4 weeks) or griseofulvin (Microsporum, 6-8+ weeks); adjunct sporicidal shampoo; screen family.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral terbinafine
before.explanation: Oral terbinafine is correct: black-dot tinea capitis with endothrix spores is typically caused by Trichophyton tonsurans, the most common US cause, and the British Association of Dermatologists 2014 guideline recommends oral therapy because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle; terbinafine is preferred for Trichophyton species (weight-based: 62.5 mg daily for 10-20 kg, 125 mg for 20-40 kg, 250 mg for >40 kg, for 4 weeks per BAD; this 24-kg child would receive 125 mg daily), whereas griseofulvin (microsize 20-25 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks or longer in US pediatric practice) is more effective for Microsporum species and remains an acceptable alternative. Topical clotrimazole is incorrect because topical therapy alone does not eradicate infection of the hair shaft. Ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo is used as an adjunct to reduce spore shedding, not as monotherapy. Hydrocortisone is incorrect because steroids do not treat fungal infection. Oral nystatin is not absorbed and has no activity against dermatophytes. Takeaway: tinea capitis requires oral antifungal therapy, terbinafine for Trichophyton and griseofulvin for Microsporum.

references.label: Fuller LC et al. British Association of Dermatologists' guidelines for the management of tinea capitis 2014. Br J Dermatol 2014

before.scenario: A 30-year-old woman reports 3 weeks of intense itching that is worst at night. Her partner has similar symptoms. Examination shows excoriated papules on the finger webs, flexor wrists, periumbilical area, and waistband, with several short, gray, wavy lines in the finger webs. Mineral oil scraping of a burrow shows a mite and eggs. She is not pregnant.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Topical triamcinolone alone", "Lindane lotion as first-line therapy", "Oral cephalexin for 7 days", "Permethrin 5% cream applied from the neck down and washed off after 8-14 hours, with simultaneous treatment of her partner", "Permethrin 1% cream rinse applied to the scalp"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "classic scabies treatment", "keyTakeaway": "Scabies: permethrin 5% cream neck down (wash off 8-14 h) or ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO repeated in 14 days; treat contacts simultaneously; wash bedding; itch can persist ~2 weeks.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Permethrin 5% cream applied from the neck down and washed off after 8-14 hours, with simultaneous treatment of her partner
before.explanation: Permethrin 5% cream from the neck down, washed off after 8-14 hours, with simultaneous treatment of close contacts, is correct: the CDC recommends permethrin 5% cream or oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg (repeated in 14 days) for classic scabies, with treatment of sexual and household contacts and decontamination of bedding and clothing. Itching may persist up to 2 weeks after successful treatment. Permethrin 1% cream rinse is a lice treatment and is not adequate for scabies. Lindane is not first-line because of neurotoxicity risk and is contraindicated in several groups. Topical steroids alone relieve itching but do not kill mites. Cephalexin treats secondary bacterial infection, not the infestation. Takeaway: scabies = permethrin 5% (or ivermectin) for the patient and all close contacts at the same time.

references.label: CDC: Clinical Care of Scabies
Workowski KA et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021

before.scenario: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes requests 'pills for toenail fungus.' The great toenails and two smaller toenails are thickened, yellow, and crumbly with subungual debris and distal onycholysis for 3 years. He has no nail pitting, skin plaques, or history of nail trauma. He has never had nail testing. Liver enzymes are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before prescribing oral terbinafine?
before.options: {"options": ["Perform a Wood lamp examination", "Obtain a nail fold capillaroscopy", "Send nail clippings and subungual debris for KOH preparation with fungal culture or PAS stain", "Start oral terbinafine 250 mg daily without testing", "Obtain a plain radiograph of the foot"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "confirming onychomycosis before systemic therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Onychomycosis: confirm with KOH + culture or nail PAS before systemic therapy; terbinafine 250 mg daily x 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails) is first line.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Send nail clippings and subungual debris for KOH preparation with fungal culture or PAS stain
before.explanation: Sending nail clippings and subungual debris for KOH with fungal culture or PAS histology is correct: only about half of dystrophic nails are fungal, and nail psoriasis, trauma, and lichen planus mimic onychomycosis, so the British Association of Dermatologists 2014 onychomycosis guideline and AAD-published clinical reviews recommend mycologic confirmation before committing a patient to systemic therapy (oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks for toenails) with its cost, drug interactions, and rare hepatotoxicity. Empiric terbinafine without testing risks treating a nonfungal dystrophy. Capillaroscopy evaluates connective tissue disease. A foot radiograph is not used to diagnose nail infection. A Wood lamp examination does not diagnose dermatophyte onychomycosis because dermatophytes in nails do not fluoresce. Takeaway: confirm onychomycosis with KOH plus culture or PAS before oral antifungal therapy.

references.label: Ameen M et al. British Association of Dermatologists' guidelines for the management of onychomycosis 2014. Br J Dermatol 2014
Lipner SR, Scher RK. Onychomycosis: Clinical overview and diagnosis. J Am Acad Dermatol 2019

before.scenario: A 47-year-old asymptomatic man with a BMI of 32 has screening laboratory studies. A single fasting blood sample shows a fasting plasma glucose of 134 mg/dL and an HbA1c of 6.7%. He has no anemia, hemoglobinopathy, kidney disease, or recent blood loss or transfusion.
before.question: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
before.options: {"options": ["Diabetes is suspected but a repeat HbA1c on a separate day is required", "The results are indeterminate; a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is required", "Prediabetes is present; repeat testing in 1 year", "Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed without further testing", "Diabetes cannot be diagnosed without symptoms of hyperglycemia"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "confirming a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes", "keyTakeaway": "ADA 2026 diabetes: A1c ≥6.5%, FPG ≥126, 2-h OGTT ≥200, or random ≥200 + symptoms; confirm with 2 abnormal results (same sample or separate samples). Prediabetes: A1c 5.7-6.4%, FPG 100-125, 2-h 140-199.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed without further testing
before.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed without further testing: the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026 define diabetes as FPG ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour 75-g OGTT glucose ≥200 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms; in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results, which may come from the same sample or from two separate samples. Both his FPG and HbA1c exceed the thresholds in the same sample. Prediabetes (FPG 100-125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7%-6.4%) is incorrect because both values are in the diabetes range. An OGTT is unnecessary because the diagnosis is established. Repeating HbA1c on another day is needed only when a single test is abnormal or results are discordant. Symptoms are not required except when using a random glucose. Takeaway: two abnormal diabetes tests, even from one blood sample, confirm diabetes.

references.label: ADA Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026
Diabetes Care 2026 Volume 49 Supplement 1: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026

before.scenario: Investigators study the long-term health of employees at a chemical plant. They compare all-cause mortality over 20 years among currently employed plant workers with mortality in the general population of the same region. The workers have 30% lower mortality than the general population, and the company concludes that exposure at the plant is not harmful.
before.question: Which of the following best explains why this conclusion may be invalid?
before.options: {"options": ["Observer (Hawthorne) effect", "Selection bias from the healthy worker effect", "Lead-time bias", "Recall bias", "Type I error"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "healthy worker effect", "keyTakeaway": "Healthy worker effect = selection bias; employed people are healthier than the general population. Fix by comparing with an internal, unexposed worker group.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Selection bias from the healthy worker effect
before.explanation: Selection bias from the healthy worker effect is correct: people who are employed must be healthy enough to work, whereas the general population includes people too ill or disabled to work, so employed cohorts have lower baseline mortality regardless of occupational exposure; this systematic difference in how the comparison groups were selected can mask real harm. The STROBE explanation and elaboration discusses such selection bias and recommends choosing comparison groups that are comparable, such as other workers with different exposures. Recall bias arises when cases remember past exposures differently from controls in retrospective studies. Lead-time bias is a screening artifact. The Hawthorne effect is a change in behavior because subjects know they are being observed. A type I error is a false-positive statistical finding by chance, not a systematic bias. Takeaway: comparing workers with the general population underestimates occupational risk (healthy worker effect).

references.label: Vandenbroucke JP et al. STROBE: explanation and elaboration. PLoS Med 2007

before.scenario: A randomized trial compares a new topical cream with a vehicle cream for chronic hand dermatitis. The primary outcome is a clinician-rated severity score at 8 weeks. The study creams are packaged differently, and the dermatologists who rate severity are also the investigators who dispensed the creams and know each patient's assignment. The new cream shows a large benefit.
before.question: Which of the following design changes would best reduce the most important source of bias in this trial?
before.options: {"options": ["Using intention-to-treat analysis", "Extending follow-up to 6 months", "Stratifying randomization by age", "Blinding the outcome assessors to treatment assignment", "Increasing the sample size"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "blinding of outcome assessors to prevent observer bias", "keyTakeaway": "Observer/detection bias: knowledge of allocation influences outcome assessment, especially subjective outcomes; prevent with blinded assessors and identical-appearing interventions.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Blinding the outcome assessors to treatment assignment
before.explanation: Blinding the outcome assessors is correct: when a subjective outcome such as a clinician-rated severity score is judged by assessors who know the allocation, their expectations can systematically influence ratings (observer, detection, or ascertainment bias), typically exaggerating benefit; CONSORT 2025 asks trials to report who was blinded after assignment and how, and identical-appearing packaging plus independent masked assessors are standard solutions. Increasing sample size improves precision and power but does not remove systematic bias. Intention-to-treat analysis protects against bias from nonadherence and dropouts, not from unblinded assessment. Longer follow-up addresses durability, not measurement bias. Stratified randomization balances known prognostic factors between groups but does not affect how outcomes are judged. Takeaway: subjective outcomes need blinded assessors to prevent observer (detection) bias.

references.label: Hopewell S et al. CONSORT 2025 explanation and elaboration: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ 2025

before.scenario: A 46-year-old man presents for a routine health maintenance visit. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, no personal history of polyps or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer. He has never been screened. Physical examination and complete blood count are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding colorectal cancer screening?
before.options: {"options": ["Screening is not indicated because he is at average risk", "Begin screening now with any recommended test, such as annual fecal immunochemical testing or colonoscopy every 10 years", "Begin screening at age 50", "Begin with a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis", "Begin with serum carcinoembryonic antigen testing"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "colorectal cancer screening start age", "keyTakeaway": "USPSTF 2021 CRC: B for 45-49, A for 50-75, C (individualize) for 76-85. Options: FIT yearly, sDNA-FIT 1-3 y, CT colonography 5 y, sigmoidoscopy 5 y, colonoscopy 10 y.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Begin screening now with any recommended test, such as annual fecal immunochemical testing or colonoscopy every 10 years
before.explanation: Beginning screening now is correct: the USPSTF 2021 recommendation is to screen all adults aged 45 to 75 for colorectal cancer (grade B for ages 45-49 and grade A for 50-75), using options such as annual high-sensitivity FIT, stool DNA-FIT every 1-3 years, CT colonography every 5 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or colonoscopy every 10 years, with abnormal noncolonoscopy tests followed by colonoscopy. Starting at 50 reflects the older 2016 recommendation. Average-risk status is exactly the group for whom population screening is recommended. Abdominal/pelvic CT (as opposed to CT colonography) is not a screening test. CEA is a tumor marker for monitoring known cancer and is neither sensitive nor specific for screening. Takeaway: average-risk colorectal cancer screening starts at age 45 and continues through 75; selective at 76-85.

references.label: USPSTF: Colorectal Cancer: Screening (2021)
US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Colorectal Cancer: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2021

before.scenario: A 74-year-old woman who lives independently reports two falls in the past year without injury. She has mild knee osteoarthritis and takes amlodipine. Her Timed Up and Go test is 15 seconds. Vision, orthostatic vital signs, and cognition are normal. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 32 ng/mL.
before.question: According to the USPSTF, which intervention is most appropriate to prevent future falls?
before.options: {"options": ["Vitamin D supplementation 2,000 IU daily", "A hip protector worn at all times", "Routine bone density testing every year", "Restriction of walking outside the home", "Referral to an exercise program that includes balance, gait, and strength training"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "fall prevention in community-dwelling older adults", "keyTakeaway": "USPSTF 2024 falls (≥65 at increased risk): exercise (balance, gait, strength) B; multifactorial intervention C; vitamin D without deficiency does not prevent falls.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Referral to an exercise program that includes balance, gait, and strength training
before.explanation: Referral to an exercise program is correct: the USPSTF 2024 recommendation (grade B) is exercise interventions for community-dwelling adults aged 65 or older at increased risk for falls, such as those with a history of falls or impaired mobility (her Timed Up and Go above 12 seconds); effective programs include supervised individual or group classes with balance, gait, and strength training. Multifactorial interventions are a grade C recommendation offered selectively. Vitamin D supplementation is incorrect because her level is normal and supplementation has not been shown to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults without deficiency. Hip protectors do not prevent falls. Annual bone density testing does not prevent falls. Restricting activity promotes deconditioning and increases fall risk. Takeaway: older adults at increased fall risk = exercise (balance, gait, strength); not vitamin D.

references.label: USPSTF: Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024)
US Preventive Services Task Force. Interventions to Prevent Falls in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2024

before.scenario: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension is found to have persistent nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; echocardiography shows no mitral stenosis and she has no prosthetic valve. She has no history of stroke, heart failure, diabetes, or vascular disease. Heart rate is controlled on metoprolol. She weighs 70 kg; serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m2. She has no history of bleeding.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to reduce her risk of stroke?
before.options: {"options": ["Aspirin 81 mg daily", "Apixaban 5 mg twice daily", "No antithrombotic therapy", "Aspirin 81 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily", "Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "stroke prevention anticoagulant choice in atrial fibrillation", "keyTakeaway": "AF: anticoagulate if CHA2DS2-VASc >=2 (men) / >=3 (women); DOAC over warfarin; apixaban 2.5 mg BID only if 2 of age >=80, wt <=60 kg, Cr >=1.5.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
before.explanation: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily is correct: her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (female sex, age 65-74, hypertension), and the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline recommends oral anticoagulation when annual stroke risk is 2% or more (score 2 or more in men, 3 or more in women), with a DOAC preferred over warfarin in eligible patients without moderate-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. Aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is used only with at least 2 of: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or more; she meets none, so underdosing raises stroke risk. Aspirin plus clopidogrel is less effective than anticoagulation with similar bleeding. Withholding therapy ignores a 3-point score. Takeaway: AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 2 or more (men) or 3 or more (women) = DOAC at full dose unless dose criteria are met.

references.label: Joglar JA et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation 2024

before.scenario: A 28-year-old woman with asthma has daytime symptoms 4 days per week and wakes at night with cough twice a month despite good adherence and correct inhaler technique. She takes fluticasone propionate 100 mcg twice daily and uses albuterol as needed. She has had no exacerbations requiring oral glucocorticoids in the past year. She does not smoke, and allergic rhinitis is controlled.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Add a 5-day burst of oral prednisone each month", "Add salmeterol and discontinue fluticasone", "Increase fluticasone to high dose and continue albuterol", "Add tiotropium to her current regimen", "Replace her regimen with low-dose budesonide-formoterol daily and as needed for symptoms"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "asthma step-up to ICS-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Uncontrolled on low-dose ICS (age >=12): switch to ICS-formoterol (e.g., budesonide-formoterol) daily + as-needed (SMART/MART).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Replace her regimen with low-dose budesonide-formoterol daily and as needed for symptoms
before.explanation: Low-dose budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy is correct: she is uncontrolled on low-dose ICS plus SABA, and both the 2020 NAEPP focused update (ages 12 and older, steps 3-4) and GINA prefer single ICS-formoterol inhaler therapy taken daily and as needed, which reduces severe exacerbations compared with a higher-dose ICS or ICS-LABA plus SABA reliever. LABA monotherapy (salmeterol without ICS) increases asthma-related death and is contraindicated. Adding a LAMA (tiotropium) is a step 5 option after medium-dose ICS-LABA, not the next step here. Escalating to high-dose ICS increases adverse effects with less benefit than adding formoterol. Repeated oral glucocorticoid bursts are not a controller strategy and cause cumulative toxicity. Takeaway: asthma uncontrolled on low-dose ICS (age 12+) = step up to ICS-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy.

references.label: NAEPP Expert Panel Working Group. 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines. J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020
Global Initiative for Asthma. GINA Strategy Reports

before.scenario: A 42-year-old man with dyspepsia has a positive Helicobacter pylori stool antigen test. He has never been treated for H pylori, has no drug allergies, and takes no medications. Antibiotic susceptibility testing is not available. He received clarithromycin for sinusitis 2 years ago.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["PPI and amoxicillin for 7 days", "PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 14 days", "PPI, levofloxacin, and amoxicillin for 10 days", "Metronidazole alone for 14 days", "PPI, bismuth subcitrate or subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole for 14 days"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "first-line Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy", "keyTakeaway": "H pylori first line (susceptibility unknown): 14-day bismuth quadruple therapy; avoid empiric clarithromycin triple; test of cure (ACG 2024).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: PPI, bismuth subcitrate or subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole for 14 days
before.explanation: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days is correct: the 2024 ACG H pylori guideline recommends optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI twice daily, bismuth, tetracycline 500 mg four times daily, and metronidazole 500 mg three to four times daily) as preferred empiric first-line therapy when susceptibility is unknown; rifabutin triple therapy or vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy are acceptable alternatives in patients without penicillin allergy. Clarithromycin triple therapy is no longer recommended empirically because clarithromycin resistance is common in the US, and his prior macrolide exposure raises that risk further. Levofloxacin triple therapy is not recommended first line because of fluoroquinolone resistance and toxicity. Seven-day PPI-amoxicillin is not a recommended regimen and is too short. Metronidazole monotherapy promotes resistance and fails. Takeaway: treatment-naive H pylori with unknown susceptibility = 14-day bismuth quadruple therapy; confirm eradication.

references.label: Chey WD et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection. Am J Gastroenterol 2024

before.scenario: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis due to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis is brought in by her husband for 2 days of confusion and day-night reversal. She has been constipated for 4 days. She is disoriented to date but follows commands. Asterixis is present. There is no fever, abdominal tenderness, or GI bleeding; diagnostic paracentesis is negative for infection, and electrolytes, glucose, and urinalysis are normal. Noncontrast CT of the head is normal. This is her first episode.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Lactulose 25 mL every 1 to 2 hours until 2 soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily", "Lorazepam 1 mg IV for agitation", "Neomycin 1 g orally every 6 hours", "Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily as monotherapy", "Withhold therapy until a serum ammonia level returns elevated"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "overt hepatic encephalopathy first-line therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Overt HE: correct precipitant + lactulose (25 mL q1-2h until 2 BMs, then 2-3 soft stools/day); add rifaximin 550 mg BID for recurrence.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Lactulose 25 mL every 1 to 2 hours until 2 soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily
before.explanation: Lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily is correct: the 2014 AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy guideline recommends identifying and correcting precipitants (here, constipation) and treating overt HE with lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least 2 soft bowel movements, then titrating to 2-3 per day; lactulose is also first-line secondary prophylaxis. Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily is added to lactulose to prevent recurrence after a second episode, not used alone first. Neomycin is an alternative with ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Benzodiazepines worsen encephalopathy. Ammonia levels do not add diagnostic, staging, or prognostic value in cirrhosis, and a normal value should prompt reevaluation rather than delay; treatment is clinical. Takeaway: overt HE = treat precipitants plus lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools; add rifaximin after recurrence.

references.label: Vilstrup H et al. Hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease: 2014 Practice Guideline by the AASLD and EASL. Hepatology 2014

before.scenario: A 24-year-old man has 8 months of low back and buttock pain that began gradually. The pain and stiffness are worst in the early morning and after prolonged sitting, wake him in the second half of the night, and improve with exercise but not rest. He had an episode of painful red left eye with photophobia last year. Examination shows tenderness over both sacroiliac joints and reduced lumbar flexion on the modified Schober test. Pelvic radiograph shows bilateral grade 3 sacroiliitis with erosions and sclerosis. HLA-B27 is positive. CRP is mildly elevated.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Mechanical low back strain", "Lumbar disc herniation", "Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis)", "Spinal stenosis", "Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "ankylosing spondylitis", "keyTakeaway": "AS: inflammatory back pain <40 y, better with exercise; sacroiliitis on imaging, HLA-B27, uveitis; NSAIDs first-line, then TNF inhibitor.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis)
before.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is correct: inflammatory back pain (onset before age 40, insidious, nocturnal, better with exercise and not rest) lasting over 3 months, prior acute anterior uveitis, HLA-B27, and bilateral radiographic sacroiliitis meet the modified New York criteria; the 2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN guideline recommends NSAIDs as first-line therapy, with TNF inhibitors for persistent activity, plus physical therapy. Disc herniation causes acute radicular pain with dermatomal signs and no sacroiliitis. Mechanical strain worsens with activity and improves with rest. DISH affects older adults, with flowing anterior osteophytes and preserved sacroiliac joints. Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication in older adults, relieved by flexion. Takeaway: young man + inflammatory back pain + uveitis + sacroiliitis + HLA-B27 = ankylosing spondylitis; NSAIDs first.

references.label: Ward MM et al. 2019 Update of the ACR/SAA/SPARTAN Recommendations for the Treatment of Ankylosing Spondylitis and Nonradiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis. Arthritis Rheumatol 2019

before.scenario: A 24-year-old competitive swimmer has 3 days of right ear pain, itching, and a sense of fullness. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F). Pulling the pinna and pressing on the tragus cause marked pain. The external auditory canal is erythematous and edematous with scant white debris; after gentle cleaning, the tympanic membrane is visualized and is intact and normal. There is no periauricular cellulitis or lymphadenopathy. She does not have diabetes or immunocompromise.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days", "Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days", "Oral prednisone for 5 days", "Oral fluconazole as a single dose", "Ofloxacin 0.3% otic solution, 10 drops in the affected ear once daily for 7 days"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "topical therapy for acute otitis externa", "keyTakeaway": "Uncomplicated AOE: topical drops (e.g., ofloxacin 0.3% 10 drops daily x7 days) + analgesia; no systemic antibiotics unless spread or high-risk host.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ofloxacin 0.3% otic solution, 10 drops in the affected ear once daily for 7 days
before.explanation: Ofloxacin 0.3% otic solution, 10 drops once daily for 7 days, is correct: tragal and pinna tenderness with canal edema after swimming indicates diffuse acute otitis externa, and the 2014 AAO-HNS guideline recommends topical preparations as initial therapy, with analgesia and aural toilet; with an intact tympanic membrane any approved topical agent works, and a non-ototoxic fluoroquinolone is preferred if the membrane is not intact or tympanostomy tubes are present. The guideline recommends against systemic antimicrobials for uncomplicated AOE unless infection extends outside the canal or the host is immunocompromised or diabetic; oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and ciprofloxacin therefore add adverse effects without benefit. Oral fluconazole is not first-line, because otomycosis is treated topically and is less likely. Oral prednisone does not treat infection. Takeaway: uncomplicated otitis externa = topical antibiotic drops, not oral antibiotics.

references.label: Rosenfeld RM et al. Clinical practice guideline: acute otitis externa. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014

before.scenario: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, has 2 days of left lower abdominal pain and light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She had chlamydial infection 4 years ago. Pulse is 88/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. There is mild left adnexal tenderness without peritoneal signs; the cervical os is closed. Quantitative serum hCG is 3,900 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an empty uterus with a thin endometrium and a 2.5-cm complex left adnexal mass separate from the ovary, with a small amount of free fluid in the pelvis.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Tubal ectopic pregnancy", "Ruptured hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst with intrauterine pregnancy too early to see", "Completed spontaneous abortion", "Complete hydatidiform mole", "Threatened abortion"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "tubal ectopic pregnancy", "keyTakeaway": "Ectopic: positive hCG, no IUP on TVUS above discriminatory zone (up to 3,500), adnexal mass separate from ovary; stable -> MTX or surgery.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Tubal ectopic pregnancy
before.explanation: Tubal ectopic pregnancy is correct: ACOG Practice Bulletin 193 notes that an hCG above the discriminatory zone (as high as 3,500 mIU/mL) without an intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound, especially with an extraovarian adnexal mass, is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; prior chlamydia (tubal damage) is a risk factor. Because she is stable, methotrexate or laparoscopy are options depending on hCG level, mass size, and follow-up reliability. Threatened abortion requires a visible intrauterine pregnancy with a closed os. A completed abortion would show falling hCG and a history of passed tissue, not an adnexal mass. An hCG of 3,900 is above the level at which a normal intrauterine gestational sac is usually seen, and the mass is separate from the ovary. Complete mole shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with very high hCG. Takeaway: hCG above the discriminatory zone + empty uterus + adnexal mass = ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol 2018

before.scenario: A randomized trial reports that a new antihypertensive lowered systolic blood pressure by 4 mm Hg more than the comparator, with p = 0.03. The prespecified significance level was 0.05.
before.question: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the p-value?
before.options: {"options": ["There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true", "If there were truly no difference, a difference this large or larger would be observed about 3% of the time by chance", "The difference is clinically important", "The probability of a type II error is 3%", "There is a 97% probability that the new drug is more effective"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "interpreting a p-value", "keyTakeaway": "p-value = probability of data at least this extreme if H0 true; not P(H0 true); significance is not clinical importance.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: If there were truly no difference, a difference this large or larger would be observed about 3% of the time by chance
before.explanation: The first statement is correct: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 15 explains that a p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true; p = 0.03 is below the alpha of 0.05, so the result is statistically significant. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor is 1 - p the probability that the treatment works. Statistical significance does not establish clinical importance; a 4-mm Hg difference must be judged by its effect size and confidence interval. Type II error (beta) is the probability of missing a true effect and is determined by power, not by the observed p-value. Takeaway: a p-value measures how compatible the data are with the null hypothesis, not the probability that a hypothesis is true or that a result matters.

references.label: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (current version), Chapter 15: Interpreting results and drawing conclusions

before.scenario: A noninferiority trial compares a new 5-day antibiotic course with a standard 10-day course for pneumonia. The prespecified noninferiority margin is a 10-percentage-point higher clinical failure rate. Failure occurred in 9.0% with the new course and 7.5% with the standard course, a difference of 1.5 percentage points (95% CI, -1.8 to 4.8).
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
before.options: {"options": ["The new course has a 4.8% higher failure rate than the standard course", "The new course is noninferior to the standard course", "The new course is superior to the standard course", "The trial is inconclusive because the confidence interval crosses zero", "The new course is inferior to the standard course"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "interpreting a noninferiority trial", "keyTakeaway": "Noninferiority: whole CI for difference within prespecified margin (upper bound < margin); superiority requires CI entirely beyond zero.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: The new course is noninferior to the standard course
before.explanation: The new course is noninferior: the CONSORT extension for noninferiority trials (Piaggio G et al., JAMA 2012) explains that noninferiority is shown when the confidence interval for the difference lies entirely on the favorable side of the prespecified margin; the upper bound of 4.8 points is below the 10-point margin. Superiority would require the entire interval to favor the new course (below zero). Inferiority would require the interval to lie entirely beyond the margin. A CI crossing zero means superiority is not shown, but in a noninferiority design that does not make the trial inconclusive. The upper bound of 4.8 is the largest difference compatible with the data, not the estimated difference, which is 1.5 points. Takeaway: noninferiority = the entire CI for harm stays within the margin; crossing zero is acceptable.

references.label: Piaggio G et al. Reporting of noninferiority and equivalence randomized trials: extension of the CONSORT 2010 statement. JAMA 2012

before.scenario: A PA in a primary care practice has a patient with hypertension and diabetes who has repeatedly shouted obscenities at front-desk staff, threatened to post false reviews, and refused to follow agreed treatment plans despite several documented discussions. The practice decides to end the professional relationship. The patient is not in an acute crisis.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to end the relationship?
before.options: {"options": ["Instruct staff to cancel his future appointments without telling him", "Discharge him today and decline to refill any medications", "Notify the patient in writing, provide care for emergencies during a reasonable transition period, and help transfer care and records", "Tell him at his next visit that he must find another clinician immediately", "Release his records to a new clinician only after his outstanding balance is paid"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "terminating a patient-clinician relationship", "keyTakeaway": "Terminating care: advance written notice, interim emergency care/refills, help transferring records and care; abrupt withdrawal = abandonment.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Notify the patient in writing, provide care for emergencies during a reasonable transition period, and help transfer care and records
before.explanation: Written notice, interim emergency care, and help transferring care is correct: AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 1.1.5 states that clinicians may withdraw from a case but must notify the patient long enough in advance to permit the patient to secure another clinician and must facilitate transfer of care when appropriate; a reasonable transition (often about 30 days, per state rules) with continued emergency care and prescriptions prevents abandonment. Silently canceling appointments gives no notice and is abandonment. Stopping medications immediately endangers a patient with chronic disease. Withholding records pending payment obstructs continuity of care and violates HIPAA access rights. Demanding an immediate change without a transition period also risks abandonment. Takeaway: end a relationship with advance written notice, interim care, and a facilitated transfer, never abruptly.

references.label: AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 1.1.5: Terminating a Patient-Physician Relationship

before.scenario: A PA in an internal medicine clinic is reviewing how the practice handles protected health information for a patient with newly diagnosed heart failure. Several disclosures and uses of the patient's records are planned this week.
before.question: To which of the following is the HIPAA minimum necessary standard NOT applicable?
before.options: {"options": ["Allowing scheduling staff to view the record", "Sharing records with the clinic's internal quality-improvement committee", "Providing records to a contracted billing company", "Sending the complete record to the consulting cardiologist who will treat the patient", "Submitting a claim to the patient's insurer for payment"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "HIPAA minimum necessary standard exceptions", "keyTakeaway": "HIPAA minimum necessary does not apply to treatment disclosures between providers, to the patient, under authorization, or as required by law.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Sending the complete record to the consulting cardiologist who will treat the patient
before.explanation: Sending records to the treating cardiologist is correct: under the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR 164.502), covered entities must make reasonable efforts to limit uses and disclosures of protected health information to the minimum necessary, but the standard does not apply to disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment, disclosures to the individual, disclosures made under the individual's authorization, or disclosures required by law. Claims for payment, workforce access such as scheduling staff, disclosures to business associates such as a billing company, and health care operations such as quality improvement are all subject to the minimum necessary standard, so only the information needed for each task should be shared. Takeaway: minimum necessary applies to payment, operations, and workforce access, but not to provider-to-provider disclosures for treatment.

references.label: eCFR 45 CFR 164.502: Uses and disclosures of protected health information: General rules
HHS. Minimum Necessary Requirement (HIPAA guidance)

before.scenario: On a hospital ward, a nurse administers hydromorphone instead of morphine to a patient, who requires naloxone and recovers fully. Review shows that both drugs are stocked in adjacent bins in the automated dispensing cabinet with similar packaging, that the nurse was covering 7 patients during a staffing shortage, and that a similar near miss occurred last month on another unit.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate institutional response?
before.options: {"options": ["Terminate the nurse to deter future errors", "Post a memo reminding staff to be more careful", "Require the nurse alone to complete remedial training", "Analyze contributing system factors and redesign storage and safeguards for these look-alike high-alert opioids", "Take no action because the patient recovered"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "systems approach to a medication error", "keyTakeaway": "Systems approach/just culture: errors stem from latent system flaws; fix design (forcing functions, separation, barcode) rather than blame.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Analyze contributing system factors and redesign storage and safeguards for these look-alike high-alert opioids
before.explanation: Analyzing contributing system factors and redesigning safeguards is correct: the AHRQ PSNet primer on the systems approach explains that most errors arise from latent conditions in system design (the Swiss cheese model) rather than individual failings, so the response should identify root causes, such as look-alike adjacent storage and staffing, and implement stronger system fixes (separating high-alert drugs, barcode scanning, tall-man lettering) within a just culture. Firing the nurse ignores latent hazards and discourages reporting. Remediating only the individual leaves the hazard for every other nurse, as last month's near miss shows. A harmful error that required naloxone warrants analysis even with recovery. Memos urging vigilance are weak interventions that rarely change outcomes. Takeaway: respond to errors with systems analysis and strong design fixes in a just culture, not blame.

references.label: AHRQ PSNet. Systems Approach (Patient Safety Primer)

before.scenario: A 76-year-old woman is admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. She brings a bag of pill bottles from 3 prescribers and 2 pharmacies. The admission orders were copied from her discharge summary from 8 months ago. Her daughter mentions that the cardiologist recently stopped one blood pressure medication and started apixaban.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate step to prevent a medication error?
before.options: {"options": ["Obtain a complete, current medication list from the patient, family, bottles, and pharmacies, and compare it with the admission orders to resolve discrepancies", "Continue the medications listed on the 8-month-old discharge summary", "Hold all home medications until discharge", "Ask the patient's cardiologist to manage all medications during the admission", "Rely on the pharmacy dispensing record alone"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "medication reconciliation at hospital admission", "keyTakeaway": "Medication reconciliation: best possible medication history from multiple sources, compared with orders at admission, transfer, and discharge.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Obtain a complete, current medication list from the patient, family, bottles, and pharmacies, and compare it with the admission orders to resolve discrepancies
before.explanation: Building a complete current list from multiple sources and comparing it with admission orders is correct: the AHRQ PSNet primer on medication reconciliation describes the process as creating the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking (best possible medication history from the patient, family, bottles, pharmacy, and prescribers) and comparing it against admission, transfer, and discharge orders to identify and resolve omissions, duplications, and dosing errors. Using an outdated discharge summary would omit apixaban and continue a stopped antihypertensive. Holding all home medications indiscriminately risks harm, such as stroke from interrupted anticoagulation. Delegating all medications to one specialist fragments responsibility. Pharmacy records alone miss over-the-counter drugs, samples, other pharmacies, and discontinued therapies. Takeaway: reconcile medications at every transition using a best possible medication history from multiple sources.

references.label: AHRQ PSNet. Medication Reconciliation (Patient Safety Primer)

before.scenario: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history has 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea and 2-pillow orthopnea. She has bibasilar crackles and trace ankle edema; there is no wheezing. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with possible mild vascular congestion. It is unclear whether her symptoms are from heart failure or her known COPD.
before.question: Which of the following laboratory tests is most useful to support or exclude heart failure as the cause of her dyspnea?
before.options: {"options": ["High-sensitivity troponin T", "Serum procalcitonin", "N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)", "Arterial blood gas", "D-dimer"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "natriuretic peptide testing in dyspnea of uncertain cause", "keyTakeaway": "BNP/NT-proBNP is Class 1 to support or exclude HF in dyspnea; falsely low in obesity, high with age, CKD, AF.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)
before.explanation: NT-proBNP is correct: the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline gives a Class 1 recommendation for measuring BNP or NT-proBNP in patients presenting with dyspnea to support a diagnosis of heart failure or to exclude it; very low levels make HF unlikely, while elevated levels prompt echocardiography. Levels can be falsely low in obesity and elevated by age, kidney disease, AF, and PE, so results are interpreted in context. D-dimer helps exclude venous thromboembolism in low-probability patients but does not assess HF.
