Troponin identifies myocardial injury and helps risk stratify but does not establish HF as the cause of dyspnea. Procalcitonin assesses bacterial infection. ABG shows gas exchange but cannot distinguish HF from COPD. Takeaway: dyspnea with HF vs lung disease uncertain = natriuretic peptide; low value argues strongly against HF.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

before.scenario: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped apixaban 1 month ago because of cost has 3 hours of sudden severe pain in the left leg. The left foot and calf are pale and cold, with no palpable femoral, popliteal, or pedal pulses. He has decreased light-touch sensation on the dorsum of the foot and mild weakness of toe dorsiflexion. Arterial Doppler signals are absent at the ankle; venous Doppler signals are audible. The right leg is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Begin aspirin and cilostazol and arrange a supervised exercise program", "Intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion with emergent vascular surgery consultation for revascularization", "Obtain a resting ankle-brachial index before any treatment", "Resume apixaban and obtain an outpatient arterial duplex study", "Observe with the leg elevated and reassess pulses in 12 hours"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism", "keyTakeaway": "Acute limb ischemia: 6 Ps, absent arterial Doppler; immediate IV heparin + emergent revascularization (motor/sensory loss = threatened limb).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion with emergent vascular surgery consultation for revascularization
before.explanation: IV heparin with emergent vascular consultation is correct: sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, and early motor weakness with an absent arterial but present venous Doppler signal indicate acute limb ischemia (Rutherford class IIb, immediately threatened) from cardioembolism. The 2024 ACC/AHA multisociety PAD guideline recommends systemic anticoagulation with heparin unless contraindicated and emergent revascularization by thrombectomy, embolectomy, or catheter-directed therapy, because muscle and nerve become irreversibly damaged within about 4-6 hours. Resuming apixaban with outpatient imaging ignores a limb-threatening emergency. Aspirin, cilostazol, and exercise treat chronic claudication. ABI is a chronic PAD test and delays care. Elevating the leg lowers perfusion pressure and worsens ischemia. Takeaway: the 6 Ps with motor or sensory loss = anticoagulate with heparin and revascularize emergently.

references.label: Gornik HL et al. 2024 ACC/AHA multisociety Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease. Circulation 2024

before.scenario: A 34-year-old man who moved from Haiti 1 year ago has 2 months of productive cough, night sweats, and a 6-kg weight loss. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe cavitary lesion. Sputum smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli, and nucleic acid amplification testing detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex without rifampin-resistance mutations. HIV testing is negative, and liver enzymes are normal. He weighs 70 kg.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Isoniazid and rifampin for 6 months without pyrazinamide or ethambutol", "Bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid for 6 months", "Rifampin alone for 4 months", "Isoniazid alone for 9 months", "Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "initial regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis", "keyTakeaway": "Active drug-susceptible TB: RIPE 2 months then INH/RIF 4 months (DOT, pyridoxine); monotherapy regimens are for latent TB only.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months
before.explanation: The 4-drug intensive phase followed by isoniazid and rifampin is correct: the ATS/CDC/IDSA drug-susceptible TB guideline recommends 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (stopping ethambutol once susceptibility is confirmed) then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin, with directly observed therapy and pyridoxine to prevent isoniazid neuropathy; the 2025 ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA update adds a 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen as an option for eligible patients. Isoniazid alone for 9 months and rifampin alone for 4 months are latent TB regimens and would select for resistance in active disease. Two drugs without pyrazinamide require 9 months and ethambutol guards against unrecognized isoniazid resistance. BPaL-based regimens are for drug-resistant TB. Takeaway: active drug-susceptible pulmonary TB = RIPE x 2 months, then INH + RIF x 4 months.

references.label: Nahid P et al. Official ATS/CDC/IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis. Clin Infect Dis 2016 (ERS-endorsed version)
Saukkonen JJ et al. Updates on the Treatment of Drug-Susceptible and Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis: An Official ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2025

before.scenario: A 42-year-old man who smoked half a pack per day for 10 years, quitting 8 years ago, has progressive exertional dyspnea. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.56 and FEV1 is 52% of predicted. Chest CT shows panlobular emphysema most pronounced in the lower lobes. ALT is mildly elevated at 62 U/L. His father died of cirrhosis at age 58 and did not drink alcohol.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to establish the underlying cause?
before.options: {"options": ["Sweat chloride test", "Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with phenotyping or genotyping", "Hepatitis C antibody only", "Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level", "Exhaled nitric oxide measurement"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency testing in early-onset emphysema", "keyTakeaway": "Early-onset, lower-lobe panlobular emphysema + liver disease = alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; GOLD: screen every COPD patient once.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with phenotyping or genotyping
before.explanation: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with phenotyping or genotyping is correct: early-onset COPD with modest smoking, basilar panlobular emphysema, unexplained liver disease, and a family history of cirrhosis suggest AATD, most often the PiZZ genotype; the 2026 GOLD report endorses the WHO recommendation that every patient with COPD be screened once for AATD, especially in areas of high prevalence, and confirmed severe deficiency can justify augmentation therapy and family testing. Sweat chloride tests for CF, which causes bronchiectasis and upper-lobe disease rather than basilar emphysema. ACE level is nonspecific for sarcoidosis, which is restrictive and not emphysematous. Hepatitis C serology may explain abnormal ALT but not basilar emphysema. Exhaled nitric oxide measures type 2 airway inflammation in asthma. Takeaway: COPD before 45, basilar emphysema, or liver disease = test AAT level and genotype.

references.label: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD). 2026 GOLD Report

before.scenario: A 79-year-old woman has 1 day of a painful, warm, swollen right knee. She was hospitalized 3 days ago for pneumonia. Temperature is 37.8 C (100.0 F). Arthrocentesis yields cloudy fluid with 28,000 WBC/mm3 (85% neutrophils); Gram stain is negative. Compensated polarized light microscopy shows rhomboid-shaped intracellular crystals that are weakly positively birefringent. Knee radiographs show linear calcification of the menisci and articular cartilage.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Septic arthritis", "Lyme arthritis", "Acute gout", "Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis", "Osteoarthritis flare"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis", "keyTakeaway": "CPPD: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals + chondrocalcinosis; gout = needle-shaped, negatively birefringent; always culture.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis
before.explanation: Acute CPP crystal arthritis is correct: an acute inflammatory monoarthritis of the knee in an older adult, often triggered by illness or surgery, with rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid and chondrocalcinosis on imaging meets the 2023 ACR/EULAR CPPD classification criteria, in which crystal identification and imaging evidence of CPPD carry heavy weight. Gout shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals. Septic arthritis must be excluded with culture, and crystals can coexist with infection, but a negative Gram stain and characteristic crystals support CPP arthritis here pending culture. An osteoarthritis flare produces noninflammatory fluid with under 2,000 WBC/mm3. Lyme arthritis affects younger patients in endemic areas with a large effusion and positive serology. Takeaway: older adult + acute knee arthritis + rhomboid weakly positive crystals + chondrocalcinosis = acute CPP arthritis.

references.label: Abhishek A et al. The 2023 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease. Arthritis Rheumatol 2023

before.scenario: A 24-year-old man rolled his right ankle inward while playing basketball 3 hours ago. He walked off the court and in the emergency department takes 4 steps unaided, though with a limp. There is swelling and ecchymosis anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus with tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament. There is no tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, at the base of the fifth metatarsal, or over the navicular. The anterior drawer test is mildly positive.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Three-view ankle radiographs", "CT of the ankle", "Foot radiographs", "Manage as a lateral ankle sprain without radiographs", "MRI of the ankle"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "Ottawa ankle rules in a lateral ankle sprain", "keyTakeaway": "Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray only with posterior-edge/tip malleolar tenderness, 5th MT base or navicular tenderness, or inability to take 4 steps.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Manage as a lateral ankle sprain without radiographs
before.explanation: Managing as a lateral ankle sprain without radiographs is correct: under the Ottawa ankle rules, which the ACR Appropriateness Criteria for acute ankle trauma endorse for deciding on imaging, ankle radiographs are indicated only for malleolar-zone pain plus bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately and in the ED; foot radiographs are indicated for midfoot pain with tenderness at the fifth metatarsal base or navicular or inability to bear weight. He has none, so fracture is very unlikely (sensitivity near 100%). Treatment is functional support, early weight bearing, and exercise. MRI and CT are reserved for persistent symptoms, suspected occult osteochondral or syndesmotic injury, or surgical planning. Takeaway: no posterior malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness and can walk 4 steps = no X-ray; it is a sprain.

references.label: Expert Panel on Musculoskeletal Imaging. ACR Appropriateness Criteria Acute Trauma to the Ankle. J Am Coll Radiol 2020

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has had bleeding from the right nostril for 20 minutes that began after he blew his nose. He is anxious and has been tilting his head back and swallowing blood. Blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg and pulse 92/min. He takes no anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. Bleeding is seen from the anterior septum; there is no bleeding into the posterior pharynx after he spits out the blood.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
before.options: {"options": ["Posterior nasal packing with a balloon device", "Firm sustained compression of the lower third of the nose for at least 5 minutes with the head tilted slightly forward", "Continue tilting the head back and apply ice to the forehead", "IV labetalol to lower blood pressure before treating the bleeding", "Emergent referral for sphenopalatine artery embolization"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "initial management of anterior epistaxis", "keyTakeaway": "Epistaxis: firm compression of lower third of nose >=5 min, leaning forward (+/- topical vasoconstrictor); then cautery or packing.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Firm sustained compression of the lower third of the nose for at least 5 minutes with the head tilted slightly forward
before.explanation: Firm sustained compression of the lower third of the nose for 5 minutes or more is correct: the 2020 AAO-HNSF nosebleed guideline recommends firm sustained compression, with or without a topical vasoconstrictor, for active bleeding requiring prompt management; most bleeding arises from the anterior septum (Kiesselbach plexus). If bleeding persists, nasal packing or cautery of an identified site follows. Leaning forward prevents swallowing blood, which causes nausea and obscures the volume of loss. Posterior packing is reserved for posterior bleeding that persists after anterior measures. Embolization or surgical arterial ligation is for persistent or recurrent bleeding not controlled by packing or cautery. Elevated blood pressure is common from anxiety; the guideline does not advise routine acute BP lowering before local control. Tilting the head back lets blood drain into the pharynx. Takeaway: anterior epistaxis = lean forward and pinch the soft nose for 5 minutes or more.

references.label: Tunkel DE et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2020

before.scenario: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks' gestation is seen for a routine prenatal visit. Her blood type is O, Rh(D)-negative, and her antibody screen repeated today is negative. Her first child was Rh(D)-positive, and she received Rh D immune globulin after that delivery. The paternity and Rh status of the father of this pregnancy are uncertain. She has had no bleeding, trauma, or invasive procedures in this pregnancy.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Withhold Rh D immune globulin until delivery and give it only if the newborn is Rh(D)-positive", "Perform a Kleihauer-Betke test now to determine whether Rh D immune globulin is needed", "Repeat the antibody screen monthly and give Rh D immune globulin only if it becomes positive", "Give Rh D immune globulin only if she has vaginal bleeding later in pregnancy", "Administer 300 mcg of Rh D immune globulin now"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "routine antenatal Rh D immune globulin at 28 weeks", "keyTakeaway": "Unsensitized Rh(D)-negative: RhIG 300 mcg at 28 wk and within 72 h of delivery of Rh+ infant, plus after sensitizing events; not useful once alloimmunized.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Administer 300 mcg of Rh D immune globulin now
before.explanation: Administering 300 mcg of Rh D immune globulin now is correct: ACOG Practice Bulletin 181 recommends routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks for unsensitized Rh D-negative patients (unless the father is reliably known to be Rh-negative), followed by another dose within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh D-positive infant, and after events such as bleeding, trauma, or invasive procedures; the 2024 ACOG update allows forgoing it for abortion or loss before 12 weeks. Waiting until delivery misses the roughly 1-2% of patients who become sensitized during the third trimester. Kleihauer-Betke testing quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage after a sensitizing event to dose additional immune globulin, and it is not a screening test. Once the antibody screen is positive, she is already alloimmunized and immune globulin no longer helps. Takeaway: Rh-negative and antibody-negative = Rh D immune globulin at 28 weeks and again after delivery of an Rh-positive infant.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 181: Prevention of Rh D Alloimmunization. Obstet Gynecol 2017
ACOG Clinical Practice Update: Rh D Immune Globulin Administration After Abortion or Pregnancy Loss at Less Than 12 Weeks of Gestation. Obstet Gynecol 2024

before.scenario: A 31-year-old lean man (BMI 21 kg/m2) has 4 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and an 8-kg unintentional weight loss. His sister has autoimmune thyroiditis. Plasma glucose is 342 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 11.2%. Serum bicarbonate is 23 mEq/L, anion gap is 11, and urine ketones are trace. He is not acutely ill. He is started on insulin.
before.question: Which of the following tests is most appropriate to determine the type of diabetes?
before.options: {"options": ["HLA genotyping", "Oral glucose tolerance test", "Serum fructosamine", "Islet autoantibodies, starting with GAD65 antibody", "Fasting insulin level"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "islet autoantibodies to classify new-onset diabetes in an adult", "keyTakeaway": "ADA 2026: suspect T1D in adults (lean, weight loss, autoimmunity) -> islet autoantibodies, GAD65 first; C-peptide if antibody negative.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Islet autoantibodies, starting with GAD65 antibody
before.explanation: Islet autoantibodies, starting with GAD65, are correct: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes) recommend islet autoantibody testing in adults with features suggesting type 1 diabetes, such as younger age, low BMI, weight loss, rapid progression, or personal or family history of autoimmunity, testing GAD65 first and adding IA-2, ZnT8, or insulin antibodies when needed; positive antibodies confirm autoimmune type 1 diabetes, and C-peptide can help when antibodies are negative. HLA genotyping indicates risk but cannot diagnose type 1 diabetes in an individual. Fasting insulin is unreliable once insulin therapy begins and is not a classification test. An OGTT is unnecessary when the diagnosis of diabetes is already established by glucose and A1c. Fructosamine reflects short-term glycemia, not autoimmunity. Takeaway: adult with new diabetes and type 1 features = check islet autoantibodies (GAD65 first) before labeling it type 2.

references.label: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026

before.scenario: A 42-year-old woman has 9 months of suprapubic pressure and pain that worsens as her bladder fills and improves after voiding, with urinary frequency every hour and nocturia 3 times nightly. Coffee and citrus foods worsen it. Four urine cultures during symptomatic periods were negative, and empiric antibiotics did not help. She has no hematuria, fever, or vaginal discharge. Pelvic examination shows tenderness of the anterior vaginal wall and bladder base without masses. Urinalysis, urine cytology, and postvoid residual (30 mL) are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome", "Recurrent bacterial cystitis", "Urethral diverticulum", "Overactive bladder", "Urothelial carcinoma in situ"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome", "keyTakeaway": "IC/BPS (AUA 2022): bladder-related pain/pressure + LUTS >6 weeks, negative cultures; worse with filling, better after voiding; dietary triggers.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome
before.explanation: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome is correct: the 2022 AUA IC/BPS guideline defines it as an unpleasant sensation (pain, pressure, discomfort) perceived to be related to the bladder, with lower urinary tract symptoms for more than 6 weeks without infection or other identifiable cause; diagnosis rests on history, examination, urinalysis, and culture, with cystoscopy for complicated cases. Recurrent bacterial cystitis requires positive cultures and responds to antibiotics. Overactive bladder causes urgency and frequency without pain that is relieved by voiding. Carcinoma in situ can mimic IC/BPS, but cytology is normal and she lacks hematuria and smoking-related risk; cytology and cystoscopy are indicated if hematuria appears. A urethral diverticulum causes a tender anterior vaginal wall mass with postvoid dribbling and discharge. Takeaway: bladder pain that worsens with filling and eases with voiding, lasting over 6 weeks with negative cultures = IC/BPS.

references.label: Clemens JQ et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome. J Urol 2022

before.scenario: A 61-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with PCI 9 months ago. He also has type 2 diabetes and symptomatic peripheral artery disease. He takes atorvastatin 80 mg daily with good adherence and no muscle symptoms, as well as aspirin, metformin, and lisinopril. Fasting lipid panel: LDL cholesterol 86 mg/dL, HDL 42 mg/dL, triglycerides 140 mg/dL, non-HDL cholesterol 114 mg/dL. ALT is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid management?
before.options: {"options": ["Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily", "Reduce atorvastatin to 40 mg daily and add niacin", "Continue the current regimen because LDL cholesterol is below 100 mg/dL", "Add fenofibrate 145 mg daily", "Add over-the-counter fish oil capsules"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "adding ezetimibe to reach the LDL-C goal after myocardial infarction", "keyTakeaway": "2026 ACC/AHA: very-high-risk ASCVD goals LDL-C <55 and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL; if above goal on max statin, add ezetimibe (then PCSK9 pathway).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily
before.explanation: Adding ezetimibe is correct: the 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety dyslipidemia guideline reintroduces LDL-C goals and, for very-high-risk clinical ASCVD (recent MI plus diabetes and PAD), recommends LDL-C below 55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C below 85 mg/dL; on maximally tolerated high-intensity statin, the guideline adds ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody, chosen by the LDL-C reduction needed and patient preference; ezetimibe (oral, inexpensive, lowers LDL-C about 20-25%) is the only such option listed. Continuing therapy accepts an outdated threshold and leaves him above goal. Fenofibrate has no ASCVD benefit on top of statin and triglycerides are normal. OTC fish oil has not reduced events. Lowering statin intensity and adding niacin reduces LDL-lowering and niacin adds harm without benefit. Takeaway: very-high-risk ASCVD on max statin with LDL-C >=55 mg/dL = add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 antibody.

references.label: Blumenthal RS et al. 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia. Circulation 2026
Siddiqi AK et al. Top 10 Concepts in Secondary ASCVD Prevention From the 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline. Curr Atheroscler Rep 2026

before.scenario: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 2 AM with a barking cough and noisy breathing that began tonight after 2 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever. Temperature is 38.1 C (100.6 F), respiratory rate 36/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. He is playful and drinking from a cup. He has a hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor when crying that is absent at rest, with mild suprasternal retractions. He is not drooling. Immunizations are up to date.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Bacterial tracheitis", "Retropharyngeal abscess", "Aspirated foreign body", "Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)", "Acute epiglottitis"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "viral croup in a toddler", "keyTakeaway": "Croup: barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor after URI in 6 mo-3 y; dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once (max 16 mg); racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)
before.explanation: Croup is correct: an acute barking (seal-like) cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor after a viral prodrome in a well-appearing child aged 6 months to 3 years is classic. A single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg in most studies; lower doses such as 0.15 mg/kg appear similarly effective) reduces symptoms and return visits, as summarized in the 2023 Cochrane review; nebulized epinephrine is added for stridor at rest. Epiglottitis causes high fever, toxicity, drooling, and tripod posture without a barking cough, and is rare after Hib immunization. Bacterial tracheitis follows croup with high fever, toxicity, and failure to respond to epinephrine. Retropharyngeal abscess causes fever, neck stiffness, dysphagia, and drooling. Foreign body causes sudden choking without a viral prodrome or fever. Takeaway: barky cough + stridor after URI in a toddler = croup; single-dose dexamethasone.

references.label: Gates A et al. Glucocorticoids for croup in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023

before.scenario: An 81-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped apixaban 2 weeks ago because of bruising has 4 hours of sudden, severe, diffuse periumbilical pain and 1 episode of forceful bowel evacuation. She is writhing in pain, but the abdomen is soft and only mildly tender without guarding or rebound. Pulse is 112/min and irregularly irregular; blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. WBC count is 18,000/mm3 and serum lactate is 3.8 mmol/L.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Ischemic colitis", "Small bowel obstruction from adhesions", "Acute mesenteric ischemia from superior mesenteric artery embolism", "Diverticulitis", "Acute pancreatitis"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "acute mesenteric arterial embolism in an older adult", "keyTakeaway": "Acute mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion to exam + embolic source (AF); immediate CTA, IV heparin, urgent revascularization; lactate is late.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Acute mesenteric ischemia from superior mesenteric artery embolism
before.explanation: Acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolism is correct: sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to a benign examination, gut emptying, and an embolic source (AF off anticoagulation) in an older adult are classic; leukocytosis and lactate rise but are neither sensitive nor specific early. The 2022 WSES guideline recommends immediate CT angiography, IV heparin, fluid resuscitation, and urgent revascularization (endovascular or open embolectomy) with laparotomy for nonviable bowel. Ischemic colitis causes milder left-sided pain with hematochezia and usually resolves with supportive care. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated lipase. Adhesive obstruction follows prior surgery with distension and obstipation. Diverticulitis causes localized left lower quadrant pain and tenderness with fever. Takeaway: pain out of proportion + AF = mesenteric embolism; CTA now, heparin, revascularize.

references.label: Bala M et al. Acute mesenteric ischemia: updated guidelines of the World Society of Emergency Surgery. World J Emerg Surg 2022

before.scenario: A 48-year-old woman is admitted with acute gallstone pancreatitis: 12 hours of epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase 2400 U/L, and ultrasound showing gallstones without bile duct dilation. Pulse is 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, and urine output is reduced. She weighs 70 kg. Hematocrit is 46%, BUN 24 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. She has no heart failure or kidney disease. There are no signs of cholangitis.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid management?
before.options: {"options": ["Total parenteral nutrition with 0.9% saline at 250 mL/h", "Lactated Ringer solution with moderate goal-directed resuscitation (10 mL/kg bolus, then about 1.5 mL/kg/h) and frequent reassessment", "Restrict IV fluids to keep-vein-open and give furosemide to prevent pulmonary edema", "Maintenance 5% dextrose in water at 75 mL/h with nothing by mouth for 7 days", "Lactated Ringer 20 mL/kg bolus followed by 3 mL/kg/h for 48 hours regardless of response"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "goal-directed fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis", "keyTakeaway": "Acute pancreatitis: moderate goal-directed LR (avoid aggressive fluids per WATERFALL), early oral feeding, no prophylactic antibiotics.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Lactated Ringer solution with moderate goal-directed resuscitation (10 mL/kg bolus, then about 1.5 mL/kg/h) and frequent reassessment
before.explanation: Moderate goal-directed LR is correct: the 2024 ACG acute pancreatitis guideline recommends moderately aggressive, goal-directed fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution, reassessing heart rate, urine output, BUN, and hematocrit; the 2022 WATERFALL trial found aggressive resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) increased fluid overload without improving outcomes. Fixed aggressive infusion ignores this harm. D5W at maintenance rates fails to correct hypovolemia, and prolonged NPO is not recommended; early oral feeding within 24-48 hours as tolerated is advised, with enteral rather than parenteral nutrition if needed. Fluid restriction with diuretics worsens hypoperfusion and necrosis risk. TPN is not indicated early. Takeaway: acute pancreatitis = moderate goal-directed LR, early oral feeding, cholecystectomy during admission for gallstone disease.

references.label: Tenner S et al. American College of Gastroenterology Guidelines: Management of Acute Pancreatitis. Am J Gastroenterol 2024

before.scenario: A 38-year-old woman has 5 days of right-sided low back pain that began after moving furniture. The pain does not radiate below the knee. She has no fever, weight loss, history of cancer, injection drug use, trauma, or bowel or bladder symptoms. She has paraspinal muscle tenderness; straight-leg raise and lower extremity neurologic examination are normal. She has no GI, renal, or cardiovascular disease.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Strict bed rest for 1 week", "Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed", "Lumbar spine radiographs", "Superficial heat, staying active, and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug if needed, without imaging", "Lumbar spine MRI"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "initial management of acute low back pain without red flags", "keyTakeaway": "Acute LBP without red flags: no imaging; heat, massage, acupuncture, or manipulation; NSAID or muscle relaxant if medication is needed; stay active.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Superficial heat, staying active, and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug if needed, without imaging
before.explanation: Superficial heat with activity and an NSAID, without imaging, is correct: the ACP low back pain guideline recommends that most patients with acute or subacute low back pain first receive nonpharmacologic treatment (superficial heat, massage, acupuncture, or spinal manipulation) and, if medication is desired, an NSAID or skeletal muscle relaxant, since most improve within weeks; ACP and Choosing Wisely advise against imaging without red flags. MRI and radiographs do not improve outcomes, find incidental degenerative changes, and increase procedures; they are reserved for red flags or persistent radicular symptoms in surgical candidates. Opioids carry dependence risk and are not first-line. Bed rest prolongs disability compared with staying active. Takeaway: acute low back pain without red flags = heat, activity, NSAID or muscle relaxant if needed; no imaging.

references.label: Qaseem A et al. Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians. Ann Intern Med 2017

before.scenario: A 62-year-old woman, whose last menstrual period was at age 51, has had 2 episodes of light vaginal spotting over the past month. She does not take hormone therapy. She has obesity and hypertension. Pelvic examination shows atrophic vaginal mucosa with no visible lesion, and the cervix appears normal. Her most recent cervical cancer screening, 2 years ago, was negative.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
before.options: {"options": ["Repeat cervical cytology alone", "CT of the abdomen and pelvis", "Serum CA-125", "Observation and reevaluation in 6 months", "Transvaginal ultrasonography to measure endometrial thickness"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "transvaginal ultrasonography for postmenopausal bleeding", "keyTakeaway": "Postmenopausal bleeding: TVUS or endometrial biopsy first; endometrial thickness <=4 mm is reassuring; >4 mm or persistent bleeding needs sampling.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Transvaginal ultrasonography to measure endometrial thickness
before.explanation: Transvaginal ultrasonography is correct: ACOG Committee Opinion 734 states that either transvaginal ultrasonography or endometrial sampling is an appropriate first step for postmenopausal bleeding, because endometrial cancer must be excluded; an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has a negative predictive value above 99% and usually does not require sampling, whereas a thickness over 4 mm, a poorly visualized endometrium, or persistent bleeding requires endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy. CA-125 is not a screening or diagnostic test for endometrial cancer. CT does not evaluate the endometrium adequately. Cervical cytology does not evaluate the endometrium. Observation risks delayed diagnosis because about 90% of endometrial cancers present with bleeding. Takeaway: any postmenopausal bleeding = TVUS (stripe <=4 mm reassuring) or endometrial biopsy.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 734: The Role of Transvaginal Ultrasonography in Evaluating the Endometrium of Women With Postmenopausal Bleeding. Obstet Gynecol 2018

before.scenario: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 1, at 10 weeks' gestation has chronic hypertension controlled with nifedipine extended-release. Blood pressure today is 128/82 mm Hg. She has no history of bleeding disorders, peptic ulcer, or aspirin allergy. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, platelet count, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to reduce her risk of preeclampsia?
before.options: {"options": ["No aspirin unless she develops proteinuria", "Aspirin 81 mg daily starting at 12 weeks (ideally before 16 weeks) and continuing until delivery", "Aspirin 325 mg daily starting at 32 weeks", "Vitamin C and E supplementation", "Prophylactic enoxaparin throughout pregnancy"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention in chronic hypertension", "keyTakeaway": "Preeclampsia prevention: 1 high-risk factor (chronic HTN, prior preeclampsia, multifetal, diabetes, CKD, autoimmune) or >=2 moderate -> aspirin 81 mg from 12-16 wk to delivery.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Aspirin 81 mg daily starting at 12 weeks (ideally before 16 weeks) and continuing until delivery
before.explanation: Aspirin 81 mg daily from 12 weeks is correct: the USPSTF recommends low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) after 12 weeks of gestation for pregnant people at high risk of preeclampsia, which includes chronic hypertension, prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, pregestational diabetes, renal disease, and autoimmune disease; ACOG advises starting between 12 and 28 weeks, optimally before 16 weeks, and continuing until delivery. Starting at 32 weeks misses the window for placental benefit, and 325 mg is not the studied dose. Low-molecular-weight heparin has not been shown to prevent preeclampsia in this setting. Waiting for proteinuria means waiting for the disease. Antioxidant vitamins C and E did not reduce preeclampsia in large trials. Takeaway: 1 high-risk factor (or 2+ moderate) = aspirin 81 mg/day from 12-16 weeks until delivery.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2021

before.scenario: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation is admitted in active labor with the cervix 5 cm dilated and intact membranes. A rectovaginal culture at 36 weeks grew group B Streptococcus. She has no drug allergies. Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F).
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate intrapartum regimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours until delivery", "Penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM once", "Penicillin G 5 million units IV, then 2.5 to 3 million units IV every 4 hours until delivery", "Vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours until delivery", "Amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours until delivery"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "intrapartum GBS prophylaxis dosing", "keyTakeaway": "Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: penicillin G 5 MU IV then 2.5-3 MU q4h (ampicillin 2 g then 1 g q4h alternative); cefazolin if low-risk allergy; >=4 h before delivery.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Penicillin G 5 million units IV, then 2.5 to 3 million units IV every 4 hours until delivery
before.explanation: Penicillin G 5 million units IV then 2.5-3 million units every 4 hours is correct: ACOG Committee Opinion 797 recommends intrapartum prophylaxis for GBS-colonized patients with penicillin G as the preferred agent because of its narrow spectrum, with ampicillin 2 g IV then 1 g every 4 hours as an alternative; prophylaxis is considered adequate if given at least 4 hours before delivery. Clindamycin is reserved for patients at high risk of anaphylaxis to penicillin whose isolate is susceptible. Vancomycin is for high-risk penicillin allergy with clindamycin resistance or unknown susceptibility. Oral amoxicillin does not achieve adequate intrapartum levels and is not a recommended regimen. Benzathine penicillin provides low serum and amniotic levels and is used for syphilis, not GBS prophylaxis. Takeaway: GBS-positive in labor without allergy = IV penicillin G 5 MU then 2.5-3 MU q4h (ideally >=4 h before delivery).

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 797: Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns. Obstet Gynecol 2020

before.scenario: A 76-year-old woman reports 3 years of gradually worsening hearing in both ears. She has the most trouble understanding speech in noisy restaurants and hearing her grandchildren's high-pitched voices, and she often thinks people mumble. She has no ear pain, drainage, vertigo, or tinnitus asymmetry, and no history of occupational noise exposure or ototoxic medications. Otoscopy is normal. The Weber test is midline and Rinne testing shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Audiometry shows symmetric, bilateral sloping high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Meniere disease", "Vestibular schwannoma", "Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis)", "Otosclerosis", "Cerumen impaction"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "age-related hearing loss (presbycusis)", "keyTakeaway": "Presbycusis: bilateral symmetric high-frequency SNHL, trouble with speech in noise; audiometry; hearing aids (OTC for mild-moderate); asymmetric loss warrants MRI.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis)
before.explanation: Presbycusis is correct: gradual, bilateral, symmetric high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with difficulty discriminating speech in background noise in an older adult, a normal otoscopic examination, and no other cause is classic. The 2024 AAO-HNSF age-related hearing loss guideline recommends screening adults 50 and older, audiometry when hearing loss is identified, and counseling on and referral for amplification (hearing aids, including over-the-counter devices for mild to moderate loss), and cochlear implant evaluation if needed. Otosclerosis is a conductive loss beginning in young adults. Meniere disease causes episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Vestibular schwannoma causes asymmetric hearing loss and tinnitus. Cerumen impaction is visible on otoscopy and causes conductive loss. Takeaway: older adult with symmetric high-frequency SNHL and poor speech-in-noise = presbycusis; offer hearing aids.

references.label: Tsai Do BS et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Age-Related Hearing Loss. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2024

before.scenario: A 73-year-old woman has 2 years of gradually worsening, painless blurring of distance vision in both eyes and glare from oncoming headlights while driving at night. She has noticed she can now read without her reading glasses. She does not use corticosteroids and has no diabetes. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/50 in both eyes, and refraction shows a myopic shift. Intraocular pressure is normal. The red reflex is diminished, and slit-lamp examination shows bilateral yellow-brown opacification of the central lens. The fundus, as visualized, shows a normal macula and optic disc.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Posterior subcapsular cataract", "Dry age-related macular degeneration", "Nuclear sclerotic cataract", "Primary open-angle glaucoma", "Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "nuclear sclerotic cataract", "keyTakeaway": "Nuclear cataract: gradual blur, glare, myopic shift with 'second sight', diminished red reflex, yellow-brown nucleus; surgery when vision limits daily activities.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Nuclear sclerotic cataract
before.explanation: Nuclear sclerotic cataract is correct: gradual, painless, bilateral blurring with glare, a myopic shift that temporarily improves near vision ('second sight'), a diminished red reflex, and yellow-brown central lens opacity are characteristic of age-related nuclear cataract. The AAO Cataract in the Adult Eye Preferred Practice Pattern recommends surgery when visual impairment interferes with the patient's activities, such as night driving. Posterior subcapsular cataract is associated with corticosteroids and diabetes, causes marked glare and worse near vision. Dry macular degeneration causes central distortion with drusen. Open-angle glaucoma causes painless peripheral field loss with optic disc cupping and often elevated pressure. Diabetic retinopathy requires diabetes and shows microaneurysms and hemorrhages. Takeaway: older adult with glare, myopic shift, improved near vision, and yellow-brown lens = nuclear cataract; surgery when function is impaired.

references.label: Miller KM et al. Cataract in the Adult Eye Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2022

before.scenario: A 79-year-old man with stable angina and prior percutaneous coronary intervention reports fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation for 6 months. TSH is 26 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.5) and free T4 is 0.5 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are positive. He weighs 75 kg. He takes aspirin, atorvastatin, and metoprolol, and his angina occurs only with heavy exertion.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg daily (about 120 mcg)", "Liothyronine 25 mcg three times daily", "Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily, titrated slowly with TSH rechecked in 6 to 8 weeks", "Levothyroxine 300 mcg IV loading dose", "No treatment; recheck TSH in 12 months"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "cautious levothyroxine initiation in an older adult with coronary disease", "keyTakeaway": "Overt hypothyroidism in older adults or CAD: levothyroxine 12.5-25 mcg daily, titrate every 6-8 wk by TSH; full 1.6 mcg/kg only in young healthy adults.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily, titrated slowly with TSH rechecked in 6 to 8 weeks
before.explanation: Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily with slow titration is correct: the ATA hypothyroidism treatment guideline recommends a low starting dose (12.5-25 mcg daily) with gradual increases in older adults and in patients with coronary artery disease, because rapid restoration of metabolic rate increases myocardial oxygen demand and can precipitate angina, MI, or arrhythmia; TSH is rechecked 6-8 weeks after each dose change, and age-appropriate targets may be somewhat higher in older adults. Full replacement at 1.6 mcg/kg is appropriate for young, healthy adults. Liothyronine has a short half-life, causes peaks in T3, and is not recommended as monotherapy. An IV loading dose is for myxedema coma, which he does not have. Overt hypothyroidism with symptoms requires treatment rather than observation. Takeaway: older adult or CAD with hypothyroidism = start levothyroxine low (12.5-25 mcg) and go slow.

references.label: Jonklaas J et al. Guidelines for the treatment of hypothyroidism: American Thyroid Association task force on thyroid hormone replacement. Thyroid 2014

before.scenario: A 6-day-old girl born at term weighing 3.4 kg has a newborn screening result showing a TSH of 92 mIU/L. She is feeding well. Examination shows a large anterior fontanelle and mild jaundice but is otherwise normal. Her mother has no thyroid disease and took no antithyroid medications.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Obtain thyroid ultrasonography and radionuclide scan before treatment", "Start levothyroxine 2 mcg/kg daily after confirmatory results return", "Start levothyroxine only if developmental delay appears at the 2-month visit", "Obtain serum TSH and free T4, then start levothyroxine 10 to 15 mcg/kg daily the same day without waiting for results", "Repeat the newborn screen in 2 weeks before any treatment"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "immediate treatment of congenital hypothyroidism after abnormal newborn screen", "keyTakeaway": "Congenital hypothyroidism: confirm with serum TSH/FT4 and start levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg/day immediately (by 2 weeks); imaging must not delay treatment.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Obtain serum TSH and free T4, then start levothyroxine 10 to 15 mcg/kg daily the same day without waiting for results
before.explanation: Drawing serum TSH and free T4 and starting levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg/day the same day is correct: the 2023 AAP congenital hypothyroidism report recommends confirmatory serum testing immediately after an abnormal screen and, when the screening TSH is markedly elevated, beginning treatment right after the confirmatory sample is drawn, ideally by 2 weeks of age, because early adequate treatment prevents intellectual disability; the starting dose is 10-15 mcg/kg/day of crushed tablets, avoiding soy formula or iron given at the same time. Repeating the screen delays therapy. Imaging is optional and must not delay treatment. A 2-mcg/kg dose is an adult replacement dose and is inadequate for neonates. Waiting for developmental delay causes irreversible harm. Takeaway: abnormal newborn screen with high TSH = confirmatory labs and levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg/day the same day.

references.label: Rose SR et al. Congenital Hypothyroidism: Screening and Management. Pediatrics 2023

before.scenario: A 15-year-old girl has had 2 months of persistent sadness, irritability, loss of interest in soccer, insomnia, poor concentration, and falling grades. PHQ-A score is 17. She has passive thoughts that life is not worth living but no plan, intent, or prior attempts, and a safety plan is completed with her parents, who secure medications and firearms at home. She has no history of mania, psychosis, or substance use. TSH and CBC are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to start along with cognitive behavioral therapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Paroxetine 20 mg daily", "Venlafaxine extended-release 75 mg daily", "Fluoxetine 10 mg daily with close monitoring for suicidal thoughts", "Amitriptyline 25 mg nightly", "Alprazolam 0.25 mg three times daily"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "fluoxetine plus CBT for moderate adolescent depression", "keyTakeaway": "Adolescent MDD: CBT/IPT + SSRI for moderate-severe; fluoxetine (age 8+) or escitalopram (12+); monitor for suicidality (boxed warning); avoid TCAs and paroxetine.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Fluoxetine 10 mg daily with close monitoring for suicidal thoughts
before.explanation: Fluoxetine with close monitoring is correct: the 2023 AACAP guideline for depressive disorders in youth recommends CBT or interpersonal psychotherapy and SSRIs, with combination treatment favored for moderate to severe depression; fluoxetine and escitalopram are FDA-approved for adolescent MDD, and fluoxetine is typically started at 10 mg and increased to 20 mg after about a week. The boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in youth calls for close follow-up and safety planning, not avoidance. Paroxetine has not shown efficacy in adolescents and has more adverse effects and discontinuation symptoms. Tricyclic antidepressants are ineffective in youth and dangerous in overdose. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression and can cause disinhibition and dependence. Venlafaxine has weaker evidence and higher rates of suicidal events in youth. Takeaway: moderate adolescent MDD = CBT plus fluoxetine (or escitalopram) with suicidality monitoring.

references.label: Walter HJ et al. AACAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Major and Persistent Depressive Disorders. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2023

before.scenario: An 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease living in a memory care unit has had 2 weeks of evening agitation, pacing, calling out, and resisting help with bathing. He has not struck anyone and is not at risk of injuring himself. He grimaces when moved and has had no bowel movement for 5 days. He is not febrile. Medications are donepezil and acetaminophen as needed, which staff rarely give. Staff ask for a medication to calm him.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Assess and treat reversible contributors such as pain and constipation, and begin individualized nonpharmacologic interventions", "Lorazepam 1 mg every evening", "Scheduled haloperidol 2 mg twice daily", "Diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime", "Quetiapine 50 mg twice daily indefinitely"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "initial approach to agitation in dementia", "keyTakeaway": "Agitation in dementia: look for pain, constipation, infection, delirium, drugs, unmet needs; nonpharmacologic first; antipsychotic only if severe/dangerous, with consent and early taper.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Assess and treat reversible contributors such as pain and constipation, and begin individualized nonpharmacologic interventions
before.explanation: Assessing contributors and starting nonpharmacologic care is correct: the APA practice guideline on antipsychotics for agitation or psychosis in dementia recommends a comprehensive assessment for medical and environmental causes (pain, constipation, infection, delirium, drugs) and use of nonpharmacologic strategies first, reserving antipsychotics for severe, dangerous, or very distressing symptoms after these measures fail, with consent about mortality risk and an attempted taper within 4 months. His grimacing and constipation suggest pain and discomfort driving the behavior Haloperidol carries mortality, stroke, and extrapyramidal risk. Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls. Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and worsens cognition. Indefinite quetiapine without a cause search or reassessment is inappropriate. Takeaway: agitation in dementia = find causes (pain, constipation, infection) and use nonpharmacologic care before antipsychotics.

references.label: Reus VI et al. The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline on the Use of Antipsychotics to Treat Agitation or Psychosis in Patients With Dementia. Am J Psychiatry 2016

before.scenario: A 7-year-old girl has refused to go to school for 2 months. On school mornings she reports stomachaches and cries and clings to her mother, but symptoms resolve if she is allowed to stay home. She worries that her mother will be in a car crash, refuses sleepovers, insists on sleeping in her parents' bed, and has nightmares about getting lost. The symptoms began 6 months ago after her grandmother died. She plays happily with peers when her mother is present. Physical examination is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Specific phobia", "Major depressive disorder", "Social anxiety disorder", "Separation anxiety disorder", "Generalized anxiety disorder"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "separation anxiety disorder", "keyTakeaway": "Separation anxiety disorder: excessive fear of separation >=4 wk in children (6 mo in adults), worry about harm to caregiver, school refusal, somatic complaints; CBT +/- SSRI.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Separation anxiety disorder
before.explanation: Separation anxiety disorder is correct: developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear of separation from an attachment figure lasting at least 4 weeks in children, with worry about harm to the parent, school refusal, reluctance to sleep away from home, nightmares of separation, and somatic complaints when separation is anticipated, is diagnostic The AACAP anxiety disorders guideline recommends CBT and SSRIs, with combination most effective. Generalized anxiety disorder involves multiple worries about everyday matters (school, health, performance) for 6 months, not focused on separation. Social anxiety centers on fear of scrutiny or embarrassment by peers, whereas she socializes comfortably with her mother present. Specific phobia targets one object or situation. Depression involves pervasive low mood and anhedonia. Takeaway: child with school refusal and fears of harm to a parent when apart = separation anxiety disorder; CBT first.

references.label: Walter HJ et al. AACAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Anxiety Disorders. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2020

before.scenario: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI 34 kg/m2), and hypertension has hepatic steatosis on ultrasonography. He drinks 2 alcoholic drinks per week. Hepatitis B and C serologies are negative. AST is 48 U/L, ALT is 52 U/L, and platelet count is 190,000/mm3. His calculated FIB-4 index is 1.9.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating his liver disease?
before.options: {"options": ["Reassurance with repeat FIB-4 in 5 years", "Abdominal CT with contrast", "Vibration-controlled transient elastography (or enhanced liver fibrosis test)", "Start ursodeoxycholic acid", "Immediate liver biopsy"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "FIB-4 followed by elastography for fibrosis risk in fatty liver disease", "keyTakeaway": "Fatty liver with metabolic risk: FIB-4 first; 1.3-2.67 -> VCTE or ELF; >2.67 or high stiffness -> hepatology.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Vibration-controlled transient elastography (or enhanced liver fibrosis test)
before.explanation: Elastography or the ELF test is correct: the 2023 AASLD practice guidance (steatotic liver disease) recommends FIB-4 as the first fibrosis risk test in people with fatty liver and metabolic risk factors. A FIB-4 below 1.3 is low risk with repeat testing in 1-2 years for those with diabetes or multiple risk factors; 1.3-2.67 is indeterminate and should be followed by a second test such as VCTE or ELF; above 2.67 warrants hepatology referral. With a FIB-4 of 1.9 and diabetes, reassurance would miss advanced fibrosis. Biopsy is reserved for discordant or uncertain results, not used first. CT does not stage fibrosis. Ursodiol has no proven benefit in MASLD; weight loss and cardiometabolic management are central. Takeaway: fatty liver: FIB-4 first; indeterminate (1.3-2.67) -> elastography or ELF.

references.label: Rinella ME et al. AASLD Practice Guidance on the clinical assessment and management of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Hepatology 2023

before.scenario: A 52-year-old man has 2 days of left lower quadrant pain and low-grade fever. He is otherwise healthy, immunocompetent, and tolerating oral fluids. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 88/min, and there is localized left lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. WBC count is 11,800/mm3. CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis without abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction. He had a normal colonoscopy 2 years ago.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Elective sigmoid colectomy after this first episode", "Outpatient care with analgesia and diet as tolerated, using antibiotics selectively rather than routinely", "Urgent colonoscopy during this episode", "CT-guided percutaneous drainage", "Hospital admission for IV piperacillin-tazobactam"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "outpatient management of uncomplicated diverticulitis without routine antibiotics", "keyTakeaway": "Mild uncomplicated diverticulitis, immunocompetent: outpatient care; antibiotics selectively, not routinely.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Outpatient care with analgesia and diet as tolerated, using antibiotics selectively rather than routinely
before.explanation: Outpatient care with selective antibiotic use is correct: the AGA clinical practice update on diverticulitis (2021) advises that antibiotics be used selectively rather than routinely in immunocompetent patients with mild uncomplicated diverticulitis, because trials show no difference in recovery, complications, or recurrence. Antibiotics are reserved for those with comorbidities, frailty, immunosuppression, sepsis, or failure to improve. Admission and IV antibiotics are for complicated disease, inability to tolerate oral intake, or systemic toxicity. Colonoscopy is avoided acutely and is needed after recovery only if not recently performed. Elective colectomy is individualized and not indicated after one uncomplicated episode. Drainage is for an abscess. Takeaway: mild uncomplicated diverticulitis in an immunocompetent patient: outpatient, antibiotics only selectively.

references.label: Peery AF et al. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Medical Management of Colonic Diverticulitis: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2021

before.scenario: A 6-year-old girl fell from monkey bars onto her outstretched right hand. Her elbow is swollen and tender, and radiographs show a displaced extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture. The radial pulse is palpable and the hand is warm and pink. Before splinting, the clinician performs a focused neurologic examination of the hand.
before.question: Which of the following maneuvers specifically tests the nerve most commonly injured in this fracture?
before.options: {"options": ["Asking her to make an 'OK' sign by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint", "Testing sensation over the lateral shoulder", "Testing sensation over the dorsal first web space", "Asking her to cross her index and middle fingers", "Testing wrist extension against resistance"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "anterior interosseous nerve injury with supracondylar humerus fracture", "keyTakeaway": "Extension supracondylar fracture: AIN (median branch) most often injured; test with the OK sign. Always document neurovascular status.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Asking her to make an 'OK' sign by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint
before.explanation: The OK sign is correct: the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve is the nerve most often injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures; it is purely motor, so injury causes loss of flexor pollicis longus and index flexor digitorum profundus function with normal sensation, and the child cannot make a round OK sign. The AAOS supracondylar fracture guideline emphasizes documenting a neurovascular examination before and after treatment. Dorsal first web space sensation and wrist extension test the radial nerve, which is also injured (especially with posteromedial displacement) but less commonly. Crossing fingers tests ulnar-innervated interossei, injured mainly with flexion-type fractures or medial pinning. Lateral shoulder sensation tests the axillary nerve. Takeaway: extension supracondylar fracture: check the OK sign (AIN), radial and ulnar function, and perfusion.

references.label: Howard A et al. AAOS clinical practice guideline: the treatment of pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012

before.scenario: A 19-year-old woman, gravida 1, at 37 weeks of gestation had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting 1 minute. She arrives drowsy but breathing, with blood pressure 168/112 mm Hg, 3+ proteinuria, and hyperreflexia. She is positioned on her left side and receiving supplemental oxygen, and an IV line is in place. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to prevent recurrent seizures?
before.options: {"options": ["Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV", "Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV loading dose over 20-30 minutes, then 1-2 g/hour", "Levetiracetam 1,500 mg IV", "Lorazepam 4 mg IV as maintenance therapy", "Magnesium sulfate 1 g IV once"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "magnesium sulfate loading dose for eclampsia", "keyTakeaway": "Eclampsia: MgSO4 4-6 g IV load then 1-2 g/h (10 g IM if no IV); treat severe BP; deliver; calcium gluconate for toxicity.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV loading dose over 20-30 minutes, then 1-2 g/hour
before.explanation: Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV over 20-30 minutes, then 1-2 g/hour is correct: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 recommends magnesium sulfate as the drug of choice to treat eclampsia and prevent recurrence, with a 4-6 g IV loading dose followed by 1-2 g/hour (or 10 g IM if IV access is unavailable), continued for 24 hours postpartum, while lowering severe-range blood pressure with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral nifedipine and planning delivery. Magnesium is superior to phenytoin and diazepam in preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures. Benzodiazepines are reserved for status not responding to magnesium. Levetiracetam is not the standard for eclampsia. A 1-g dose is subtherapeutic. Monitor reflexes, respirations, and urine output; calcium gluconate reverses toxicity. Takeaway: eclampsia: magnesium 4-6 g IV load then 1-2 g/h, control BP, deliver.

references.label: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 222. Obstet Gynecol 2020

before.scenario: A 21-year-old woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, and vaginal discharge. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). She is tolerating oral intake. Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness without a mass. Urine hCG is negative. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows no tubo-ovarian abscess. NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia is pending. She has no drug allergies.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once alone", "Azithromycin 1 g orally once", "Oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days alone", "Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days", "Admission for IV clindamycin and gentamicin"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease regimen", "keyTakeaway": "Outpatient PID (CDC 2021): ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100 mg BID + metronidazole 500 mg BID x14 days.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
before.explanation: Ceftriaxone plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole is correct: pelvic or abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness meets CDC minimum criteria for PID, and empiric treatment should begin without waiting for NAAT results. The 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if 150 kg or more), plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 days, covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes. Single-dose azithromycin and ceftriaxone alone leave the polymicrobial infection inadequately treated. Metronidazole alone treats bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis. Hospitalization is for pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness, inability to tolerate oral therapy, or outpatient failure. Retest in 3 months and treat partners. Takeaway: outpatient PID: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days.

references.label: Workowski KA et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

before.scenario: A 38-year-old man has right flank pain radiating to the groin that began 8 hours ago. Pain is controlled with ketorolac. He is afebrile. Urinalysis shows hematuria without pyuria or nitrites. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm stone in the distal right ureter with mild hydronephrosis. He has a normal left kidney and no history of stones.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Emergency ureteral stent placement", "Immediate percutaneous nephrolithotomy", "Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily with analgesics and follow-up imaging", "Ciprofloxacin for 7 days", "Potassium citrate to dissolve the stone"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "tamsulosin medical expulsive therapy for a distal ureteral stone", "keyTakeaway": "Uncomplicated distal ureteral stone <=10 mm: medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin; urgent decompression if obstructed + infected.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily with analgesics and follow-up imaging
before.explanation: Tamsulosin is correct: the AUA/Endourological Society stone surgery guideline (2016; superseded by the 2026 AUA guideline series) recommends offering observation with an alpha-blocker (medical expulsive therapy) to patients with uncomplicated distal ureteral stones 10 mm or smaller whose pain is controlled, with no infection and adequate renal function, and follow-up imaging within about 4-6 weeks; ureteroscopy or shock wave lithotripsy follows if the stone does not pass. Emergency decompression is reserved for obstruction with infection, intractable pain, or renal failure. Antibiotics are not indicated without infection. Potassium citrate does not dissolve calcium stones; it is used for prevention and uric acid stones. PCNL is for large renal stones. Takeaway: uncomplicated distal ureteral stone <=10 mm: tamsulosin and observation; decompress if infected.

references.label: Pearle MS et al. Surgical Management of Kidney and Ureteral Stones: AUA Guideline (2026) Part I. J Urol 2026
Assimos D et al. Surgical Management of Stones: AUA/Endourological Society Guideline, Part I. J Urol 2016

before.scenario: A 7-year-old boy wets the bed 5 nights per week and has never had a dry period longer than 2 weeks. He has no daytime wetting, urgency, constipation, or snoring. Growth and examination are normal, and urinalysis shows normal specific gravity without glucose or protein. He is going to a 1-week summer camp in 3 weeks and is distressed about it. The family wants a treatment that will work quickly for camp.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Oxybutynin twice daily as monotherapy", "Renal and bladder ultrasonography before any treatment", "Desmopressin at bedtime with fluid restriction from 1 hour before until 8 hours after the dose", "Imipramine at bedtime", "Waking him with punishment for wet nights"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "desmopressin for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis", "keyTakeaway": "Monosymptomatic enuresis: alarm or desmopressin first line; desmopressin acts fast (camps) and requires evening fluid restriction.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Desmopressin at bedtime with fluid restriction from 1 hour before until 8 hours after the dose
before.explanation: Desmopressin with evening fluid restriction is correct: this is monosymptomatic enuresis (no daytime symptoms) in a child over 5 years. The 2020 International Children's Continence Society document lists the enuresis alarm and desmopressin as first-line therapies; desmopressin works within days and suits short-term needs such as camp, whereas alarms take weeks to work. Fluid intake must be limited from 1 hour before to 8 hours after dosing to prevent hyponatremia. Imipramine is a later option because of cardiotoxicity in overdose. Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder symptoms, not monotherapy here. Imaging is unnecessary when history, examination, and urinalysis are normal. Punishment is harmful. Takeaway: monosymptomatic enuresis: alarm or desmopressin first line; desmopressin for quick or situational control with fluid restriction.

references.label: Nevéus T et al. Management and treatment of nocturnal enuresis: an updated standardization document from the International Children's Continence Society. J Pediatr Urol 2020

before.scenario: A 44-year-old man has passed his third calcium oxalate kidney stone in 4 years; stone analysis confirmed calcium oxalate monohydrate. He is now pain free. He drinks about 1 L of fluid daily and eats a high-sodium diet. Serum calcium, creatinine, uric acid, and bicarbonate are normal. He asks what can be done to prevent more stones.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to guide prevention?
before.options: {"options": ["No further testing; restrict dietary calcium to under 400 mg/day", "24-hour urine collection for volume, pH, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, and creatinine", "Random spot urine calcium only", "Serum PTH and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without urine studies", "Repeat noncontrast CT every 3 months"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "24-hour urine metabolic evaluation in a recurrent calcium stone former", "keyTakeaway": "Recurrent stone former: serum chemistries + 24-hour urine (volume, pH, Ca, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, Na, creatinine); keep normal calcium intake.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: 24-hour urine collection for volume, pH, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, and creatinine
before.explanation: A 24-hour urine collection is correct: the AUA medical management of kidney stones guideline (2026) recommends metabolic evaluation for recurrent or high-risk stone formers and interested first-time formers, including serum chemistry and 1 or 2 24-hour urine collections measuring volume, pH, calcium, oxalate, uric acid, citrate, sodium, potassium, and creatinine, to direct diet (fluid for at least 2.5 L urine daily, sodium restriction) and drugs such as thiazides or potassium citrate. Spot urine calcium cannot characterize risk. PTH testing is reserved for high serum or urine calcium. Frequent CT adds radiation without guiding prevention. Dietary calcium restriction raises oxalate absorption and stone risk; normal calcium intake (1,000-1,200 mg/day) is advised. Takeaway: recurrent calcium stones: 24-hour urine to tailor prevention; do not restrict calcium.

references.label: Pearle MS et al. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline (2026) Part I: Evaluation of Patients With Kidney Stones and Dietary Management of Patients With Calcium Stones. J Urol 2026

before.scenario: A 76-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and CKD (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m2) has had 2 days of fever, cough, and myalgias, and a home antigen test is positive for SARS-CoV-2. SpO2 is 96% on room air and she is not hypoxic or dyspneic. Her medications are metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. She has no liver disease.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Azithromycin for 5 days", "Nirmatrelvir 300 mg with ritonavir 100 mg twice daily for 5 days", "Nirmatrelvir 150 mg with ritonavir 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, temporarily holding atorvastatin", "Oral dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days", "Symptomatic care only because she is not hypoxic"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "renally adjusted nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for high-risk outpatient COVID-19", "keyTakeaway": "High-risk outpatient COVID-19 within 5 days: nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (150/100 mg BID if eGFR 30-59); check CYP3A4 interactions; no steroids unless hypoxic.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Nirmatrelvir 150 mg with ritonavir 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, temporarily holding atorvastatin
before.explanation: Renally adjusted nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is correct: she is at high risk for progression (age, diabetes, CKD) and is within 5 days of symptom onset. The IDSA COVID-19 treatment guideline suggests nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for ambulatory high-risk patients; for eGFR 30 to below 60 the dose is reduced to nirmatrelvir 150 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg twice daily for 5 days. Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, so atorvastatin can be held during treatment. The standard 300-mg dose is for eGFR 60 or higher. Dexamethasone is recommended only for patients who need supplemental oxygen and can harm those who do not. Azithromycin has no antiviral benefit. Withholding antivirals forgoes reduced hospitalization risk in high-risk patients. Takeaway: high-risk outpatient COVID-19 within 5 days: nirmatrelvir-ritonavir, adjusted for eGFR 30-59, after an interaction review.

references.label: IDSA Guidelines on the Treatment and Management of Patients with COVID-19

before.scenario: A 79-year-old man from a nursing home has fever, confusion, and hypotension from pyelonephritis. Blood cultures were drawn and IV piperacillin-tazobactam was given within 1 hour of arrival. He has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 3 hours. Mean arterial pressure remains 56 mm Hg, lactate is 4.6 mmol/L, and lungs now have bibasilar crackles. A peripheral IV catheter in a large forearm vein is functioning well, and central access is being arranged.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Give another 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus", "Delay vasopressors until central venous access is placed", "Start IV hydrocortisone as the only additional therapy", "Start norepinephrine, through the peripheral IV if needed, titrated to a mean arterial pressure of 65 mm Hg", "Start dopamine as the first-line vasopressor"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor in septic shock", "keyTakeaway": "Septic shock not responding to fluids: norepinephrine first-line, MAP target 65, start peripherally rather than delay.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Start norepinephrine, through the peripheral IV if needed, titrated to a mean arterial pressure of 65 mm Hg
before.explanation: Norepinephrine titrated to MAP 65 mm Hg is correct: persistent hypotension and elevated lactate after initial fluids indicate septic shock. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, an initial MAP target of 65 mm Hg (60-65 is suggested for patients 65 or older), and starting vasopressors peripherally rather than delaying until central access is obtained. Further large fluid boluses risk pulmonary edema, already suggested by new crackles; additional fluid should be guided by reassessment. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine. Low-dose hydrocortisone is an adjunct for persistent vasopressor requirement, not a replacement for vasopressors. Takeaway: septic shock after initial fluids: norepinephrine first, MAP about 65, peripherally if necessary.

references.label: Prescott HC et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026

before.scenario: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after nearly fainting at home. He is lightheaded and diaphoretic but responsive. Blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg and pulse is 36/min. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with normal QRS duration and no AV block. Glucose and potassium levels are normal. Intravenous access is in place.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
