before.options: {"options": ["Atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg", "Metoprolol 5 mg IV", "Epinephrine 1 mg IV push", "Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push", "Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "atropine 1 mg for symptomatic sinus bradycardia", "keyTakeaway": "Unstable bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV q3-5 min (max 3 mg); if no response, transcutaneous pacing or epinephrine/dopamine infusion.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg
before.explanation: Atropine 1 mg IV is correct: this is bradycardia causing hypotension and presyncope (hemodynamically unstable). AHA adult ALS guidance (2020, carried forward in the 2025 guidelines) recommends atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes up to 3 mg; if ineffective, use transcutaneous pacing or an infusion of epinephrine (2-10 mcg/min) or dopamine (5-20 mcg/kg/min) while preparing transvenous pacing. Epinephrine 1 mg IV push is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause dangerous hypertension and arrhythmias in a patient with a pulse. Adenosine and amiodarone treat tachyarrhythmias and would worsen bradycardia. Metoprolol slows the heart further. Atropine may be ineffective after heart transplant and in infranodal high-grade block. Takeaway: unstable bradycardia: atropine 1 mg (max 3 mg), then pacing or a chronotropic infusion.

references.label: Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support: 2025 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Circulation 2025

before.scenario: A 32-year-old woman has 40 minutes of rapid, regular palpitations that began suddenly while she was bending over. She feels anxious but has no chest pain or dyspnea. Blood pressure is 122/80 mm Hg and pulse is 188/min. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves. She has no medical problems.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
before.options: {"options": ["Synchronized cardioversion", "IV amiodarone", "Modified Valsalva maneuver with supine leg elevation", "Oral metoprolol and discharge home", "IV procainamide"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "vagal maneuver as initial therapy for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia", "keyTakeaway": "Stable regular narrow-complex SVT: modified Valsalva first, then adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg; synchronized cardioversion if unstable.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Modified Valsalva maneuver with supine leg elevation
before.explanation: A modified Valsalva maneuver is correct: a stable patient with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia most likely has AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. The 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline and the AHA ALS tachycardia algorithm recommend vagal maneuvers first, followed by IV adenosine (6 mg rapid push, then 12 mg) if the rhythm persists. Straining against resistance for 15 seconds and then lying flat with the legs raised converts more patients than the standard Valsalva. Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamic instability or failure of drug therapy. Amiodarone is not first line for SVT. Oral metoprolol and discharge leaves the tachycardia untreated. Procainamide is used for stable wide-complex or pre-excited tachycardia. Takeaway: stable regular narrow-complex SVT: vagal maneuvers first, then adenosine; cardiovert only if unstable.

references.label: Page RL et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. J Am Coll Cardiol 2016
Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support: 2025 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Circulation 2025

before.scenario: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 90 minutes after the onset of substernal chest pressure that lasted 30 minutes and has resolved. She has hypertension. Vital signs are normal. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. The initial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T level is detectable but below the 99th percentile upper reference limit.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Immediate exercise treadmill testing", "Repeat the high-sensitivity troponin measurement in 1 to 3 hours", "Discharge home with no further testing", "Measure creatine kinase-MB", "Urgent invasive coronary angiography"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "repeat high-sensitivity troponin 1 to 3 hours after a nondiagnostic early result", "keyTakeaway": "Single hs-cTn rules out MI only if below detection limit and >=3 h after symptom onset; otherwise repeat at 1-3 h. CK-MB is obsolete.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Repeat the high-sensitivity troponin measurement in 1 to 3 hours
before.explanation: Repeating the hs-troponin in 1-3 hours is correct: the 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline and the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline use clinical decision pathways in which a single hs-cTn rules out MI only if it is below the assay's limit of detection and symptoms began at least 3 hours earlier. This patient presented within 3 hours and has a detectable level, so serial testing at 1-3 hours is needed to look for a significant change. Discharge without serial testing could miss NSTEMI. Stress testing should wait until MI is excluded. Angiography is for high-risk features such as dynamic ECG changes or a rising troponin. CK-MB adds nothing when hs-troponin is available. Takeaway: early presenter with detectable but normal hs-troponin: repeat at 1-3 hours per the pathway before ruling out MI.

references.label: Gulati M et al. 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain. Circulation 2021
Rao SV et al. 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes. Circulation 2025

before.scenario: A 29-year-old woman with asthma comes to the emergency department with a severe exacerbation. Over the past hour she has received three doses of nebulized albuterol with ipratropium, oral prednisone 50 mg, and oxygen. She still speaks in short phrases and uses accessory muscles. Respiratory rate is 28/min, pulse is 118/min, and oxygen saturation is 93% on oxygen. Peak expiratory flow is 35% of predicted. She is alert.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Inhaled salmeterol", "IV ceftriaxone", "Oral montelukast", "Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes", "IV aminophylline"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "IV magnesium sulfate for severe asthma exacerbation unresponsive to initial therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Severe asthma exacerbation not responding to SABA + ipratropium + systemic steroid: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min; avoid aminophylline.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes
before.explanation: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is correct: the GINA 2025 strategy report advises considering IV magnesium for adults with severe exacerbations who do not respond to initial treatment with repeated SABA (with ipratropium in severe attacks), systemic corticosteroids, and controlled oxygen; it reduces hospital admission in this group. She should continue frequent or continuous albuterol, be monitored for fatigue and rising PaCO2, and be admitted if PEF stays below 60%. IV aminophylline adds toxicity without meaningful benefit and is not recommended. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of bacterial infection. Montelukast has no established role in acute severe attacks. Salmeterol is a slow-onset LABA and must never be used alone or as rescue. Takeaway: severe asthma not improving after an hour of SABA/ipratropium and steroids: IV magnesium 2 g over 20 minutes.

references.label: Global Initiative for Asthma. GINA Strategy Report 2025

before.scenario: A 62-year-old woman with a 40-pack-year smoking history has progressive exertional dyspnea. Spirometry shows a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58 and FEV1 of 55% of predicted, with a 6% improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator. Lung volumes show total lung capacity of 118% of predicted and residual volume of 160% of predicted.
before.question: Which of the following additional pulmonary function findings is most likely and best supports emphysema rather than chronic asthma?
before.options: {"options": ["Reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)", "Reduced total lung capacity", "Normal DLCO", "Reduced residual volume", "Increased DLCO"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "reduced DLCO distinguishing emphysema from asthma", "keyTakeaway": "Obstruction with hyperinflation + low DLCO = emphysema; asthma and chronic bronchitis have normal (asthma possibly high) DLCO.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)
before.explanation: Reduced DLCO is correct: emphysema destroys alveolar walls and the capillary bed, decreasing gas-transfer surface, so DLCO falls in proportion to severity, while asthma usually has a normal or increased DLCO. The 2022 ERS/ATS interpretive standard uses DLCO with spirometry and lung volumes to characterize obstruction; here, persistent obstruction with hyperinflation (TLC >100%) and air trapping (high RV) plus low DLCO points to emphysema. Increased DLCO is seen in asthma, alveolar hemorrhage, polycythemia, and obesity. A normal DLCO would favor asthma or chronic bronchitis. Reduced TLC indicates restriction, not hyperinflation. Residual volume is increased by air trapping in obstructive disease, not reduced. Takeaway: obstruction + hyperinflation + low DLCO = emphysema; obstruction with normal or high DLCO = asthma.

references.label: Stanojevic S et al. ERS/ATS technical standard on interpretive strategies for routine lung function tests. Eur Respir J 2022

before.scenario: A 58-year-old woman who has never smoked has 2 months of cough and hip pain. Imaging shows a 4-cm left upper lobe mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and lytic lesions in the pelvis and spine. CT-guided biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma of the lung. Brain MRI is negative. Performance status is good.
before.question: Before first-line systemic therapy is selected, which of the following is the most appropriate testing?
before.options: {"options": ["Serial serum CEA measurements only", "PD-L1 testing alone", "No further testing; begin platinum-based chemotherapy immediately", "Sputum cytology", "Broad molecular profiling, preferably next-generation sequencing, for actionable driver alterations plus PD-L1 testing"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "broad molecular biomarker testing before first-line therapy for metastatic lung adenocarcinoma", "keyTakeaway": "Metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC: broad NGS (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, MET, RET, NTRK, HER2) + PD-L1 before choosing first-line therapy.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Broad molecular profiling, preferably next-generation sequencing, for actionable driver alterations plus PD-L1 testing
before.explanation: Broad molecular profiling plus PD-L1 is correct: the 2025 NCCN NSCLC guideline recommends testing all patients with advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC, ideally by broad-panel NGS on tissue and/or plasma, for EGFR, ALK, KRAS, ROS1, BRAF, NTRK1/2/3, MET exon 14 skipping, RET, and ERBB2 (HER2) alterations, together with PD-L1 immunohistochemistry. A never-smoker with adenocarcinoma has a high likelihood of a targetable driver such as EGFR or ALK, for which oral targeted therapy is preferred over chemoimmunotherapy, and immunotherapy given first can increase toxicity of later targeted agents. CEA is not used to select therapy. PD-L1 alone misses actionable drivers. Sputum cytology adds nothing after tissue diagnosis. Starting chemotherapy without biomarker results forgoes better first-line options. Takeaway: metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC: broad NGS + PD-L1 before first-line therapy.

references.label: Riely GJ et al. NCCN Guidelines Insights: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 7.2025. J Natl Compr Canc Netw 2025

before.scenario: A 6-year-old boy has had vomiting and watery nonbloody diarrhea for 1 day; several classmates have similar symptoms. He has vomited after each attempt to drink. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F) and pulse is 118/min. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill is 2 seconds, and he is alert and interactive. The abdomen is soft and nontender.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["IV normal saline bolus of 20 mL/kg and admission", "Empiric oral azithromycin", "A single dose of oral ondansetron followed by oral rehydration solution in small frequent amounts", "Rehydration with apple juice and sports drinks", "Oral loperamide"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "ondansetron then oral rehydration for vomiting child with mild-to-moderate dehydration", "keyTakeaway": "Pediatric gastroenteritis with mild-moderate dehydration: ORS first-line; ondansetron (>4 y) for vomiting; no loperamide; IV only for severe dehydration.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: A single dose of oral ondansetron followed by oral rehydration solution in small frequent amounts
before.explanation: Ondansetron followed by ORS is correct: this child has acute viral gastroenteritis with mild-to-moderate dehydration and vomiting that is preventing oral intake. The 2017 IDSA infectious diarrhea guideline recommends reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution as first-line therapy for mild to moderate dehydration and states that an antiemetic such as ondansetron may be given to children older than 4 years and adolescents with vomiting to facilitate oral rehydration; it reduces the need for IV fluids and admission. IV fluids are for severe dehydration, shock, altered mental status, or ORS failure. Antimotility drugs such as loperamide should not be given to children with acute diarrhea. Antibiotics are not indicated for watery diarrhea without bloody stools, travel, or toxicity. Juices and sports drinks have inappropriate sugar and electrolyte content and can worsen diarrhea. Takeaway: vomiting child older than 4 with mild-moderate dehydration: ondansetron, then ORS.

references.label: Shane AL et al. 2017 IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea. Clin Infect Dis 2017

before.scenario: A 16-year-old girl has cramping lower abdominal pain that begins with each menstrual period and lasts 2 days; it has caused her to miss school twice this semester. Menarche was at age 12, and the pain began about a year later. Cycles are regular, and bleeding is not heavy. She is not sexually active. She takes acetaminophen without relief. Abdominal examination is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Oxycodone as needed", "Pelvic ultrasonography and CA-125 before any therapy", "Naproxen started at the onset of menses (or 1 to 2 days before) and taken on a scheduled basis", "Diagnostic laparoscopy", "Leuprolide acetate"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "NSAIDs for primary dysmenorrhea in an adolescent", "keyTakeaway": "Primary dysmenorrhea: scheduled NSAID starting 1-2 days before/at menses onset; add hormonal contraception; evaluate for endometriosis if refractory 3-6 months.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Naproxen started at the onset of menses (or 1 to 2 days before) and taken on a scheduled basis
before.explanation: Scheduled naproxen is correct: crampy pain that starts with menses, begins after ovulatory cycles are established, and occurs with a normal history and examination is primary dysmenorrhea, mediated by endometrial prostaglandins. ACOG Committee Opinion 760 recommends NSAIDs as first-line therapy, started 1-2 days before or at the onset of menses and taken on a schedule rather than as needed, with hormonal contraception as a further option; if symptoms persist after 3-6 months of NSAIDs and hormonal therapy, evaluate for secondary causes such as endometriosis. Laparoscopy is for refractory symptoms. GnRH agonists are reserved for suspected endometriosis not responding to first-line therapy and need add-back therapy. Opioids are inappropriate. Routine imaging and CA-125 are unnecessary with a normal history and examination. Takeaway: adolescent primary dysmenorrhea: scheduled NSAID, then hormonal contraception; evaluate if refractory.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 760: Dysmenorrhea and Endometriosis in the Adolescent. Obstet Gynecol 2018

before.scenario: A 51-year-old woman has had no menses for 14 months. She has 10-12 hot flashes daily with night sweats that wake her several times per night and impair her work. She has an intact uterus. She has no history of breast or endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism, stroke, coronary disease, liver disease, or unexplained vaginal bleeding. Blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg and BMI is 24 kg/m2.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Transdermal estradiol plus oral micronized progesterone", "Testosterone gel", "Low-dose vaginal estradiol alone", "Transdermal estradiol alone", "Black cohosh extract"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "estrogen plus progestogen for vasomotor symptoms in a woman with a uterus", "keyTakeaway": "Moderate-severe VMS, age <60/within 10 y of menopause, no contraindications: systemic estrogen; add progestogen if uterus intact; nonhormonal options if contraindicated.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Transdermal estradiol plus oral micronized progesterone
before.explanation: Estrogen plus a progestogen is correct: hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms, and the 2022 NAMS hormone therapy position statement finds that for women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, benefits generally outweigh risks; transdermal estrogen carries less VTE risk than oral. A woman with a uterus needs a progestogen to prevent estrogen-induced endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, so estrogen alone is inappropriate. Low-dose vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause but not hot flashes. Testosterone is not indicated for vasomotor symptoms. Black cohosh is not shown to be effective. For women who cannot take hormones, options include SSRIs or SNRIs (paroxetine 7.5 mg), gabapentin, or fezolinetant. Takeaway: bothersome hot flashes, under 60, no contraindications, uterus present: estrogen plus progestogen.

references.label: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society. Menopause 2022

before.scenario: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, aspirin, metoprolol, and lisinopril. Hemoglobin A1c is 8.1%. BMI is 33 kg/m2. eGFR is 75 mL/min/1.73 m2 with a normal urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. LVEF is 55% without heart failure symptoms. He has no personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or pancreatitis.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Pioglitazone", "Subcutaneous semaglutide once weekly", "Glipizide", "Insulin glargine", "Sitagliptin"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit in type 2 diabetes with ASCVD", "keyTakeaway": "T2D + established ASCVD: add GLP-1 RA (e.g., semaglutide) and/or SGLT2i with proven CV benefit, independent of A1c; SGLT2i preferred if HF/CKD.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Subcutaneous semaglutide once weekly
before.explanation: Weekly semaglutide is correct: the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026 recommend, for adults with type 2 diabetes and established ASCVD, a GLP-1 receptor agonist and/or SGLT2 inhibitor with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, independent of A1c or metformin use; a GLP-1 RA is especially attractive with obesity. Semaglutide is started at 0.25 mg weekly for 4 weeks, then 0.5 mg, titrated to 1-2 mg as tolerated. Sulfonylureas lower glucose but lack cardiovascular benefit and cause hypoglycemia and weight gain. DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascular-neutral (saxagliptin increases HF hospitalization). Pioglitazone causes weight gain and fluid retention. Basal insulin adds weight gain and hypoglycemia and lacks CV benefit; a GLP-1 RA is preferred before insulin. Takeaway: type 2 diabetes with ASCVD: add a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven CV benefit regardless of A1c.

references.label: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026
American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026

before.scenario: An 8-year-old boy has had 3 episodes in 6 months, each shortly after falling asleep, in which his parents found him awake but unable to speak, drooling, with twitching of the left side of his face and gurgling sounds, lasting about 1 minute. One episode evolved into a generalized convulsion. He develops and performs normally at school, and his examination is normal. EEG shows high-amplitude biphasic centrotemporal spikes activated by drowsiness and sleep, with a normal background.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Childhood absence epilepsy", "Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy", "Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes", "Lennox-Gastaut syndrome", "Night terrors"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes in a school-age child", "keyTakeaway": "Nocturnal hemifacial twitching, drooling, speech arrest in normal child 4-10 y + centrotemporal spikes = SeLECTS; remits by adolescence; treatment often unnecessary.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
before.explanation: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS, formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) is correct: the 2022 ILAE childhood-onset syndrome classification describes onset at about 4-10 years, brief focal seizures in sleep with hemifacial sensorimotor symptoms, speech arrest, drooling, and gurgling that may become bilateral tonic-clonic, normal development, and EEG centrotemporal spikes activated by sleep. Seizures remit by mid-adolescence; many need no medication. Childhood absence epilepsy causes many daily brief staring spells with 3-Hz spike-wave. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy begins in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks and generalized polyspike-wave. Lennox-Gastaut causes multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and slow spike-wave. Night terrors are nonepileptic arousals with screaming and no facial clonus. Takeaway: nocturnal hemifacial seizures with drooling in a normal school-age child + centrotemporal spikes = SeLECTS.

references.label: Specchio N et al. ILAE classification and definition of epilepsy syndromes with onset in childhood. Epilepsia 2022

before.scenario: A 72-year-old man falls forward down a flight of stairs and strikes his forehead. He reports burning pain in both hands. Examination shows marked weakness of both arms, worse distally in the hands, with mild weakness of the legs. Sensation is patchy below C5, sacral sensation is preserved, and he has urinary retention. Cervical radiographs show severe degenerative spondylosis without fracture.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Anterior cord syndrome", "Posterior cord syndrome", "Cauda equina syndrome", "Central cord syndrome", "Brown-Sequard syndrome"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "acute traumatic central cord syndrome after hyperextension in an older adult", "keyTakeaway": "Hyperextension injury in older adult with cervical spondylosis; arm (hand) weakness > leg weakness, sacral sparing = central cord syndrome; keep MAP 85-90.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Central cord syndrome
before.explanation: Central cord syndrome is correct: hyperextension of a spondylotic cervical spine, typically in an older adult after a forward fall, compresses the central cord, producing upper-extremity weakness greater than lower-extremity weakness (distal arm fibers lie centrally in the corticospinal tract), variable sensory loss, sacral sparing, and bladder dysfunction. The 2013 AANS/CNS guideline on acute traumatic central cord syndrome recommends ICU or monitored care with mean arterial pressure maintained at 85-90 mm Hg for the first week, MRI,, and selected early decompression. Anterior cord syndrome causes bilateral motor loss and pain/temperature loss with preserved proprioception. Brown-Sequard causes ipsilateral weakness and proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss. Cauda equina syndrome produces lower motor neuron leg findings with saddle anesthesia. Takeaway: older spondylotic neck + hyperextension + arms weaker than legs = central cord syndrome.

references.label: Aarabi B et al. Management of acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS). Neurosurgery 2013

before.scenario: A 35-year-old competitive bodybuilder who eats a high-protein diet and takes creatine supplements has a serum creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL on routine testing; creatinine-based eGFR is 56 mL/min/1.73 m2. He has no hypertension or diabetes, urinalysis is normal, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 8 mg/g. Repeat creatinine 3 months later is unchanged. Renal ultrasonography is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next test to assess his kidney function?
before.options: {"options": ["Serum cystatin C to calculate a combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR", "Serum creatine kinase every month", "Renal biopsy", "24-hour urine protein", "Renal artery Doppler ultrasonography"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "cystatin C-based eGFR to confirm CKD in a muscular adult", "keyTakeaway": "When creatinine eGFR may be inaccurate (high muscle mass, creatine, diet) or to confirm CKD at eGFR 45-59 without albuminuria: measure cystatin C, use eGFRcr-cys.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Serum cystatin C to calculate a combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR
before.explanation: Cystatin C is correct: the KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline recommends measuring cystatin C and using the combined creatinine-cystatin C equation (eGFRcr-cys) when creatinine-based eGFR may be inaccurate, as with high muscle mass, high protein intake, or creatine supplements, all of which raise serum creatinine without reduced GFR, and when confirming CKD at eGFR 45-59 mL/min/1.73 m2 without albuminuria. Cystatin C is less affected by muscle mass; measured GFR (iohexol clearance) is an option when greater accuracy is needed. Renal biopsy is unwarranted with normal urinalysis, albuminuria, and imaging. CK identifies muscle injury, not GFR. A 24-hour urine protein adds little when albumin-to-creatinine ratio is normal. Renal artery Doppler evaluates renovascular hypertension, which he does not have. Takeaway: suspect creatinine overestimates kidney dysfunction (muscle, creatine, diet): use cystatin C and eGFRcr-cys.

references.label: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease. Kidney Int 2024

before.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia has 2 weeks of fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and dark urine. She is pale and mildly jaundiced with splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL (3 months ago, 12.5 g/dL), reticulocyte count is 9%, LDH is elevated, haptoglobin is undetectable, and indirect bilirubin is elevated. Peripheral smear shows many spherocytes and no schistocytes. Platelet count is normal.
before.question: Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the cause of her anemia?
before.options: {"options": ["Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity", "Osmotic fragility test", "Hemoglobin electrophoresis", "ADAMTS13 activity", "Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for IgG with or without C3"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "direct antiglobulin test confirming warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia", "keyTakeaway": "Hemolysis + spherocytes, esp. with CLL/SLE: DAT positive for IgG (+/- C3) = warm AIHA; prednisone 1 mg/kg first line; HS has negative DAT.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for IgG with or without C3
before.explanation: DAT positive for IgG is correct: hemolysis (high reticulocytes, high LDH and indirect bilirubin, undetectable haptoglobin) with spherocytes in a patient with CLL, a common cause of secondary warm AIHA, points to warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The 2020 First International Consensus Meeting recommendations on AIHA state that diagnosis requires evidence of hemolysis plus a positive DAT, typically IgG with or without C3 in warm AIHA (C3 alone suggests cold agglutinin disease); first-line treatment is prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, with rituximab for relapse or refractory disease. Osmotic fragility identifies hereditary spherocytosis, which also has spherocytes but a negative DAT and a family history. Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies. G6PD deficiency causes bite cells and Heinz bodies after oxidant stress. ADAMTS13 is for TTP, which has schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. Takeaway: hemolysis + spherocytes + CLL = warm AIHA; confirm with DAT (IgG), treat with prednisone.

references.label: Jäger U et al. Diagnosis and treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia in adults: Recommendations from the First International Consensus Meeting. Blood Rev 2020

before.scenario: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 28%) and stage 4 chronic kidney disease has NYHA class II symptoms. She takes sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, and furosemide. Blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Today potassium is 5.4 mEq/L and eGFR is 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, both unchanged from 3 months ago. Her cardiologist is reviewing whether to add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate decision regarding mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Start spironolactone 25 mg daily and recheck potassium in 3 months", "Start eplerenone 50 mg daily", "Start spironolactone 12.5 mg daily and stop furosemide", "Start spironolactone 25 mg daily", "Do not start a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist because eGFR is below 30 and potassium is above 5.0"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "withholding mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist when eGFR is below 30 or potassium exceeds 5.0", "keyTakeaway": "MRA in HFrEF only if eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and K <5.0 mEq/L; otherwise withhold because of hyperkalemia risk.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Do not start a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist because eGFR is below 30 and potassium is above 5.0
before.explanation: Not starting an MRA is correct. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline recommends spironolactone or eplerenone in HFrEF only when eGFR is greater than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and potassium is less than 5.0 mEq/L, with potassium and creatinine checked within about 1 week of starting and then often; in other patients, life-threatening hyperkalemia outweighs benefit. Spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone 50 mg in this woman would be unsafe at any dose. Stopping furosemide to make room for spironolactone removes a potassium-wasting drug and makes hyperkalemia worse. Rechecking potassium 3 months after starting is far too late even in eligible patients. Takeaway: MRA in HFrEF requires eGFR >30 and K <5.0, with close lab follow-up; older adults with CKD are at highest risk.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis has no history of ascites, bleeding, or encephalopathy. Screening endoscopy shows large esophageal varices without red wale signs. Blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min. He has no asthma. Platelets are 92,000/mm3, and liver stiffness is 32 kPa.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Pantoprazole 40 mg daily", "Spironolactone 100 mg daily", "Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily", "Carvedilol 6.25 mg once daily, increased to 6.25 mg twice daily as tolerated", "Isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg daily as monotherapy"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "carvedilol to prevent decompensation in cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension", "keyTakeaway": "Compensated cirrhosis with CSPH or large varices: nonselective beta-blocker, carvedilol preferred (6.25 mg daily to 6.25 mg twice daily).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Carvedilol 6.25 mg once daily, increased to 6.25 mg twice daily as tolerated
before.explanation: Carvedilol is correct. The 2024 AASLD portal hypertension practice guidance recommends a nonselective beta-blocker, with carvedilol preferred, for patients with compensated cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension to prevent decompensation; for large varices, it is the preferred alternative to band ligation for preventing a first bleed. Carvedilol starts at 6.25 mg daily and is increased to 6.25 mg twice daily (12.5 mg/day) if systolic BP stays above 90 mm Hg. Cardioselective metoprolol does not lower portal pressure enough. Nitrate monotherapy is ineffective and may harm. PPIs do not prevent variceal bleeding. Spironolactone treats ascites, which he does not have. Takeaway: CSPH or large varices in compensated cirrhosis = carvedilol 6.25 mg daily to 12.5 mg/day.

references.label: Kaplan DE et al. AASLD Practice Guidance on risk stratification and management of portal hypertension and varices in cirrhosis. Hepatology 2024

before.scenario: A 34-year-old woman with newly diagnosed systemic lupus erythematosus is starting hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily; she weighs 70 kg. She has normal kidney function, no tamoxifen use, and no retinal disease. She asks how her eyes will be monitored.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate screening plan?
before.options: {"options": ["Baseline eye examination within the first year, then annual screening with automated visual fields and SD-OCT starting after 5 years of use", "No eye examinations are needed at a dose below 5 mg/kg", "Monthly visual acuity checks during the first year", "Annual Amsler grid self-testing only", "Fundus photography every 5 years"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening schedule", "keyTakeaway": "Hydroxychloroquine: dose <=5 mg/kg real body weight; baseline eye exam, then annual SD-OCT + visual fields after 5 years (sooner with risk factors).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Baseline eye examination within the first year, then annual screening with automated visual fields and SD-OCT starting after 5 years of use
before.explanation: Baseline examination within the first year, then annual screening after 5 years, is correct. The 2016 AAO revised recommendations advise a baseline fundus examination to exclude maculopathy, then annual screening beginning after 5 years for patients without major risk factors, using automated visual fields plus spectral-domain OCT. Annual screening starts earlier with risk factors such as dose above 5 mg/kg real weight, kidney disease, tamoxifen, or preexisting macular disease. Her dose (about 4.3 mg/kg) is within the recommended maximum, but a safe dose lowers risk and does not remove it. Amsler grid testing and fundus photography are insensitive for early toxicity. Monthly acuity checks detect damage late. Takeaway: HCQ = dose ≤5 mg/kg real weight, baseline exam, then annual SD-OCT plus visual fields after 5 years.

references.label: Marmor MF et al. Recommendations on Screening for Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy (2016 Revision). Ophthalmology 2016

before.scenario: A 24-year-old woman uses a 21/7 combined oral contraceptive (ethinyl estradiol 30 mcg/levonorgestrel). She calls on day 10 of her pack because she forgot the day 8 and day 9 pills; she last took an active pill on day 7, 72 hours ago. She had unprotected intercourse 2 days ago, during week 2. Earlier pills in this pack were taken correctly.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?
before.options: {"options": ["Take one missed pill now, continue the pack, and use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive active pills are taken", "Take all missed pills at once and no backup is needed", "Take emergency contraception and stop the pills", "Double the daily dose for the rest of the pack", "Stop the pack and start a new pack after a 7-day break"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "two missed combined oral contraceptive pills in week 2", "keyTakeaway": "Two or more missed combined pills: take the latest missed pill now, continue daily, backup or abstinence until 7 consecutive active pills; EC if missed in week 1 with unprotected sex.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Take one missed pill now, continue the pack, and use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive active pills are taken
before.explanation: Taking one pill now, continuing the pack, and using backup for 7 days is correct. The 2024 CDC US Selected Practice Recommendations treat two or more missed combined pills (48 hours or more since the last pill) by taking the most recent missed pill as soon as possible, discarding the other, continuing daily pills (even two in one day), and using condoms or abstaining until 7 consecutive active pills are taken. If the missed pills were in the last week of hormones, the hormone-free interval is skipped. Emergency contraception is considered when pills were missed in week 1 or late in the previous cycle with unprotected sex; after 7 correct pills in week 1, ovulation is unlikely, so it is not routinely needed here. Stopping the pack or a 7-day break raises ovulation risk. Taking all missed pills at once is unnecessary, and no backup is wrong. Doubling the daily dose is not recommended. Takeaway: 2+ missed COCs = take one now, continue, backup 7 days.

references.label: Curtis KM et al. U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024. MMWR Recomm Rep 2024

before.scenario: A 49-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer has taken tamoxifen for 1 year. She has 10 to 12 hot flashes daily that disrupt sleep. She has no history of seizures, uncontrolled hypertension, or bipolar disorder. She wants pharmacologic treatment. Her oncologist advises against hormone therapy.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Fluoxetine 20 mg daily", "Bupropion 150 mg daily", "Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily, increased to 75 mg daily", "Conjugated estrogens 0.3 mg daily", "Paroxetine 7.5 mg nightly"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "nonhormonal therapy for vasomotor symptoms in a woman taking tamoxifen", "keyTakeaway": "Vasomotor symptoms on tamoxifen: venlafaxine (or gabapentin, citalopram, escitalopram); avoid strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily, increased to 75 mg daily
before.explanation: Venlafaxine is correct. The 2023 Menopause Society nonhormone therapy position statement recommends SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentin, fezolinetant, and oxybutynin for vasomotor symptoms. In women taking tamoxifen, venlafaxine (or citalopram, escitalopram, or gabapentin) is preferred because it only weakly inhibits CYP2D6. Paroxetine and fluoxetine are strong CYP2D6 inhibitors that reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen and may reduce its anticancer effect, so they are unsafe here, even though low-dose paroxetine is FDA approved for hot flashes in other women. Estrogen is contraindicated in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Bupropion is also a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor and is not an evidence-based hot flash therapy. Takeaway: hot flashes on tamoxifen = venlafaxine or gabapentin; avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine, and bupropion.

references.label: The 2023 nonhormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society. Menopause 2023

before.scenario: A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 12 years has an HbA1c of 9.6% despite metformin 1000 mg twice daily and semaglutide 1 mg weekly. Fasting glucose readings are 190 to 230 mg/dL. She weighs 80 kg, has normal kidney function, and has had no hypoglycemia. She lives with her husband, is cognitively intact, and can check fingerstick glucose. The plan is to add basal insulin.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate starting regimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Regular insulin sliding scale before meals only", "Insulin glargine 0.8 units/kg (64 units) daily", "Stop metformin and semaglutide and start glargine 10 units", "Premixed 70/30 insulin 30 units twice daily", "Insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime, increased by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches target"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "starting and titrating basal insulin in type 2 diabetes", "keyTakeaway": "Start basal insulin at 10 units/day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day, titrate (e.g., +2 units every 3 days) to fasting goal; continue metformin and GLP-1 RA.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime, increased by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose reaches target
before.explanation: Glargine 10 units with titration of 2 units every 3 days is correct. The ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Section 9) recommends starting basal insulin at 10 units/day or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg/day, then titrating, for example by 2 units every 3 days, to a fasting target (often 80 to 130 mg/dL, individualized), while reducing the dose by 10% to 20% for hypoglycemia. Metformin and the GLP-1 receptor agonist are continued for glycemic and weight benefits. A starting dose of 0.8 units/kg is too high and risks hypoglycemia, especially in an older adult. Sliding-scale insulin alone is discouraged as reactive and ineffective. Premixed insulin at this dose is too aggressive as a first step. Stopping metformin and semaglutide removes effective agents. Takeaway: add basal insulin at 10 units or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, titrate to fasting target, and keep other agents.

references.label: ADA Professional Practice Committee. 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026

before.scenario: A 76-year-old man was admitted 3 hours ago with an acute left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke and received IV thrombolysis. He is alert and has right hemiparesis and mild dysarthria. He asks for a sandwich and water. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before he eats or drinks?
before.options: {"options": ["Allow a regular diet because he is alert", "Start total parenteral nutrition", "Place a percutaneous gastrostomy tube today", "A formal dysphagia screen before any oral intake, including medications", "Allow thin liquids only, as tolerated"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "dysphagia screening before oral intake after acute stroke", "keyTakeaway": "Acute stroke: dysphagia screen before any oral intake or oral medication; SLP evaluation if failed; NG tube early, PEG only if persistent (2-3 weeks).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: A formal dysphagia screen before any oral intake, including medications
before.explanation: A dysphagia screen before any oral intake is correct. The AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline (2026) recommends dysphagia screening before patients start eating, drinking, or taking oral medications, because dysphagia is common after stroke and silent aspiration causes pneumonia. Patients who fail the screen get a speech-language pathology evaluation and an instrumental study if needed. Allowing liquids or a regular diet before screening risks aspiration, even in alert patients with mild dysarthria. Gastrostomy is considered only when dysphagia persists beyond about 2 to 3 weeks; nasogastric feeding is used in the meantime. Parenteral nutrition is not needed when the gut works. Takeaway: every stroke patient gets a dysphagia screen before anything by mouth.

references.label: Prabhakaran S et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (AHA/ASA). Stroke 2026

before.scenario: A 77-year-old woman has taken lorazepam 1 mg three times daily for 8 years for anxiety and sleep. She had two falls in the past 6 months and wants to stop the medication. She has no seizure history or alcohol use. She is willing to start cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to discontinuation?
before.options: {"options": ["Stop lorazepam today and start zolpidem", "Stop lorazepam today and monitor for withdrawal", "Switch to alprazolam and stop it after 2 weeks", "Reduce the dose by 50% each week", "Reduce the total daily dose by about 5% to 10% every 2 to 4 weeks, adjusted to symptoms"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "gradual benzodiazepine taper in an older adult", "keyTakeaway": "Long-term benzodiazepine taper: reduce by 5-10% every 2-4 weeks (max ~25% every 2 weeks), pause as needed, combine with CBT; never stop abruptly.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Reduce the total daily dose by about 5% to 10% every 2 to 4 weeks, adjusted to symptoms
before.explanation: Reducing the dose by about 5% to 10% every 2 to 4 weeks is correct. The 2025 joint clinical practice guideline on benzodiazepine tapering (ASAM and partner societies) recommends tapering long-term users gradually, usually by 5% to 10% of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks and generally no more than 25% every 2 weeks, with pauses for withdrawal symptoms and supported by psychological therapy such as CBT-I. Older adults gain fewer falls and better cognition with tapering. Abrupt discontinuation risks seizures, delirium, and severe withdrawal. Switching to a Z-drug substitutes another sedative-hypnotic with similar fall risk. Halving weekly is too fast after 8 years of use. Switching to short-acting alprazolam increases rebound and withdrawal. Takeaway: long-term benzodiazepine = slow taper of 5-10% every 2-4 weeks with CBT support.

references.label: Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (ASAM and partner societies). J Gen Intern Med 2025

before.scenario: A 15-year-old boy is seen for a sports preparticipation examination. He has no complaints. He lives with his parents and is doing well in school. His history is unremarkable, and his examination is normal. The clinic has the staff and systems to confirm diagnoses and arrange treatment and follow-up.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding depression screening?
before.options: {"options": ["Screen with a urine drug screen instead", "Screen only after age 18 years", "Screen for major depressive disorder with a validated tool such as the PHQ-A", "Screen only if the parents report mood changes", "Do not screen because he has no symptoms"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "routine depression screening in adolescents", "keyTakeaway": "USPSTF 2022: screen all adolescents 12-18 years for MDD with a validated tool (e.g., PHQ-A) when follow-up systems are in place (grade B).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Screen for major depressive disorder with a validated tool such as the PHQ-A
before.explanation: Screening with a validated tool such as the PHQ-A is correct. The 2022 USPSTF recommendation advises screening all adolescents 12 to 18 years old for major depressive disorder (grade B), using tools such as the PHQ for Adolescents, with systems for accurate diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Relying on parent report or symptoms misses many affected teens, who often hide symptoms. Adult screening recommendations apply after 18, but adolescents are already included. A urine drug screen is not a depression screening tool. Positive results need clinical evaluation, including suicide risk assessment, and treatment such as psychotherapy or an SSRI. Takeaway: screen every 12- to 18-year-old for depression with a validated tool.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Depression and Suicide Risk in Children and Adolescents: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2022

before.scenario: A 63-year-old man with diabetic chronic kidney disease, stage G4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2), has fatigue and diffuse bone aches. He takes no calcium, vitamin D, or phosphate binders. Laboratory studies are pending.
before.question: Which of the following laboratory patterns is most likely?
before.options: {"options": ["Normal calcium, low phosphorus, high PTH, high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D", "Low-normal calcium, high phosphorus, high PTH, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D", "High calcium, low phosphorus, high PTH, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D", "Low calcium, low phosphorus, low PTH, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D", "High calcium, high phosphorus, low PTH, high 25-hydroxyvitamin D"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "laboratory pattern of secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD-mineral bone disorder", "keyTakeaway": "CKD-MBD: phosphate retention, low calcitriol, high FGF-23 and PTH, low or low-normal calcium; monitor Ca, P, PTH, ALP from G3a.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Low-normal calcium, high phosphorus, high PTH, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
before.explanation: Low-normal calcium, high phosphorus, high PTH, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D is correct. In advanced CKD, phosphate retention, rising FGF-23, reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D, and lower calcium absorption all drive secondary hyperparathyroidism. The KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline update recommends monitoring calcium, phosphate, PTH, and alkaline phosphatase from stage G3a on, and checking 25(OH)D with repletion as for the general population. High calcium with low phosphorus and high PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism. High calcium and phosphorus with low PTH suggests vitamin D toxicity or granulomatous disease. Low calcium, phosphorus, and PTH suggests hypoparathyroidism with poor intake, which is not typical. High calcitriol with low phosphorus does not fit CKD. Takeaway: CKD-MBD = high phosphorus, high PTH, low or low-normal calcium, low vitamin D.

references.label: Ketteler M et al. Executive summary of the 2017 KDIGO CKD-MBD Guideline Update. Kidney Int 2017

before.scenario: A newborn delivered at term is examined in the nursery. The external genitalia show a phallus with a proximal (penoscrotal) urethral opening and chordee. Neither testis is palpable in the scrotum, inguinal canals, or perineum. The infant is otherwise well, and vital signs are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step based on these findings?
before.options: {"options": ["Referral for orchiopexy at 1 year", "Reassurance and recheck of the testes at 6 months", "Circumcision before hospital discharge", "Urgent evaluation for a disorder of sex development, including karyotype and electrolytes", "Hormone therapy with testosterone before any testing"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "hypospadias with bilateral nonpalpable testes requiring DSD evaluation", "keyTakeaway": "Bilateral nonpalpable testes or undescended testis with hypospadias: urgent DSD evaluation (karyotype, electrolytes, 17-OHP for CAH); no circumcision.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Urgent evaluation for a disorder of sex development, including karyotype and electrolytes
before.explanation: Urgent evaluation for a disorder of sex development is correct. The AUA cryptorchidism guideline states that newborns with bilateral nonpalpable testes, or with undescended testes plus hypospadias or other ambiguity, should be evaluated urgently for DSD, because congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX infant can mimic this and cause life-threatening salt wasting. Evaluation includes karyotype, electrolytes, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and specialist consultation. Reassurance and rechecking at 6 months is appropriate only for an isolated, unilateral palpable undescended testis in a boy with normal genitalia. Circumcision is avoided in hypospadias because the foreskin is used in repair. Orchiopexy timing does not come before diagnosis. Hormone therapy is not given before evaluation. Takeaway: hypospadias + nonpalpable testes = urgent DSD workup (rule out CAH).

references.label: Kolon TF et al. Evaluation and Treatment of Cryptorchidism: AUA Guideline. J Urol 2014

before.scenario: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity has passed a second kidney stone. Stone analysis shows 100% uric acid. Urine pH on repeated testing is 5.2, and 24-hour urine uric acid is normal. Serum uric acid is normal. eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73 m2 and potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. He has no gout.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent recurrence?
before.options: {"options": ["Calcium carbonate supplements", "Allopurinol as first-line therapy", "Potassium citrate to raise urine pH to about 6.0 to 6.5", "Hydrochlorothiazide", "Acetohydroxamic acid"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "potassium citrate for uric acid nephrolithiasis", "keyTakeaway": "Uric acid stones: potassium citrate to urine pH 6.0-6.5 and high fluid intake; allopurinol only if recurrent or hyperuricosuric.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Potassium citrate to raise urine pH to about 6.0 to 6.5
before.explanation: Potassium citrate is correct. The 2026 AUA medical management of kidney stones guideline recommends potassium citrate for uric acid stones to raise urine pH to about 6.0 to 6.5, because low urine pH, common with diabetes and obesity, is the main cause of uric acid stones; alkalinization can also dissolve existing stones. Allopurinol is not first line and is used only for recurrence despite alkalinization or with hyperuricosuria. Thiazides treat hypercalciuria in calcium stones. Acetohydroxamic acid is for struvite (infection) stones. Calcium supplements do not prevent uric acid stones. Fluids are also needed. Takeaway: uric acid stones = alkalinize urine with potassium citrate (pH 6.0-6.5) plus fluids.

before.scenario: A 74-year-old woman had a right total knee arthroplasty 3 years ago. For 6 weeks she has had increasing knee pain and swelling, but no fever. She is hemodynamically stable. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion; there is no sinus tract. ESR is 58 mm/h and CRP is 4.2 mg/dL. Radiographs show no loosening or fracture. She has not taken antibiotics.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Empiric IV vancomycin, then arthrocentesis in 2 weeks", "Technetium bone scan", "Reassurance and repeat ESR and CRP in 3 months", "Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, and culture before antibiotics", "Empiric oral cephalexin for 6 weeks"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "arthrocentesis before antibiotics for suspected prosthetic joint infection", "keyTakeaway": "Suspected PJI: ESR/CRP, then arthrocentesis (cell count, differential, cultures) before antibiotics in stable patients; avoid empiric antibiotics before sampling.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, and culture before antibiotics
before.explanation: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid studies before antibiotics is correct. The IDSA prosthetic joint infection guideline recommends ESR and CRP in suspected PJI, and diagnostic arthrocentesis (total cell count, differential, aerobic and anaerobic culture) when infection is suspected, unless surgery is already planned; antibiotics should be held for at least 2 weeks before sampling when the patient is stable, to improve culture yield. Synovial WBC and neutrophil percentage thresholds for chronic PJI are much lower than for native joints. Empiric antibiotics before cultures, oral or IV, make organism identification and the right surgical plan much harder. Bone scans are not routine. Reassurance and repeat markers delay diagnosis. Takeaway: suspected PJI + elevated ESR/CRP = arthrocentesis with cell count and culture before antibiotics.

references.label: Osmon DR et al. Diagnosis and management of prosthetic joint infection: IDSA clinical practice guidelines. Clin Infect Dis 2013

before.scenario: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of dysuria and fever and new confusion. Temperature is 39.3 C, pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. IV access is established.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Obtain CT of the abdomen before any treatment", "Wait for urine culture results before giving antibiotics", "Obtain blood cultures and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, and start balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg", "Start dopamine as the first-line vasopressor before fluids", "Give oral ciprofloxacin and observe"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "cultures and antimicrobials within 1 hour for septic shock", "keyTakeaway": "Septic shock: blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, norepinephrine for MAP >=65.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Obtain blood cultures and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, and start balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg
before.explanation: Cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid are correct. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guidelines (2021, with the 2026 update) recommend giving antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour, in possible septic shock, after obtaining blood cultures if this does not delay therapy, plus at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid (balanced solutions preferred) within the first 3 hours for hypoperfusion, and norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor for MAP of at least 65 mm Hg. Waiting for urine culture results delays lifesaving treatment. Oral antibiotics are inadequate in shock. Dopamine is not first line and causes more arrhythmias. Imaging may help with source control but should not delay antibiotics. Takeaway: septic shock = cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, norepinephrine.

before.scenario: An 84-year-old man with end-stage heart failure (NYHA class IV), recurrent hospitalizations despite optimal therapy, and progressive weight loss tells his primary care physician assistant that he wants to stop hospital visits and focus on comfort at home. He has Medicare Part A. His family supports his choice.
before.question: Which of the following is required for him to begin the Medicare hospice benefit?
before.options: {"options": ["Certification by a physician that his life expectancy is 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course", "Documentation that he has refused all medications", "A prognosis of 30 days or less", "A do-not-resuscitate order signed before admission", "Placement in a skilled nursing facility"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "physician certification of terminal prognosis for hospice eligibility", "keyTakeaway": "Medicare hospice: physician certification of terminal illness (prognosis <=6 months if usual course) + patient election; DNR and stopping all meds not required.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Certification by a physician that his life expectancy is 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course
before.explanation: Physician certification of a life expectancy of 6 months or less is correct. Under Medicare regulations (42 CFR 418.22), hospice eligibility requires written certification by a physician (the hospice medical director and the attending physician, if any, for the first period) that the patient is terminally ill, meaning a prognosis of 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course, with a brief narrative supporting it. The patient elects hospice and waives curative Medicare coverage for the terminal illness. He may still take medications for symptom control, including heart failure drugs. A 30-day prognosis is not required. A DNR order is not a condition of eligibility. Hospice is delivered wherever the patient lives, including at home. Takeaway: Medicare hospice = physician certification of prognosis ≤6 months; DNR not required.

before.scenario: A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after learning that her husband died. She has substernal chest pressure and dyspnea. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse is 102/min. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2 through V5. High-sensitivity troponin is mildly elevated. Emergency coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease. Left ventriculography shows akinesis of the mid and apical segments with a hyperkinetic base, extending beyond a single coronary artery territory.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Acute viral myocarditis", "Anterior STEMI from left anterior descending artery occlusion", "Takotsubo syndrome", "Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina", "Acute type A aortic dissection"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy with apical ballooning", "keyTakeaway": "Stress, postmenopausal woman, STEMI-like ECG, nonobstructive coronaries, and apical ballooning beyond one territory: takotsubo syndrome.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Takotsubo syndrome
before.explanation: Takotsubo syndrome is correct. The AHA scientific statement on MINOCA lists takotsubo as a key alternative diagnosis in patients with infarct-like presentation and no obstructive coronary disease: it typically follows emotional or physical stress in postmenopausal women and shows transient regional wall-motion abnormality (classically apical ballooning) that extends beyond one coronary territory, with recovery over weeks. An LAD occlusion is excluded by the angiogram. Myocarditis usually follows a viral prodrome and causes patchy injury on cardiac MRI rather than this apical-basal pattern. Vasospastic angina causes transient episodes, often at night, without a fixed ballooning pattern. Aortic dissection causes tearing pain and would not produce this ventriculogram. Cardiac MRI can confirm and follow recovery.

references.label: Tamis-Holland JE et al. Contemporary Diagnosis and Management of Patients With MINOCA: AHA Scientific Statement. Circulation 2019

before.scenario: A 72-year-old man with coronary artery disease takes atorvastatin 80 mg daily. Ten days ago he started clarithromycin for sinusitis. He now has diffuse, symmetric thigh and shoulder pain, difficulty rising from a chair, and dark urine. Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F). Proximal muscles are tender with 4/5 strength.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Check TSH and continue atorvastatin until the result returns", "Add coenzyme Q10 and continue atorvastatin", "Continue atorvastatin and recheck a lipid panel in 4 weeks", "Switch atorvastatin to rosuvastatin 40 mg today", "Stop atorvastatin and measure creatine kinase, serum creatinine, and urinalysis"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "stopping the statin and checking CK for severe statin-associated muscle symptoms", "keyTakeaway": "Severe statin muscle symptoms (weakness, dark urine): stop the statin, check CK, creatinine, and urinalysis; look for interacting drugs like CYP3A4 inhibitors.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Stop atorvastatin and measure creatine kinase, serum creatinine, and urinalysis
before.explanation: Stopping the statin and checking CK, creatinine, and urinalysis is correct. The 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline advises that severe statin-associated muscle symptoms, especially weakness or dark urine, warrant measuring CK and assessing for rhabdomyolysis and kidney injury, and stopping the statin. Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and raises atorvastatin levels. Continuing the statin and checking lipids ignores possible rhabdomyolysis. Switching immediately to high-dose rosuvastatin is premature before CK and kidney function are known. Coenzyme Q10 is not recommended as a treatment. TSH can be checked because hypothyroidism predisposes to myopathy, but the statin should not be continued while serious muscle injury is possible.

references.label: Grundy SM et al. 2018 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol. Circulation 2019

before.scenario: An 84-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation takes digoxin 0.25 mg daily. After 3 days of vomiting she is brought to the emergency department with confusion and yellow-tinged vision. Pulse is 38/min and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a slow regular ventricular rhythm and frequent multifocal premature ventricular complexes. Potassium is 6.1 mEq/L and creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). Serum digoxin concentration is 4.2 ng/mL.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Emergency hemodialysis to remove digoxin", "IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes", "Sodium polystyrene sulfonate orally as the only therapy", "Digoxin-specific immune Fab fragments IV", "Observation with repeat digoxin level in 6 hours"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "digoxin-specific immune Fab for life-threatening digoxin toxicity", "keyTakeaway": "Digoxin toxicity with dysrhythmia, shock, or K >5-6 mEq/L: give digoxin Fab; digoxin is not dialyzable.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Digoxin-specific immune Fab fragments IV
before.explanation: Digoxin-specific immune Fab is correct. The 2023 AHA focused update on poisoning recommends digoxin Fab for digoxin poisoning with life-threatening dysrhythmias, shock, or marked hyperkalemia; this patient has symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, ventricular ectopy, potassium above 6, and AKI that slows digoxin clearance. Hemodialysis does not remove digoxin because of its large volume of distribution, although it may help hyperkalemia from kidney failure. Amiodarone raises digoxin levels and can worsen conduction block. A potassium binder alone is too slow and does not reverse digoxin. Observation is unsafe with hemodynamic instability. Note that hyperkalemia in digoxin toxicity reflects Na-K-ATPase blockade and improves after Fab.

references.label: Lavonas EJ et al. 2023 AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning. Circulation 2023

before.scenario: A 58-year-old man has had palpitations for 5 days. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 96/min after oral metoprolol. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg and he has no chest pain or dyspnea. He has hypertension only (CHA2DS2-VASc score 1) and takes no anticoagulant. He would like rhythm control.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to cardioversion?
before.options: {"options": ["IV amiodarone loading today for chemical cardioversion without anticoagulation", "Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before cardioversion, or transesophageal echocardiography to exclude thrombus, then anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks afterward", "Immediate electrical cardioversion today without anticoagulation", "IV heparin bolus, electrical cardioversion today, then no further anticoagulation", "Electrical cardioversion today followed by aspirin 81 mg daily"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "3 weeks of anticoagulation or TEE before cardioversion of atrial fibrillation lasting longer than 48 hours", "keyTakeaway": "Stable AF >=48 hours: 3 weeks anticoagulation (or TEE) before cardioversion and >=4 weeks after, by either electrical or drug cardioversion.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before cardioversion, or transesophageal echocardiography to exclude thrombus, then anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks afterward
before.explanation: Three weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a TEE-guided strategy, followed by at least 4 weeks of anticoagulation, is correct. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline states that when AF has lasted 48 hours or longer (or duration is unknown) in a stable patient, cardioversion requires 3 weeks of uninterrupted anticoagulation or TEE to exclude left atrial thrombus, and anticoagulation should continue at least 4 weeks afterward regardless of stroke risk score because atrial stunning persists. Immediate cardioversion without anticoagulation risks embolism. Aspirin is not adequate stroke prevention. A single heparin bolus without post-cardioversion anticoagulation leaves the stunning period unprotected. Pharmacologic cardioversion with amiodarone carries the same embolic risk as electrical cardioversion.

references.label: Joglar JA et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation 2024

before.scenario: A 3-year-old girl is brought for a well-child visit. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has no history of kidney, heart, or urologic disease. She takes no medications. Her height and weight are at the 50th percentile. Her parents ask whether her blood pressure needs to be checked.
before.question: Which of the following is the recommended approach to blood pressure screening in this child?
before.options: {"options": ["Begin blood pressure measurement at age 13 years", "Measure blood pressure at this visit and then annually", "Measure blood pressure only if her BMI reaches the 95th percentile", "Measure blood pressure at every health care encounter since birth", "Begin blood pressure measurement at age 6 years"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "annual blood pressure measurement starting at age 3 in healthy children", "keyTakeaway": "Healthy children: BP annually from age 3; at every visit if risk factors; under 3 only if risk factors (e.g., prematurity, CHD, kidney disease).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Measure blood pressure at this visit and then annually
before.explanation: Measuring blood pressure now and annually is correct. The 2017 AAP clinical practice guideline for high blood pressure in children recommends annual blood pressure measurement in all children starting at age 3 years. Children with risk factors such as obesity, kidney disease, diabetes, aortic arch obstruction, or medications that raise blood pressure should be measured at every encounter, and children younger than 3 years are measured only when they have risk factors such as prematurity, congenital heart disease, or kidney disease. Waiting until age 6 or 13 delays detection of secondary hypertension. Limiting screening to obese children misses others. Measuring at every encounter from birth applies only to infants and toddlers with risk factors.

references.label: Flynn JT et al. Clinical Practice Guideline for Screening and Management of High Blood Pressure in Children and Adolescents (AAP). Pediatrics 2017

before.scenario: A 70-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 25%) has had 2 weeks of worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea requiring 3 pillows, and a 4-kg weight gain after running out of furosemide. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg and pulse is 98/min. He has bilateral pitting edema to the knees.
before.question: Which of the following additional physical examination findings is most likely in this patient?
before.options: {"options": ["Pulsus paradoxus of 18 mm Hg with distant heart sounds", "Wide pulse pressure with bounding peripheral pulses", "Fixed splitting of S2 with a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border", "Opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex", "Jugular venous pressure of 14 cm H2O with an S3 gallop"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "elevated jugular venous pressure with S3 in decompensated heart failure", "keyTakeaway": "Decompensated HFrEF with volume overload: elevated JVP (positive abdominojugular reflux), S3, orthopnea, edema.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Jugular venous pressure of 14 cm H2O with an S3 gallop
before.explanation: Elevated JVP with an S3 is correct. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline emphasizes bedside assessment of congestion: elevated jugular venous pressure (often with a positive abdominojugular reflux), orthopnea, edema, and an S3 reflect high filling pressures in decompensated HFrEF. Pulsus paradoxus with distant heart sounds suggests cardiac tamponade. Fixed S2 splitting with a pulmonic flow murmur indicates an atrial septal defect. Wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses suggests aortic regurgitation or a high-output state. An opening snap with a diastolic rumble indicates mitral stenosis. In this patient the findings point to volume overload from diuretic nonadherence, managed with IV loop diuretics.

references.label: Heidenreich PA et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022

before.scenario: A 52-year-old woman has left calf and thigh swelling 3 weeks after an open cholecystectomy. Compression ultrasonography shows an occlusive thrombus in the left femoral vein. She has no history of cancer or prior VTE and is now fully mobile. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, platelets are 240,000/mm3, and she takes no interacting medications. She is not pregnant.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?
before.options: {"options": ["Warfarin alone with a target INR of 2 to 3, without parenteral overlap, for 3 months", "Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily indefinitely", "Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, stopping after 3 months", "Aspirin 81 mg daily for 6 months", "Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for 2 weeks, then stop"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "3 months of a DOAC for proximal DVT provoked by recent surgery", "keyTakeaway": "Proximal DVT provoked by surgery: DOAC (apixaban 10 mg BID x7 days, then 5 mg BID) for 3 months, then stop.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, stopping after 3 months
before.explanation: Apixaban with the 7-day loading phase, stopped at 3 months, is correct. The 2021 CHEST antithrombotic guideline recommends a DOAC over warfarin for VTE without cancer and a 3-month treatment phase for proximal DVT provoked by surgery, because recurrence risk after a major transient risk factor is low; extended therapy is not advised. Indefinite apixaban is for unprovoked or persistent-risk VTE. Warfarin started alone without parenteral overlap is unsafe because early protein C depletion can be prothrombotic, and DOACs are preferred anyway. Aspirin is not adequate primary treatment of acute DVT. Two weeks of enoxaparin is shorter than the recommended 3-month course.

references.label: Stevens SM et al. Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease: Second Update of the CHEST Guideline. Chest 2021

before.scenario: A 64-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden tearing pain between the shoulder blades. Blood pressure is 186/104 mm Hg in both arms and pulse is 108/min. Peripheral pulses are intact and the neurologic examination is normal. CT angiography shows a type B aortic dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery, without malperfusion or rupture. Creatinine is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
before.options: {"options": ["IV hydralazine 20 mg bolus", "Oral amlodipine and outpatient follow-up in 1 week", "IV nitroprusside alone titrated to systolic pressure below 120 mm Hg", "IV esmolol titrated to heart rate below 60/min, then add IV nicardipine if systolic pressure remains above 120 mm Hg", "Emergency open surgical repair of the descending aorta"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "IV beta-blocker before vasodilator in acute type B aortic dissection", "keyTakeaway": "Acute aortic dissection: IV beta-blocker first (HR <60), then vasodilator to SBP <120; uncomplicated type B is medical, complicated type B or any type A is surgical/endovascular.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: IV esmolol titrated to heart rate below 60/min, then add IV nicardipine if systolic pressure remains above 120 mm Hg
before.explanation: IV beta-blockade first, then a vasodilator if needed, is correct. The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline recommends IV beta-blockers to reduce heart rate (target below 60/min) and aortic wall stress (dP/dt), and a systolic pressure goal below 120 mm Hg, adding a vasodilator only after rate control. Nitroprusside or hydralazine alone causes reflex tachycardia that increases shear stress on the dissection flap.
