Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically in an ICU; surgery or endovascular repair is reserved for complications such as malperfusion, rupture, or refractory pain. Oral therapy and outpatient follow-up are unsafe for an acute dissection.

references.label: Isselbacher EM et al. 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease. Circulation 2022

before.scenario: A 34-year-old man has exertional dyspnea and lightheadedness when climbing stairs. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 21 mm, LVEF 70%, and a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 60 mm Hg with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. He takes no medications and has no history of syncope.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Digoxin 0.125 mg daily", "Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily", "Metoprolol succinate titrated to symptom relief", "Lisinopril 10 mg daily", "Nifedipine extended-release 30 mg daily"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "nonvasodilating beta-blocker for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy", "keyTakeaway": "Symptomatic obstructive HCM: start a nonvasodilating beta-blocker; avoid vasodilators, digoxin, and aggressive diuresis.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Metoprolol succinate titrated to symptom relief
before.explanation: Metoprolol is correct. The 2024 AHA/ACC hypertrophic cardiomyopathy guideline recommends a nonvasodilating beta-blocker titrated to effect as first-line therapy for symptomatic obstructive HCM, with verapamil or diltiazem as alternatives; this slows heart rate, prolongs diastolic filling, and lowers the outflow gradient. Diuretics reduce preload and can worsen obstruction. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine and ACE inhibitors are vasodilators that lower afterload and increase the gradient. Digoxin increases contractility and can worsen obstruction. Persistent symptoms on beta-blockade lead to add-on options such as a cardiac myosin inhibitor, disopyramide, or septal reduction therapy.

references.label: Ommen SR et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy. Circulation 2024

before.scenario: A 24-year-old woman has had a heart murmur noted since early childhood. She is active, runs 5 km three times weekly, and has no symptoms. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg and pulse is 64/min. Oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The point of maximal impulse is not displaced and there is no cyanosis or clubbing. Echocardiography is scheduled.
before.question: Which of the following auscultatory findings is most consistent with a small restrictive perimembranous ventricular septal defect?
before.options: {"options": ["Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border", "Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill that does not increase with inspiration", "Continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle", "Fixed splitting of S2 with a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border", "Midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "harsh holosystolic murmur with thrill of a small restrictive ventricular septal defect", "keyTakeaway": "Small VSD: loud harsh holosystolic murmur at the LLSB with thrill; louder does not mean larger, and it does not increase with inspiration.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill that does not increase with inspiration
before.explanation: The harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a thrill is correct. The 2018 AHA/ACC adult congenital heart disease guideline describes small restrictive VSDs as having a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur, often with a thrill, because of the high pressure gradient between the ventricles; these patients have normal chamber size and often need only periodic follow-up. Unlike tricuspid regurgitation, the murmur does not increase with inspiration. A continuous machinery murmur is a patent ductus arteriosus. Fixed splitting of S2 suggests an atrial septal defect. An early diastolic decrescendo murmur suggests aortic regurgitation. A midsystolic click with a late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse.

references.label: Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease. Circulation 2019

before.scenario: A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Pulse is 112/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. She has no leg swelling or pain. A shielded chest radiograph is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?
before.options: {"options": ["D-dimer to rule out pulmonary embolism", "Bilateral lower extremity compression ultrasonography", "Transthoracic echocardiography to make the diagnosis", "Conventional pulmonary angiography", "Ventilation-perfusion lung scintigraphy"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "ventilation-perfusion scan for suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy with a normal chest radiograph", "keyTakeaway": "Suspected PE in pregnancy: leg symptoms -> compression US; otherwise chest radiograph; normal CXR -> V/Q scan; abnormal CXR -> CTPA. Do not use D-dimer.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Ventilation-perfusion lung scintigraphy
before.explanation: Lung scintigraphy (V/Q scan) is correct. The ATS/STR clinical practice guideline for suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy recommends against D-dimer testing, recommends compression ultrasonography only when there are signs of DVT, and recommends a chest radiograph first; when the radiograph is normal, V/Q scanning is preferred over CT pulmonary angiography because it is highly diagnostic and gives lower radiation to maternal breast tissue. CTPA is used when the radiograph is abnormal or the V/Q scan is nondiagnostic. D-dimer rises normally in pregnancy and is not reliable. Leg ultrasonography is low yield without leg symptoms. Pulmonary angiography is invasive and outdated. Echocardiography can show right heart strain but cannot confirm or exclude PE.

references.label: Leung AN et al. An Official ATS/STR Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation of Suspected Pulmonary Embolism in Pregnancy. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011

before.scenario: A 67-year-old man with COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1 45% predicted) was discharged 1 week ago after a hospitalization for an exacerbation. He has quit smoking and uses tiotropium-olodaterol daily with albuterol as needed. He becomes breathless walking 100 meters on level ground. Resting oxygen saturation is 93% on room air and he is clinically stable.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
before.options: {"options": ["Long-term home oxygen therapy", "Defer pulmonary rehabilitation until he has been exacerbation-free for 6 months", "Monthly prophylactic levofloxacin", "Referral to pulmonary rehabilitation starting within 4 weeks of discharge", "Long-term oral prednisone 10 mg daily"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "pulmonary rehabilitation within 4 weeks after a COPD exacerbation hospitalization", "keyTakeaway": "After a COPD exacerbation hospitalization, start pulmonary rehabilitation within 4 weeks of discharge.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Referral to pulmonary rehabilitation starting within 4 weeks of discharge
before.explanation: Pulmonary rehabilitation within 4 weeks of discharge is correct. The GOLD 2026 report recommends pulmonary rehabilitation for patients with high symptom burden and after hospitalization for an exacerbation, starting within 4 weeks of discharge, because it improves dyspnea, exercise capacity, quality of life, and reduces readmission; starting during the hospital stay is not recommended. Waiting 6 months loses that benefit. Long-term oral corticosteroids are not recommended because harms outweigh benefits. Long-term oxygen is indicated for resting PaO2 of 55 mm Hg or less or saturation of 88% or less, not 93%. Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is not a recommended strategy; azithromycin is the macrolide option in selected patients.

references.label: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2026 Report

before.scenario: A 58-year-old man has 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. He never smoked. Fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles are heard. Spirometry shows FEV1 68% predicted, FVC 64% predicted, and FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84, with no significant bronchodilator response.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm a restrictive ventilatory defect?
before.options: {"options": ["Total lung capacity by body plethysmography", "Cardiopulmonary exercise testing", "Peak expiratory flow monitoring at home", "Methacholine challenge test", "Repeat spirometry in 3 months"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "measuring total lung capacity to confirm restriction suggested by spirometry", "keyTakeaway": "Low FVC with normal/high FEV1/FVC suggests restriction, but restriction is confirmed only by TLC below the LLN (plethysmography).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Total lung capacity by body plethysmography
before.explanation: Measuring total lung capacity is correct. The 2022 ERS/ATS technical standard on interpretation of lung function tests states that a low FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio only suggests restriction; restriction is defined by a TLC below the lower limit of normal, measured by body plethysmography or gas dilution, because a low FVC can also reflect air trapping or poor effort. DLCO should also be measured, as it is usually reduced in interstitial lung disease. Methacholine challenge assesses airway hyperresponsiveness for suspected asthma. Repeating spirometry alone cannot confirm restriction. Peak flow monitoring is for asthma variability. Exercise testing evaluates exercise limitation but does not define restriction. High-resolution CT is the next step for suspected fibrosis.

references.label: Stanojevic S et al. ERS/ATS Technical Standard on Interpretive Strategies for Routine Lung Function Tests. Eur Respir J 2022

before.scenario: A 70-year-old woman develops fever of 38.6 C (101.5 F), productive cough, and a new right lower lobe infiltrate on day 6 after hip fracture surgery. She is breathing comfortably on 2 L/min nasal cannula, blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg, and she is not ventilated. She has received no IV antibiotics in the past 90 days. The hospital MRSA prevalence among S. aureus isolates is below 20%. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and she has no drug allergies.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
before.options: {"options": ["Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam plus tobramycin", "Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours", "Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg orally twice daily", "Vancomycin IV alone", "Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy for hospital-acquired pneumonia without MRSA or high-mortality risk factors", "keyTakeaway": "HAP without high mortality risk or MRSA risk: one antipseudomonal agent with MSSA activity (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam); add MRSA and second antipseudomonal only if risk.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours
before.explanation: Piperacillin-tazobactam alone is correct. The 2016 IDSA/ATS hospital-acquired pneumonia guideline recommends, for HAP without high mortality risk (no ventilatory support or septic shock) and without MRSA risk factors (no IV antibiotics in 90 days, MRSA prevalence below 20%), a single agent active against Pseudomonas and MSSA, such as piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, cefepime, levofloxacin, imipenem, or meropenem. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a community-acquired regimen without antipseudomonal coverage. Adding vancomycin and an aminoglycoside is reserved for high mortality risk or recent IV antibiotics. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate lacks Pseudomonas coverage. Vancomycin alone misses gram-negative organisms.

references.label: Kalil AC et al. Management of Adults With Hospital-acquired and Ventilator-associated Pneumonia: 2016 IDSA/ATS Guideline. Clin Infect Dis 2016

before.scenario: A 60-year-old man with newly diagnosed non-Hodgkin lymphoma has 3 weeks of progressive dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows a large left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields milky white fluid that remains opaque after centrifugation.
before.question: Which of the following pleural fluid results would best confirm a chylothorax?
before.options: {"options": ["Triglyceride concentration of 240 mg/dL", "pH of 7.10", "Cholesterol concentration of 260 mg/dL with cholesterol crystals", "Amylase concentration three times the serum value", "Glucose concentration of 40 mg/dL"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "pleural fluid triglycerides confirming chylothorax", "keyTakeaway": "Milky pleural fluid: triglycerides >110 mg/dL = chylothorax (lymphoma, thoracic duct injury); cholesterol >200 mg/dL with crystals = pseudochylothorax.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Triglyceride concentration of 240 mg/dL
before.explanation: A pleural fluid triglyceride level of 240 mg/dL is correct. The 2023 BTS pleural disease guideline states that a triglyceride level above 110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L) supports chylothorax, which in adults is most often caused by lymphoma or thoracic duct injury; chylomicrons on lipoprotein analysis confirm equivocal cases. Fluid that stays milky after centrifugation suggests a lipid effusion rather than empyema. A high cholesterol level above 200 mg/dL with crystals indicates a pseudochylothorax from long-standing effusions such as rheumatoid or tuberculous pleurisy. Low pH and low glucose suggest complicated parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignancy, or rheumatoid effusion. Elevated amylase suggests pancreatitis or esophageal rupture.

references.label: Roberts ME et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for Pleural Disease. Thorax 2023

before.scenario: A 2-year-old boy has had 4 wheezing episodes in the past year, each responding to albuterol, with nighttime cough between episodes. His clinician starts a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. His parents ask which delivery device he should use.
before.question: Which of the following is the preferred inhaler delivery method for this child?
before.options: {"options": ["Pressurized metered-dose inhaler with a spacer and mouthpiece only", "Pressurized metered-dose inhaler without a spacer", "Pressurized metered-dose inhaler with a valved spacer and face mask", "Dry powder inhaler", "Breath-actuated metered-dose inhaler"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "pressurized metered-dose inhaler with valved spacer and face mask for a toddler", "keyTakeaway": "Young child asthma device: pMDI + valved spacer; face mask for ages 0-3, mouthpiece from ~4-5; DPIs not for young children.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Pressurized metered-dose inhaler with a valved spacer and face mask
before.explanation: A pMDI with a valved spacer and face mask is correct. The GINA strategy recommends that children 5 years and younger use a pMDI with a valved spacer, with a face mask for children aged 0 to 3 years and a mouthpiece once they can use one (usually from age 4 to 5); nebulizers are an alternative for children who cannot use a spacer. Dry powder inhalers need a strong, fast inspiratory flow that toddlers cannot generate. A pMDI without a spacer requires actuation-breath coordination that young children lack and deposits drug in the oropharynx. A mouthpiece needs a tight lip seal that a 2-year-old cannot reliably maintain. Breath-actuated devices also need adequate inspiratory flow.

references.label: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2025 update

before.scenario: A 30-year-old woman with asthma has symptoms 4 days a week and wakes at night with cough twice monthly. Her previous clinician prescribed salmeterol 50 mcg twice daily by dry powder inhaler and albuterol as needed. She has never used an inhaled corticosteroid. Her inhaler technique and adherence are good. Spirometry shows reversible airflow obstruction.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in therapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Stop salmeterol monotherapy and start low-dose budesonide-formoterol", "Continue salmeterol and add tiotropium", "Continue salmeterol and add montelukast", "Continue salmeterol and albuterol and reassess in 6 months", "Increase salmeterol to 100 mcg twice daily"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "replacing LABA monotherapy with an ICS-containing regimen in asthma", "keyTakeaway": "Never treat asthma with LABA alone; every patient needs an ICS-containing regimen.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Stop salmeterol monotherapy and start low-dose budesonide-formoterol
before.explanation: Stopping salmeterol monotherapy and starting budesonide-formoterol is correct. GINA states that adults and adolescents with asthma should not be treated with a long-acting beta-agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid because LABA monotherapy increases the risk of severe exacerbations and asthma-related death; every patient should receive ICS-containing controller therapy. With symptoms most days and night waking, low-dose ICS-formoterol is a preferred option, used daily and as needed. Adding montelukast or tiotropium to salmeterol still leaves her without an inhaled corticosteroid. Doubling the salmeterol dose increases adverse effects without treating airway inflammation. Waiting 6 months leaves uncontrolled asthma on an unsafe regimen.

references.label: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2025 update

before.scenario: A 19-year-old man has 10 days of cough, progressive dyspnea, fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He vapes cannabis oil cartridges bought from a friend several times daily. Temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F), respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. CT of the chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing. Respiratory viral panel, blood cultures, Legionella and pneumococcal urine antigens, and HIV test are negative. Peripheral eosinophil count is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury", "Pulmonary sarcoidosis", "Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia", "Cardiogenic pulmonary edema", "Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia"], "blueprintSystem": "pulmonary", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI)", "keyTakeaway": "Vaping (especially THC) + respiratory, GI, and constitutional symptoms + bilateral ground-glass with subpleural sparing + negative infectious workup: EVALI.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury
before.explanation: EVALI is correct. CDC interim guidance for EVALI describes vaping within 90 days, especially THC-containing products obtained from informal sources (vitamin E acetate has been implicated), with respiratory symptoms, frequent gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms, hypoxemia, and bilateral ground-glass opacities often with subpleural sparing, after other causes such as infection are reasonably excluded. Management includes stopping vaping, supportive care, and often corticosteroids. Mycoplasma pneumonia rarely causes this degree of hypoxemia with diffuse bilateral opacities, and empiric treatment is reasonable while testing. Pneumocystis pneumonia occurs with immunosuppression and his HIV test is negative. Cardiogenic edema is unlikely in a healthy young man. Sarcoidosis is subacute with hilar adenopathy.

references.label: Siegel DA et al. Update: Interim Guidance for Health Care Providers Evaluating and Caring for Patients with Suspected EVALI. MMWR 2019

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man presents with melena and lightheadedness after taking naproxen for 2 weeks. After resuscitation, upper endoscopy shows a 1.5-cm duodenal ulcer with a nonbleeding visible vessel, which is treated with bipolar electrocoagulation and epinephrine injection. Biopsies for Helicobacter pylori are sent.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate acid-suppression plan?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral PPI once daily starting at discharge", "IV octreotide infusion for 72 hours", "High-dose PPI by continuous or intermittent dosing for 3 days, then oral PPI twice daily through 2 weeks, then once daily", "IV tranexamic acid for 24 hours instead of a PPI", "Stop PPI therapy because endoscopic hemostasis was achieved"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "high-dose PPI for 3 days after endoscopic hemostasis of a high-risk peptic ulcer", "keyTakeaway": "High-risk ulcer after endoscopic therapy: high-dose PPI x3 days, then oral PPI BID to day 14, then daily; stop NSAIDs; test and treat H. pylori.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: High-dose PPI by continuous or intermittent dosing for 3 days, then oral PPI twice daily through 2 weeks, then once daily
before.explanation: High-dose PPI for 3 days, then twice daily oral PPI to 2 weeks, is correct. The 2021 ACG ulcer bleeding guideline recommends high-dose PPI therapy, continuous or intermittent (for example, 80 mg bolus followed by continuous infusion, or high-dose intermittent dosing), for 3 days after successful endoscopic treatment of a high-risk ulcer (active bleeding, visible vessel, or adherent clot), followed by twice daily oral PPI through day 14, then once daily. Stopping acid suppression increases rebleeding. Octreotide is for variceal bleeding. The guideline advises against tranexamic acid for upper GI bleeding because it does not reduce mortality and increases thrombosis. Once daily oral PPI alone is inadequate early after high-risk stigmata. NSAIDs should be stopped and H. pylori treated if present.

references.label: Laine L et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding. Am J Gastroenterol 2021

before.scenario: A 5-year-old boy has had hard, painful stools every 5 to 7 days for 4 months and stool-withholding behaviors. Last week he had fecal soiling at school. He is growing normally and passed meconium on day 1 of life. Abdominal examination shows a firm mass in the left lower quadrant. Rectal examination shows a dilated rectum filled with hard stool, normal anal position, and normal perianal sensation.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral polyethylene glycol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 to 6 days, then maintenance polyethylene glycol", "Daily sodium phosphate enemas for 2 weeks", "Daily probiotic supplement", "Increased dietary fiber as the only intervention", "Abdominal radiograph before starting any treatment"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "oral polyethylene glycol disimpaction for functional constipation in a child", "keyTakeaway": "Pediatric functional constipation with impaction: oral PEG 1-1.5 g/kg/day for 3-6 days, then maintenance PEG ~0.4 g/kg/day for months; no routine x-ray.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral polyethylene glycol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 to 6 days, then maintenance polyethylene glycol
before.explanation: Oral polyethylene glycol disimpaction followed by maintenance is correct. The ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN functional constipation recommendations advise oral PEG 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 to 6 days to treat fecal impaction, with enemas as an alternative when PEG is not available, followed by maintenance PEG (about 0.4 g/kg/day, adjusted to effect) plus toilet training and behavioral measures for at least 2 months. Daily phosphate enemas for 2 weeks are not recommended and repeated use risks electrolyte disturbance. Fiber alone will not clear impaction. An abdominal radiograph is not needed when the history and examination establish the diagnosis. Probiotics are not recommended because evidence is lacking. Red flags for Hirschsprung disease are absent here.

references.label: Tabbers MM et al. Evaluation and Treatment of Functional Constipation in Infants and Children: ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN Recommendations. J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr 2014

before.scenario: A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has 6 months of early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea, and vomiting of food eaten several hours earlier. Her hemoglobin A1c is 8.4%. Upper endoscopy shows retained food but no ulcer, mass, or outlet obstruction. She takes insulin only and no opioids or GLP-1 receptor agonists.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Liquid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy with imaging at 1 hour", "CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast", "Barium esophagram", "Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan", "Solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy with imaging over 4 hours"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "4-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy for suspected diabetic gastroparesis", "keyTakeaway": "Gastroparesis: rule out obstruction (EGD), then 4-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy off emptying-slowing drugs.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy with imaging over 4 hours
before.explanation: Solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy over 4 hours is correct. The 2022 ACG gastroparesis guideline recommends excluding mechanical obstruction with endoscopy, then confirming delayed gastric emptying with a standardized solid-meal scintigraphy study imaged for 4 hours (or a validated breath test), after stopping drugs that slow emptying and with glucose below about 275 mg/dL. Shorter studies or liquid meals miss many cases and underestimate delay. CT does not measure gastric emptying, though it can exclude obstruction. A barium esophagram evaluates the esophagus. A HIDA scan evaluates gallbladder function. Treatment then includes glycemic control, dietary changes with small low-fat low-fiber meals, and metoclopramide if needed.

references.label: Camilleri M et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Gastroparesis. Am J Gastroenterol 2022

before.scenario: A 68-year-old woman has 3 months of 6 to 8 watery, nonbloody stools daily, including at night, with mild cramping. She started sertraline 5 months ago and takes naproxen most days for knee pain. Stool culture, Clostridioides difficile testing, and tissue transglutaminase IgA are negative. Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa. Random biopsies from the right and left colon show a thickened subepithelial collagen band and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Crohn disease of the colon", "Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea", "Ulcerative colitis", "Ischemic colitis", "Microscopic (collagenous) colitis"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "collagenous microscopic colitis diagnosed by biopsy of normal-appearing colon", "keyTakeaway": "Older woman, watery nocturnal diarrhea, NSAID/SSRI/PPI use, normal colonoscopy: biopsy for microscopic colitis; treat with budesonide.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Microscopic (collagenous) colitis
before.explanation: Microscopic colitis of the collagenous type is correct. The AGA technical review on microscopic colitis describes chronic watery, often nocturnal, nonbloody diarrhea in older adults, particularly women, associated with drugs such as NSAIDs, SSRIs, and PPIs, with a normal colonoscopy and diagnosis made only by colon biopsies; a subepithelial collagen band defines collagenous colitis and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes without a thick band defines lymphocytic colitis. Budesonide is first-line therapy and offending drugs should be reviewed. IBS is excluded by the abnormal histology and nocturnal diarrhea. Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease show visible mucosal inflammation and bleeding. Ischemic colitis is acute and painful with segmental mucosal changes.

references.label: Pardi DS et al. AGA Institute Technical Review on the Medical Management of Microscopic Colitis. Gastroenterology 2016

before.scenario: An 81-year-old man has had a painful, swollen right groin for 10 hours with vomiting. He has a known right inguinal hernia that he usually pushes back in. Temperature is 38.1 C (100.6 F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. A tense, exquisitely tender, irreducible right groin mass has overlying erythema. Abdomen is distended. WBC count is 16,500/mm3 and lactate is 3.4 mmol/L.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Scheduled elective repair within 6 weeks", "Nasogastric decompression and observation for 24 hours", "Fitting a hernia truss and discharge", "Emergency surgical repair with assessment of bowel viability, without attempting manual reduction", "Manual reduction under procedural sedation, then elective repair"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "emergency repair of a strangulated incarcerated inguinal hernia without manual reduction", "keyTakeaway": "Incarcerated hernia with fever, erythema, tachycardia, leukocytosis, or high lactate: strangulation; go to emergency surgery, do not reduce.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Emergency surgical repair with assessment of bowel viability, without attempting manual reduction
before.explanation: Emergency surgery without attempted reduction is correct. The HerniaSurge international groin hernia guidelines recommend emergency surgery for incarcerated hernias with signs of strangulation, such as fever, tachycardia, skin erythema, severe tenderness, leukocytosis, or raised lactate, and advise against manual reduction in that setting because it can return ischemic or necrotic bowel to the abdomen. Manual reduction followed by elective repair is reserved for incarcerated hernias without signs of strangulation. Observation with nasogastric suction delays treatment of possible bowel ischemia. A truss has no role in an acute incarcerated hernia. Elective repair in weeks is unsafe here. Age alone is not a reason to avoid surgery.

references.label: HerniaSurge Group. International Guidelines for Groin Hernia Management. Hernia 2018

before.scenario: A 76-year-old man has taken omeprazole 40 mg daily for 6 years. It was started for heartburn, which resolved within weeks, and he has had no symptoms since. He has never had endoscopy, Barrett esophagus, severe erosive esophagitis, or peptic ulcer bleeding, and he takes no NSAIDs or antiplatelet drugs. He asks whether he still needs the medication.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
before.options: {"options": ["Measure serum gastrin and bone density and continue omeprazole unless results are abnormal", "Continue omeprazole 40 mg daily indefinitely because he is asymptomatic", "Add sucralfate and continue omeprazole", "Increase omeprazole to 40 mg twice daily to prevent recurrence", "Attempt to discontinue omeprazole, by tapering or stopping, and monitor for return of symptoms"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "deprescribing a long-term PPI without a definite ongoing indication", "keyTakeaway": "Long-term PPI with no definite indication (no Barrett, severe esophagitis, or bleeding ulcer): offer deprescribing; taper or stop and watch for rebound.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Attempt to discontinue omeprazole, by tapering or stopping, and monitor for return of symptoms
before.explanation: Attempting discontinuation is correct. The 2022 AGA clinical practice update on PPI deprescribing advises that all patients on long-term PPIs should have the indication reviewed, and those without a definitive ongoing indication, such as uncomplicated GERD that responded to short-term therapy, should be offered a trial of deprescribing; tapering or abrupt discontinuation are both acceptable, with transient rebound acid hypersecretion possible. Patients with Barrett esophagus, severe erosive esophagitis, or a history of bleeding ulcer should usually continue. Lifelong continuation or dose escalation without an indication adds cost and pill burden. The decision should not hinge on gastrin or bone density testing. Sucralfate adds nothing for an asymptomatic patient.

references.label: Targownik LE et al. AGA Clinical Practice Update on De-Prescribing of Proton Pump Inhibitors. Gastroenterology 2022

before.scenario: A 52-year-old man who drinks 8 beers daily has had recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back for 2 years. For 3 months he has had bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that are hard to flush and a 6-kg weight loss. CT shows pancreatic calcifications and a dilated pancreatic duct. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.8%.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency?
before.options: {"options": ["Fecal elastase-1 concentration", "Stool ova and parasite examination", "D-xylose absorption test", "Lactose hydrogen breath test", "Serum lipase concentration"], "blueprintSystem": "gastrointestinal", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "fecal elastase to diagnose exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis", "keyTakeaway": "Chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhea: fecal elastase confirms exocrine insufficiency; treat with pancreatic enzymes with meals; lipase is often normal.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Fecal elastase-1 concentration
before.explanation: Fecal elastase-1 is correct. The 2020 ACG chronic pancreatitis guideline recommends a fecal elastase test as the practical noninvasive test to diagnose exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in patients with chronic pancreatitis, with low values supporting pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy taken with meals. Serum lipase is often normal in advanced chronic pancreatitis and does not measure exocrine function. The D-xylose test evaluates small intestinal mucosal absorption and is normal in pancreatic disease. Ova and parasite examination evaluates parasitic diarrhea such as giardiasis. A lactose breath test detects lactose malabsorption. The CT calcifications, steatorrhea, weight loss, and new diabetes indicate advanced alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis.

references.label: Gardner TB et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Chronic Pancreatitis. Am J Gastroenterol 2020

before.scenario: A 16-year-old girl who runs cross-country has had 3 months of diffuse, aching pain around and behind both kneecaps. It worsens when she runs downhill, climbs stairs, or sits through a long movie. She recalls no injury, locking, or giving way. There is no effusion.
before.question: Which of the following examination findings most strongly supports the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Point tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella during resisted knee extension", "Medial joint line tenderness with a painful click on the McMurray test", "Painful bony prominence at the tibial tubercle", "Increased anterior tibial translation with a soft end point on the Lachman test", "Retropatellar or peripatellar pain reproduced by squatting"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "squat-provoked retropatellar pain in patellofemoral pain syndrome", "keyTakeaway": "Patellofemoral pain: anterior knee pain with squatting, stairs, prolonged sitting; diagnose clinically, treat with hip and knee strengthening.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Retropatellar or peripatellar pain reproduced by squatting
before.explanation: Pain reproduced by squatting is correct. The 2019 APTA/JOSPT patellofemoral pain guideline states that the diagnosis rests on retropatellar or peripatellar pain reproduced by squatting and by other activities that load the flexed patellofemoral joint, such as stairs, running, or prolonged sitting, after excluding other causes; it notes that tests such as patellar grind have poor accuracy. Treatment centers on hip and knee strengthening exercise. A positive Lachman test indicates an ACL tear, and there was no injury. Joint line tenderness with a McMurray click suggests a meniscal tear with mechanical symptoms. Inferior pole tenderness suggests patellar tendinopathy. A tender tibial tubercle in a younger adolescent suggests Osgood-Schlatter disease.

references.label: Willy RW et al. Patellofemoral Pain: Clinical Practice Guidelines (APTA/JOSPT). J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2019

before.scenario: A 69-year-old woman has 2 years of right groin pain that worsens with walking and improves with rest, with morning stiffness of 15 minutes. Internal rotation of the right hip is limited and painful. Radiographs show joint space narrowing and osteophytes of the right hip. She has tried acetaminophen with limited benefit. Her BMI is 24 kg/m2 and kidney function is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
before.options: {"options": ["Glucosamine and chondroitin supplementation", "Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation", "Structured exercise program such as strengthening or aquatic exercise", "Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection", "Oral alendronate"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "structured exercise as core therapy for hip osteoarthritis", "keyTakeaway": "Hip OA: exercise for everyone (plus NSAIDs, weight loss if overweight); avoid hyaluronic acid, glucosamine/chondroitin, and TENS.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Structured exercise program such as strengthening or aquatic exercise
before.explanation: A structured exercise program is correct. The 2019 ACR/Arthritis Foundation osteoarthritis guideline strongly recommends exercise, including strengthening, aerobic, aquatic, and balance or mind-body programs, for all patients with hip osteoarthritis, along with oral NSAIDs when not contraindicated and weight loss when overweight. The guideline strongly recommends against intra-articular hyaluronic acid for hip osteoarthritis, strongly recommends against glucosamine and chondroitin, and recommends against TENS for hip osteoarthritis. Bisphosphonates treat osteoporosis and do not improve osteoarthritis pain. Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection, ideally image guided, and total hip arthroplasty remain options if symptoms persist.

references.label: Kolasinski SL et al. 2019 ACR/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee. Arthritis Care Res 2020

before.scenario: A 68-year-old woman has taken alendronate 70 mg weekly for 5 years for osteoporosis diagnosed by a femoral neck T-score of -2.7. She has never had a fracture, has not lost height, and has no new risk factors. She does not take glucocorticoids. Repeat DXA shows a femoral neck T-score of -2.1. Calcium and vitamin D levels are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Switch to teriparatide for 2 years", "Stop alendronate for a drug holiday and reassess fracture risk in 2 to 3 years", "Continue alendronate indefinitely", "Add raloxifene to alendronate", "Switch to denosumab and stop it after 2 years"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "bisphosphonate drug holiday after 5 years of alendronate in a lower-risk woman", "keyTakeaway": "After 5 years oral bisphosphonate, no fractures, hip T-score > -2.5: consider a 2-3 year drug holiday; never stop denosumab without follow-on therapy.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Stop alendronate for a drug holiday and reassess fracture risk in 2 to 3 years
before.explanation: A drug holiday is correct. The ASBMR task force on long-term bisphosphonate treatment suggests reassessing after 5 years of oral (or 3 years of IV) bisphosphonate; women without a fracture before or during therapy whose hip T-score is now above -2.5 are at lower risk and may take a drug holiday of 2 to 3 years with periodic reassessment, which also lowers the risk of atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw. Continuing up to 10 years is suggested for higher-risk patients, such as those with fractures or a hip T-score at or below -2.5. Teriparatide is for very high risk. Denosumab should not be stopped without follow-up therapy because of rebound vertebral fractures. Combining raloxifene with alendronate is not recommended.

references.label: Adler RA et al. Managing Osteoporosis in Patients on Long-Term Bisphosphonate Treatment: ASBMR Task Force Report. J Bone Miner Res 2016

before.scenario: A 30-year-old man twisted his left knee playing soccer 3 hours ago. He walked into the emergency department with a limp, taking more than 4 steps without help. On examination there is a small effusion, no tenderness of the patella or fibular head, and he can flex the knee to 110 degrees. The Lachman test and McMurray test are negative and the knee is stable to varus and valgus stress.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["CT of the knee", "No imaging; provide supportive care with follow-up if not improving", "Radiographs of the knee", "Ultrasonography of the knee", "MRI of the knee"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "Ottawa knee rule to avoid radiographs after a twisting knee injury", "keyTakeaway": "Ottawa knee rule: x-ray if age >=55, isolated patellar or fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90 degrees, or cannot bear weight 4 steps; otherwise no imaging.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: No imaging; provide supportive care with follow-up if not improving
before.explanation: No imaging is correct. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria for acute knee trauma endorse clinical decision rules such as the Ottawa knee rule: radiographs are indicated after acute knee injury only for age 55 or older, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately and in the emergency department. This patient meets none, so fracture is very unlikely. A small effusion alone does not meet a criterion. MRI is reserved for suspected internal derangement such as ligament or meniscal tear with persistent symptoms or instability, which is not present. CT is used for complex fractures after radiographs. Ultrasound is not a first-line study for acute knee trauma.

references.label: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Acute Trauma to the Knee. J Am Coll Radiol 2020

before.scenario: A 2-week-old girl is brought for a weight check. She was born at term and is exclusively breastfed. She has regained her birth weight. Her mother takes a prenatal vitamin. The family asks whether the baby needs any supplements.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral vitamin D 400 IU daily starting now and continuing through the first year", "Direct sunlight exposure for 30 minutes daily instead of supplementation", "Begin vitamin D at 6 months of age when solid foods are introduced", "No supplementation because maternal prenatal vitamins provide enough vitamin D in breast milk", "Oral vitamin D 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "vitamin D 400 IU daily for an exclusively breastfed infant", "keyTakeaway": "All infants (especially breastfed) need vitamin D 400 IU daily from birth through 12 months; avoid direct sun in young infants.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral vitamin D 400 IU daily starting now and continuing through the first year
before.explanation: Vitamin D 400 IU daily from now through the first year is correct. The global consensus recommendations on nutritional rickets advise 400 IU of vitamin D daily for all infants from birth to 12 months, regardless of feeding mode, because breast milk contains little vitamin D even when the mother takes a standard prenatal vitamin. Infants who drink enough fortified formula may get adequate amounts, but this infant is exclusively breastfed. A 50,000 IU weekly regimen is a treatment dose for deficiency, not prevention. Waiting until 6 months leaves the infant at risk of deficiency and rickets. Infants younger than 6 months should be kept out of direct sunlight, so sun exposure is not a safe substitute.

references.label: Munns CF et al. Global Consensus Recommendations on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016

before.scenario: A 27-year-old woman has 3 months of symmetric small-joint arthralgia, a photosensitive malar rash, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640 and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are elevated. CBC, creatinine, and urinalysis are normal and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is normal. She weighs 60 kg, is not pregnant, and has no eye disease.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily", "Hydroxychloroquine 600 mg daily", "No drug therapy until internal organ involvement develops", "IV cyclophosphamide", "Prednisone 40 mg daily long term"], "blueprintSystem": "musculoskeletal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "hydroxychloroquine at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight for all patients with SLE", "keyTakeaway": "SLE: hydroxychloroquine for everyone, <=5 mg/kg actual body weight daily, with retinal screening; minimize glucocorticoids.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily
before.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily is correct. The 2023 EULAR SLE recommendations advise hydroxychloroquine for all patients with SLE unless contraindicated, at a dose not exceeding 5 mg/kg of actual body weight per day (300 mg for 60 kg), because it reduces flares, organ damage, and mortality; baseline and periodic retinal screening is needed. Withholding therapy until organ involvement forfeits these benefits. Long-term glucocorticoids should be minimized, with maintenance at 5 mg/day or less of prednisone equivalent and withdrawal when possible. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ-threatening disease such as lupus nephritis. A 600 mg dose exceeds 5 mg/kg and increases the risk of retinal toxicity.

references.label: Fanouriakis A et al. EULAR Recommendations for the Management of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: 2023 Update. Ann Rheum Dis 2024

before.scenario: A 31-year-old woman is seen 10 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She is exclusively breastfeeding, has no medical problems, and does not smoke. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. She wants to start an oral contraceptive now and declines an intrauterine device or implant.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive to start today?
before.options: {"options": ["Combined oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol 30 mcg", "No contraceptive until 6 weeks postpartum", "Progestin-only pill", "Combined transdermal contraceptive patch", "Combined contraceptive vaginal ring"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "progestin-only pill for a breastfeeding woman 10 days postpartum", "keyTakeaway": "Postpartum <21 days: no estrogen-containing method (MEC 4); progestin-only methods are MEC 1 even while breastfeeding.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Progestin-only pill
before.explanation: A progestin-only pill is correct. The 2024 U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria rate progestin-only methods as category 1 for breastfeeding women at any time postpartum. All combined hormonal contraceptives (pills, patch, and ring) are category 4 in the first 21 days postpartum because of the high risk of venous thromboembolism, and they remain category 2 or 3 until 6 weeks depending on breastfeeding and VTE risk factors. Delaying contraception until 6 weeks is unnecessary; ovulation can return before the postpartum visit, especially if breastfeeding is not exclusive. Lactational amenorrhea is effective only if all criteria are met, and she has asked for a pill.

references.label: Nguyen AT et al. U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024. MMWR Recomm Rep 2024

before.scenario: A 14-year-old girl has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche at age 12, lasting 8 days and requiring pad changes every hour on the heaviest days. She has frequent nosebleeds and bled for 2 days after a dental extraction. Her mother also has heavy periods. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with microcytosis. Pregnancy test is negative.
before.question: In addition to a CBC with platelet count, ferritin, PT, and aPTT, which of the following tests is most appropriate?
before.options: {"options": ["Pelvic MRI", "Von Willebrand factor antigen, von Willebrand factor activity, and factor VIII level", "Serum FSH and LH", "Endometrial biopsy", "No further testing; start a combined oral contraceptive"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "von Willebrand testing in an adolescent with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche", "keyTakeaway": "Adolescent with heavy menses since menarche plus a bleeding history: test for von Willebrand disease (VWF antigen, activity, factor VIII).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Von Willebrand factor antigen, von Willebrand factor activity, and factor VIII level
before.explanation: Von Willebrand testing is correct. ACOG Committee Opinion 785 recommends screening adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding, particularly since menarche, for bleeding disorders; a positive bleeding history (epistaxis, bleeding after dental work, family history) warrants a CBC, platelets, PT, aPTT, ferritin, and von Willebrand factor antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor), and factor VIII, ideally coordinated with hematology, because von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited cause. Pelvic MRI and endometrial biopsy look for structural or neoplastic causes that are rare in adolescents. Gonadotropins evaluate ovarian function, not bleeding. Starting hormones without testing can mask the diagnosis; testing should be done before or coordinated with treatment.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 785: Screening and Management of Bleeding Disorders in Adolescents With Heavy Menstrual Bleeding. Obstet Gynecol 2019

before.scenario: A 13-year-old girl has 4 months of monthly lower abdominal and pelvic pain lasting several days, and she has not had a menstrual period. She has Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development and normal height. She is not sexually active and a urine pregnancy test is negative. A lower midline mass is palpable.
before.question: Which of the following findings on external genital examination is most likely?
before.options: {"options": ["Clitoromegaly with labial fusion", "Vaginal discharge with cervical motion tenderness", "Bulging bluish membrane at the introitus with no visible vaginal opening", "Absent pubic and axillary hair with bilateral inguinal masses", "Normal introitus with a short blind-ending vagina and absent cervix"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "bulging bluish membrane of an imperforate hymen with hematocolpos", "keyTakeaway": "Primary amenorrhea + cyclic pelvic pain + normal puberty + midline mass: imperforate hymen with hematocolpos (bulging bluish membrane).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Bulging bluish membrane at the introitus with no visible vaginal opening
before.explanation: A bulging bluish membrane is correct. ACOG Committee Opinion 780 on hymenal variants describes imperforate hymen presenting after puberty with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and sometimes a pelvic or abdominal mass from hematocolpos, with a bulging, often bluish membrane at the introitus; treatment is surgical hymenectomy. Clitoromegaly with labial fusion suggests androgen excess such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A short blind vagina with absent cervix suggests mullerian agenesis, which usually lacks cyclic pain and a hematocolpos mass. Absent sexual hair with inguinal masses suggests androgen insensitivity syndrome, but this girl has normal pubic hair. Cervical motion tenderness suggests pelvic inflammatory disease, unlikely without sexual activity.

references.label: ACOG Committee Opinion 780: Diagnosis and Management of Hymenal Variants. Obstet Gynecol 2019

before.scenario: A 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation presents for her first prenatal visit. She has no urinary symptoms, no history of urinary tract infections, and no medical problems. Vital signs are normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria?
before.options: {"options": ["Urine culture at 28 weeks of gestation only", "Urine culture at this visit, with treatment if positive", "No screening because she has no risk factors", "Screen only if urinary symptoms develop", "Urine dipstick for nitrites and leukocyte esterase at each visit, with culture only if positive"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "urine culture screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria in early pregnancy", "keyTakeaway": "Pregnancy: screen once with urine culture at 12-16 weeks (or first visit) and treat bacteriuria; do not screen nonpregnant adults.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Urine culture at this visit, with treatment if positive
before.explanation: Urine culture at this visit is correct. The 2019 USPSTF recommendation (grade B) is to screen pregnant persons for asymptomatic bacteriuria using urine culture, generally at 12 to 16 weeks of gestation or at the first prenatal visit if later, because treating bacteriuria lowers the risk of pyelonephritis and may reduce low birth weight. Dipstick testing has poor sensitivity and is not an adequate screen. Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening. A single culture at 28 weeks is too late. Pregnancy itself is the indication, so absence of other risk factors is irrelevant. By contrast, the USPSTF recommends against screening nonpregnant adults.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Adults: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2019

before.scenario: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, is at 42 weeks 1 day of gestation by first-trimester ultrasonography. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. A nonstress test is reactive and amniotic fluid volume is normal. The cervix is 2 cm dilated, 50% effaced, and soft. She has no contraindication to vaginal birth.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Induction of labor", "Expectant management with weekly nonstress tests until 43 weeks", "Twice-weekly biophysical profiles while awaiting spontaneous labor", "Scheduled cesarean delivery", "Weekly membrane sweeping as the only intervention"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "induction of labor for an uncomplicated pregnancy at 42 weeks", "keyTakeaway": "Postterm (>=42 0/7 weeks): induce labor by 42 6/7 weeks; consider induction from 41 0/7 with fetal surveillance.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Induction of labor
before.explanation: Induction of labor is correct. ACOG Practice Bulletin 146 recommends induction of labor after 42 0/7 weeks and by 42 6/7 weeks of gestation because stillbirth, neonatal morbidity, and meconium aspiration increase beyond 42 weeks; induction may be considered from 41 0/7 weeks, and fetal surveillance is reasonable from 41 weeks. Continuing expectant management to 43 weeks exposes the fetus to rising risk even with reassuring tests. Cesarean delivery is not indicated without an obstetric indication, and she has a favorable cervix with a prior vaginal birth. Ongoing surveillance alone delays recommended delivery. Membrane sweeping may promote labor at term but does not replace induction at 42 weeks.

references.label: ACOG Practice Bulletin 146: Management of Late-Term and Postterm Pregnancies. Obstet Gynecol 2014

before.scenario: A 20-year-old woman with HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 count 520/mm3, viral load undetectable) is seen for routine care. She has never received HPV vaccine. She is sexually active with one partner and her cervical cytology last year was normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate HPV vaccination plan?
before.options: {"options": ["A single dose of 9-valent HPV vaccine", "Two doses of 9-valent HPV vaccine at 0 and 6 to 12 months", "No vaccination because she is already sexually active", "Defer vaccination until her CD4 count is above 700/mm3", "Three doses of 9-valent HPV vaccine at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "3-dose HPV vaccine series for a young adult with HIV", "keyTakeaway": "HPV vaccine: catch-up through age 26; immunocompromised (including HIV) always need 3 doses (0, 1-2, 6 months).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Three doses of 9-valent HPV vaccine at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months
before.explanation: Three doses at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months is correct. ACIP recommends HPV vaccination through age 26 for those not adequately vaccinated, and recommends a 3-dose schedule for people with immunocompromising conditions, including HIV infection, regardless of the age at which vaccination starts, because immune responses may be reduced. The 2-dose schedule applies only to immunocompetent people who start before their 15th birthday. A single-dose schedule is not recommended for immunocompromised patients. Sexual activity does not remove the benefit, since she is unlikely to have been exposed to all vaccine types. HPV vaccine is inactivated and safe in HIV, so there is no reason to wait for a higher CD4 count.

references.label: Meites E et al. Human Papillomavirus Vaccination for Adults: Updated Recommendations of the ACIP. MMWR 2019

before.scenario: A 40-year-old man woke this morning with drooping of the right side of his face and difficulty closing his right eye. He has no rash, hearing loss, limb weakness, or other neurologic symptoms. Examination shows complete weakness of the right forehead, eyelid, and lower face, with an otherwise normal neurologic and ear examination. Glucose is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["MRI of the brain before starting any treatment", "Oral prednisone 60 mg daily for 5 days, then a 5-day taper, with eye protection", "No treatment because most cases resolve spontaneously", "Oral valacyclovir alone for 7 days", "Admission for IV methylprednisolone"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "oral corticosteroids within 72 hours for Bell palsy", "keyTakeaway": "Bell palsy (forehead involved, otherwise normal exam): oral steroids within 72 hours, eye protection; no antiviral alone, no routine imaging.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral prednisone 60 mg daily for 5 days, then a 5-day taper, with eye protection
before.explanation: Oral prednisone with eye protection is correct. The AAO-HNSF Bell palsy guideline strongly recommends oral steroids within 72 hours of symptom onset for patients 16 and older, because they improve facial nerve recovery; it recommends against antiviral therapy alone, allows antivirals only in combination with steroids, and recommends eye protection (lubrication, taping) when eye closure is impaired. Antiviral monotherapy is ineffective. Routine laboratory testing and imaging are not recommended for new-onset Bell palsy; imaging is for atypical features or no recovery by 3 months. IV steroids and admission are unnecessary. Although many recover, untreated patients have higher rates of incomplete recovery.

references.label: Baugh RF et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Bell's Palsy (AAO-HNSF). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013

before.scenario: A 22-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry has had two focal seizures with impaired awareness. MRI shows mesial temporal sclerosis. His neurologist is considering carbamazepine as initial therapy. He has never taken an antiseizure medication and has no drug allergies.
before.question: Which of the following tests should be done before starting carbamazepine?
before.options: {"options": ["CYP2C19 genotyping", "Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity", "HLA-B*58:01 genotyping", "HLA-B*15:02 genotyping", "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine in a patient of Southeast Asian ancestry", "keyTakeaway": "Before carbamazepine in Asian ancestry: test HLA-B*15:02 (SJS/TEN risk); HLA-B*58:01 is for allopurinol.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: HLA-B*15:02 genotyping
before.explanation: HLA-B*15:02 genotyping is correct. The CPIC guideline for HLA genotype and carbamazepine recommends testing carbamazepine-naive patients for HLA-B*15:02, which is common in people of Southeast and East Asian ancestry, because carriers have a markedly increased risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis; carriers should not start carbamazepine and should be cautious with oxcarbazepine. HLA-A*31:01 is also associated with carbamazepine hypersensitivity across ancestries. HLA-B*58:01 predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity. TPMT guides thiopurine dosing. CYP2C19 affects clopidogrel and some SSRIs. G6PD deficiency predicts hemolysis with oxidant drugs such as dapsone or rasburicase.

references.label: Phillips EJ et al. CPIC Guideline for HLA Genotype and Use of Carbamazepine and Oxcarbazepine: 2017 Update. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2018

before.scenario: A 34-year-old woman has 2 months of drooping of both eyelids and double vision that worsen by evening, plus fatigable proximal arm weakness when she styles her hair. She has no dysphagia, dysarthria, or dyspnea, and forced vital capacity is normal. Acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies are positive, and chest CT shows no thymoma. She is not pregnant and takes no medications.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["IV immune globulin 2 g/kg", "Rituximab IV", "Pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three times daily, titrated to symptoms", "Eculizumab IV", "Plasma exchange, 5 exchanges over 10 days"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "pyridostigmine as initial symptomatic therapy for mild generalized myasthenia gravis", "keyTakeaway": "Mild AChR-positive myasthenia gravis: start pyridostigmine; IVIG or plasma exchange for crisis; add immunotherapy if goals are not met.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three times daily, titrated to symptoms
before.explanation: Pyridostigmine is correct. The 2020 international consensus guidance for myasthenia gravis recommends pyridostigmine as part of initial treatment in most patients, adjusting the dose to symptoms; a typical start is 30 mg three to four times daily, increased as needed toward 60 mg every 4 to 6 hours while watching for cramps and diarrhea. Corticosteroids or nonsteroidal immunosuppressants are added if goals are not met, and thymectomy should be considered for nonthymomatous AChR antibody-positive generalized disease at ages 18 to 50. IV immune globulin and plasma exchange are incorrect because they are short-term therapies for crisis, severe bulbar or respiratory weakness, or preoperative optimization. Eculizumab is incorrect because it is reserved for refractory AChR-positive disease. Rituximab is incorrect because it is mainly an early option for MuSK-positive disease.

references.label: Narayanaswami P et al. International Consensus Guidance for Management of Myasthenia Gravis: 2020 Update. Neurology 2021

before.scenario: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a motorcycle crash without a helmet. His eyes open only to a painful stimulus. He speaks random, inappropriate words but no conversation. With a painful stimulus to the nail bed he pulls the limb away but does not localize. Pupils are equal and reactive. Blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
before.question: Which of the following is this patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score?
before.options: {"options": ["7", "8", "9", "11", "10"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "calculating the Glasgow Coma Scale score after head trauma", "keyTakeaway": "GCS = eye (4) + verbal (5) + motor (6): to pain = 2, inappropriate words = 3, withdraws = 4; 13-15 mild, 9-12 moderate, 3-8 severe TBI.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.explanation: A score of 9 is correct. The Glasgow Coma Scale, used throughout the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines to classify traumatic brain injury, sums eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5), and motor response (1 to 6). Eye opening to pain scores 2, inappropriate words score 3, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, totaling 9, which is moderate TBI (9 to 12); severe TBI is 3 to 8, where airway protection is generally indicated. A total of 7 or 8 would require a lower motor or verbal score, such as abnormal flexion (3) or incomprehensible sounds (2). A total of 10 or 11 would require localizing pain (5) or confused conversation (4). Reassessment over time matters more than a single value.

references.label: Carney N et al. Guidelines for the Management of Severe Traumatic Brain Injury, Fourth Edition (Brain Trauma Foundation). Neurosurgery 2017

before.scenario: A 68-year-old man has sudden right arm and face weakness and aphasia that began 90 minutes ago. He takes amlodipine only and no anticoagulants, and has no known bleeding disorder or liver disease. Blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg. NIHSS score is 10. Noncontrast head CT shows no hemorrhage. Fingerstick glucose is 132 mg/dL. Platelet count, INR, aPTT, and troponin have been drawn and are pending. He meets all other criteria for IV thrombolysis.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Give IV thrombolytic therapy now without waiting for the pending laboratory results", "Wait for the troponin result to exclude myocardial infarction first", "Wait for the platelet count and INR before giving thrombolytic therapy", "Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mm Hg before giving thrombolytic therapy", "Repeat the head CT in 1 hour before deciding on thrombolysis"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "blood glucose as the only laboratory result required before IV thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke", "keyTakeaway": "Before IV thrombolysis: only glucose is required unless coagulopathy or anticoagulant use is suspected; BP must be <185/110 mm Hg.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Give IV thrombolytic therapy now without waiting for the pending laboratory results
before.explanation: Giving thrombolysis now is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline, consistent with prior versions, states that in patients without suspected coagulopathy or anticoagulant use, only the blood glucose must be known before starting IV thrombolysis, because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke; treatment should not be delayed for platelet count or coagulation results. Waiting for troponin also delays treatment without changing eligibility. The blood pressure threshold for thrombolysis is below 185/110 mm Hg, which he already meets, and pressure is kept at or below 180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours afterward. Repeating the CT wastes time, since benefit falls with every minute of delay. Vessel imaging for thrombectomy can proceed in parallel.

references.label: 2026 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke. Stroke 2026

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man has 1 year of slowly progressive numbness and tingling of both feet that has now reached his ankles. He drinks 1 glass of wine weekly and takes no medications. Examination shows decreased pinprick and vibration sense in a stocking distribution and absent ankle reflexes with normal strength. Fasting glucose is 104 mg/dL. CBC, creatinine, and TSH are normal.
before.question: Which of the following sets of tests has the highest yield for the cause of his neuropathy?
before.options: {"options": ["2-hour oral glucose tolerance test, vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid, and serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis", "Genetic testing for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease", "Sural nerve biopsy", "Lumbar puncture with CSF protein", "Serum anti-ganglioside antibody panel"], "blueprintSystem": "neurologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "glucose tolerance test, B12 with methylmalonic acid, and serum immunofixation for distal symmetric polyneuropathy", "keyTakeaway": "Distal symmetric polyneuropathy workup: glucose (OGTT if needed), B12 with MMA, and serum protein immunofixation are highest yield.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test, vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid, and serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis
before.explanation: The glucose tolerance test, B12 with methylmalonic acid, and serum immunofixation are correct. The AAN/AANEM/AAPMR practice parameter on distal symmetric polyneuropathy identifies blood glucose, serum B12 with metabolites (methylmalonic acid with or without homocysteine), and serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis as the highest-yield screening tests, with a 2-hour glucose tolerance test when routine glucose testing is not diagnostic, since impaired glucose tolerance is a common cause. Genetic testing is reserved for a cryptogenic neuropathy with a hereditary phenotype such as pes cavus or family history. Anti-ganglioside antibodies apply to motor neuropathies and Guillain-Barre variants. Nerve biopsy is invasive and reserved for suspected vasculitis or amyloidosis. CSF studies are for suspected demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

references.label: England JD et al. Practice Parameter: Evaluation of Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy: Role of Laboratory and Genetic Testing (AAN/AANEM/AAPMR). Neurology 2009

before.scenario: A 64-year-old man with COPD uses fluticasone-salmeterol twice daily and does not rinse his mouth afterward. For 1 week he has had a cottony feeling in his mouth and altered taste. He has no odynophagia or dysphagia. White plaques on the buccal mucosa and palate wipe off and leave an erythematous base. A recent HIV test was negative, and he takes no other medications.
before.question: In addition to rinsing his mouth after each inhaler use, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Permanently discontinue the inhaled corticosteroid without antifungal therapy", "Triamcinolone dental paste applied three times daily", "Voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily for 14 days", "Clotrimazole troches 10 mg dissolved in the mouth 5 times daily for 7 to 14 days", "Micafungin 150 mg IV daily"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "clotrimazole troches for mild oropharyngeal candidiasis in an inhaled corticosteroid user", "keyTakeaway": "Mild thrush: clotrimazole troches or miconazole buccal tablet for 7 to 14 days; fluconazole for moderate to severe; rinse after inhaled steroids.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Clotrimazole troches 10 mg dissolved in the mouth 5 times daily for 7 to 14 days
before.explanation: Clotrimazole troches are correct. The 2016 IDSA candidiasis guideline recommends clotrimazole troches 10 mg 5 times daily or a miconazole mucoadhesive buccal tablet 50 mg once daily for 7 to 14 days for mild oropharyngeal candidiasis, reserving oral fluconazole 100 to 200 mg daily for moderate to severe disease. Rinsing and spitting after each inhaled corticosteroid dose reduces recurrence. Voriconazole is incorrect because it is reserved for fluconazole-refractory disease and has more toxicity and interactions. Micafungin is incorrect because IV echinocandins are for esophageal or invasive candidiasis when oral therapy is not possible. Triamcinolone paste is incorrect because a topical steroid worsens fungal overgrowth. Stopping the inhaler alone is incorrect because the infection still needs treatment.

references.label: Pappas PG et al. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Candidiasis: 2016 Update by IDSA. Clin Infect Dis 2016

before.scenario: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after a soccer collision knocked out her upper front tooth. Her father brings the intact tooth wrapped in a dry tissue; it has dirt on the root. She has no loss of consciousness or other injuries. The alveolar socket is intact, and the tooth is a permanent maxillary central incisor.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Hold the tooth by the crown, rinse the root briefly with saline, and replant it in the socket now, then arrange urgent dental splinting", "Keep the tooth dry in the tissue and refer to a dentist the next day", "Store the tooth in tap water until a dentist can see her", "Do not replant because replantation is contraindicated in children", "Scrub the root with gauze to remove the dirt before replantation"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "immediate replantation of an avulsed permanent incisor", "keyTakeaway": "Avulsed permanent tooth: hold by crown, rinse without scrubbing, replant ASAP (or store in milk/saline/saliva); never replant primary teeth.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Hold the tooth by the crown, rinse the root briefly with saline, and replant it in the socket now, then arrange urgent dental splinting
before.explanation: Immediate replantation after a brief saline rinse is correct. The IADT guideline for avulsion of permanent teeth advises handling the tooth by the crown, rinsing a dirty root briefly with saline or milk without scrubbing, and replanting it as soon as possible, followed by a flexible splint for about 2 weeks, tetanus review, and dental follow-up; if replantation is not possible, storage in milk, saline, or saliva preserves periodontal ligament cells. Scrubbing destroys those cells. Dry storage longer than about 60 minutes makes cells nonviable. Replantation is recommended for permanent teeth in children; primary teeth, by contrast, should not be replanted because of risk to the developing permanent tooth. Tap water is hypotonic and damages root cells.

references.label: Fouad AF et al. IADT Guidelines for the Management of Traumatic Dental Injuries: 2. Avulsion of Permanent Teeth. Dent Traumatol 2020

before.scenario: A 62-year-old man has had constant, nonpulsatile ringing in both ears for 8 months that disturbs his sleep and concentration. He worked in a factory for 30 years. Otoscopic and neurologic examinations are normal. Audiometry shows symmetric bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss that he does not find limiting.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Oral zinc supplementation", "Gabapentin titrated to 900 mg daily", "MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium", "Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy for tinnitus", "Ginkgo biloba supplementation"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "cognitive behavioral therapy rather than imaging or drugs for bothersome bilateral tinnitus", "keyTakeaway": "Bothersome bilateral nonpulsatile tinnitus with symmetric hearing loss: audiology, hearing aid evaluation, CBT; no routine imaging, drugs, or supplements.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy for tinnitus
before.explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy is correct. The AAO-HNSF tinnitus guideline recommends CBT for persistent, bothersome tinnitus because it reduces tinnitus-related distress and improves quality of life, and recommends a hearing aid evaluation for patients with hearing loss. It recommends against imaging of the head and neck unless tinnitus is unilateral, pulsatile, or accompanied by focal neurologic findings or asymmetric hearing loss; this patient's tinnitus and hearing loss are symmetric. The guideline recommends against routine use of medications such as antidepressants, anticonvulsants like gabapentin, and anxiolytics, and against dietary supplements such as ginkgo biloba, melatonin, and zinc, because they lack benefit and carry adverse effects.

references.label: Tunkel DE et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus (AAO-HNSF). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014

before.scenario: A 3-year-old boy is brought because his parents notice that his right eye sometimes turns in toward his nose, especially when he is tired. He was born at term and is developing normally. Red reflexes are present and symmetric. The corneal light reflex appears displaced temporally in the right eye.
before.question: Which of the following cover test findings would confirm strabismus in this child?
before.options: {"options": ["Horizontal nystagmus only at extreme lateral gaze", "Equal and bright red reflexes on simultaneous red reflex testing", "Outward refixation movement of the right eye when the left eye is covered", "Symmetric corneal light reflexes with no refixation movement on cover testing", "Broad nasal bridge with symmetric corneal light reflexes"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "cover test showing refixation movement in childhood esotropia", "keyTakeaway": "Cover test: covering the fixing eye makes a deviated eye move to fixate (esotropic eye moves outward); refer all true strabismus for amblyopia risk.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Outward refixation movement of the right eye when the left eye is covered
