before.explanation: An outward refixation movement of the right eye is correct. The AAP clinical report on evaluating the visual system recommends the corneal light reflex and cover testing to detect strabismus at preschool visits: if the right eye is turned in (esotropia), covering the fixating left eye forces the right eye to take up fixation, so it moves outward. A temporally displaced light reflex in the right eye also indicates esotropia. Any true strabismus warrants referral to an eye specialist because untreated strabismus can cause amblyopia. Symmetric reflexes with no movement on cover testing are normal. A broad nasal bridge with symmetric reflexes is pseudostrabismus. End-gaze nystagmus is usually physiologic. Symmetric red reflexes are normal.

references.label: Donahue SP et al. Procedures for the Evaluation of the Visual System by Pediatricians (AAP). Pediatrics 2016

before.scenario: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent cold sores 3 to 4 times a year. One hour ago she felt tingling and burning at the right upper lip border, where her outbreaks usually occur; no vesicles have appeared yet. She is otherwise healthy, is not pregnant, has normal kidney function, and takes no medications.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Mupirocin ointment three times daily for 5 days", "Valacyclovir 2 g orally twice daily for 1 day, with doses about 12 hours apart", "Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours", "Wait until vesicles appear, then start oral antiviral therapy", "Cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "single-day high-dose valacyclovir at prodrome for recurrent herpes labialis", "keyTakeaway": "Recurrent cold sores: valacyclovir 2 g twice daily for 1 day, started at the first prodromal tingle.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Valacyclovir 2 g orally twice daily for 1 day, with doses about 12 hours apart
before.explanation: Valacyclovir 2 g twice daily for 1 day is correct. The FDA-approved regimen for recurrent herpes labialis in immunocompetent adults is valacyclovir 2 g every 12 hours for 1 day, started at the earliest prodromal symptom such as tingling, itching, or burning; in the pivotal randomized trials this shortened episodes and aborted some lesions. The dose is reduced in kidney impairment. Waiting for vesicles is incorrect because benefit depends on starting during the prodrome. IV acyclovir is incorrect because it is reserved for severe, disseminated, or immunocompromised HSV disease. Cephalexin is incorrect because it treats bacterial infection and has no antiviral activity. Mupirocin is incorrect because it is a topical antibacterial for impetigo, not HSV.

references.label: VALTREX (valacyclovir) prescribing information, GlaxoSmithKline (DailyMed)
Spruance SL et al. High-dose, short-duration, early valacyclovir therapy for episodic treatment of cold sores: two randomized trials. Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2003

before.scenario: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and empagliflozin. Two days after laparoscopic hysterectomy she has had poor oral intake, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort. She is tachypneic. Glucose is 182 mg/dL, sodium 138 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, arterial pH 7.18, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L (normal <0.6), and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Serum osmolality is 296 mOsm/kg. She does not drink alcohol.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Starvation ketosis", "Metformin-associated lactic acidosis", "Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state", "Alcoholic ketoacidosis", "Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis associated with an SGLT2 inhibitor", "keyTakeaway": "SGLT2 inhibitor + surgery/fasting/illness + high-gap acidosis + ketones with glucose <250: euglycemic DKA; treat with fluids, insulin plus dextrose; stop the SGLT2i.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
before.explanation: Euglycemic DKA is correct. The 2024 ADA/EASD hyperglycemic crises consensus report defines DKA as glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher or known diabetes, ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or higher), and metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L), recognizing that SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with surgery, fasting, or acute illness. Her anion gap is 24. Treatment requires IV fluids, insulin with dextrose, and stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor. HHS has glucose above 600 mg/dL and high osmolality without significant acidosis. Alcoholic ketoacidosis requires alcohol use. Starvation ketosis rarely lowers bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L. Her lactate is normal, excluding lactic acidosis.

references.label: Umpierrez GE et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024

before.scenario: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin 1,000 mg twice daily for 8 years. He reports 4 months of numbness in both feet. Hemoglobin A1c is 7.0%. Hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL with an MCV of 104 fL. He does not drink alcohol and takes no other medications.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?
before.options: {"options": ["Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies as the first test", "Bone marrow biopsy", "Serum vitamin B12 level", "Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 3 months", "Nerve conduction studies"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "vitamin B12 measurement in long-term metformin therapy with neuropathy and macrocytosis", "keyTakeaway": "Long-term metformin: check B12 periodically, especially with neuropathy or anemia; replace B12 and usually continue metformin.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Serum vitamin B12 level
before.explanation: Serum vitamin B12 is correct. The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Section 9) recommend periodic measurement of vitamin B12 in people taking metformin long term, especially those with peripheral neuropathy or anemia, because metformin reduces B12 absorption; methylmalonic acid can confirm borderline results. His macrocytic anemia and neuropathy make deficiency likely, and B12 deficiency neuropathy can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy. Nerve conduction studies would not identify the cause. Repeating A1c does not address the anemia. Bone marrow biopsy is unnecessary before simple tests. Intrinsic factor antibodies help diagnose pernicious anemia after B12 deficiency is confirmed. Metformin can usually be continued with B12 replacement.

references.label: ADA. 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026

before.scenario: A 29-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily. Her TSH was 1.6 mU/L 3 months ago. She now has a positive home pregnancy test, and ultrasonography confirms an intrauterine pregnancy at 5 weeks. She has no symptoms.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her levothyroxine?
before.options: {"options": ["Reduce the dose by 25% to avoid fetal hyperthyroidism", "Take two extra daily doses each week (9 doses weekly) now and check TSH every 4 weeks through mid-pregnancy", "Switch to liothyronine", "Continue the same dose and check TSH at 20 weeks", "Stop levothyroxine because hCG stimulates the thyroid"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "increasing levothyroxine by about 30% at confirmation of pregnancy", "keyTakeaway": "Hypothyroid on levothyroxine and newly pregnant: increase dose ~20-30% (2 extra doses/week) immediately; TSH every 4 weeks to mid-gestation.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Take two extra daily doses each week (9 doses weekly) now and check TSH every 4 weeks through mid-pregnancy
before.explanation: Increasing to 9 doses weekly with TSH every 4 weeks is correct. The 2017 American Thyroid Association pregnancy guideline recommends that women with treated hypothyroidism increase levothyroxine by about 20% to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, for example by taking two extra daily doses each week, because requirements rise early in gestation and fetal neurodevelopment depends on maternal thyroxine in the first trimester. TSH should be checked about every 4 weeks until mid-gestation, aiming for the lower half of the trimester-specific range (or below 2.5 mU/L). Keeping the dose unchanged risks maternal hypothyroidism. Stopping therapy is harmful. Liothyronine does not cross the placenta well and is not recommended. Reducing the dose is incorrect.

references.label: Alexander EK et al. 2017 Guidelines of the American Thyroid Association for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum. Thyroid 2017

before.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 10 years comes for a routine visit. She has no foot pain, numbness, or ulcers. Her pedal pulses are palpable and her skin is intact without calluses or deformities.
before.question: Which of the following is recommended at least annually to identify loss of protective sensation in her feet?
before.options: {"options": ["Plain radiographs of both feet", "Serum vitamin B12 level in place of a foot examination", "Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density", "10-g monofilament testing plus at least one other test such as 128-Hz tuning fork vibration", "Nerve conduction studies"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "annual 10-g monofilament plus one other sensory test for diabetic foot screening", "keyTakeaway": "Diabetes: foot exam at least annually with 10-g monofilament + one other test (vibration, pinprick, temperature, or reflexes), plus inspection and pulses.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: 10-g monofilament testing plus at least one other test such as 128-Hz tuning fork vibration
before.explanation: Monofilament testing plus another sensory test is correct. The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Section 12) recommend a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually, including inspection, assessment of pedal pulses, and testing for loss of protective sensation with a 10-g monofilament plus at least one other assessment (vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork, pinprick, temperature sensation, or ankle reflexes). More frequent examination is needed if risk factors are present. Nerve conduction studies are rarely needed unless features are atypical. Plain radiographs are for suspected Charcot foot or osteomyelitis. Skin biopsy is a research or small-fiber neuropathy tool, not a screen. B12 testing may be useful with metformin but does not replace the foot examination.

references.label: ADA. 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026. Diabetes Care 2026

before.scenario: A 52-year-old man with confirmed hypogonadism started testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks 6 months ago. His energy and libido have improved. Baseline hematocrit was 46%. Today his hematocrit is 56% and trough testosterone is in the mid-normal range. He snores loudly and his wife reports pauses in his breathing during sleep.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Add hydroxyurea and continue testosterone", "Continue the same dose and recheck hematocrit in 12 months", "Add aspirin 81 mg daily and continue the same dose", "Increase the dose to weekly injections for steadier levels", "Stop testosterone until hematocrit falls to a safe level, evaluate for sleep apnea, and then resume at a reduced dose"], "blueprintSystem": "endocrine", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "withholding testosterone therapy when hematocrit exceeds 54%", "keyTakeaway": "Testosterone therapy: check hematocrit at baseline, 3-6 months, then yearly; if >54%, stop, evaluate for OSA/hypoxia, and restart at a lower dose.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Stop testosterone until hematocrit falls to a safe level, evaluate for sleep apnea, and then resume at a reduced dose
before.explanation: Stopping testosterone, evaluating for sleep apnea, and resuming at a lower dose is correct. The 2018 Endocrine Society testosterone guideline recommends checking hematocrit at baseline, at 3 to 6 months, and then annually, and stopping therapy when hematocrit exceeds 54% until it falls to a safe level, evaluating for hypoxia and sleep apnea, and then reinitiating at a reduced dose. Erythrocytosis increases the risk of thrombosis. Continuing unchanged ignores this risk. Aspirin does not correct erythrocytosis. Increasing the total dose worsens it. Hydroxyurea is used for myeloproliferative neoplasms such as polycythemia vera, not testosterone-induced erythrocytosis. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea can be worsened by testosterone.

references.label: Bhasin S et al. Testosterone Therapy in Men With Hypogonadism: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018

before.scenario: A 24-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia is about to start olanzapine. He has no medical history and takes no medications. His BMI is 24 kg/m2. His father has type 2 diabetes.
before.question: Which of the following baseline assessments is most appropriate before starting olanzapine?
before.options: {"options": ["Weight and BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, and lipid panel", "Serum olanzapine level after the first dose", "TSH and serum creatinine only", "Absolute neutrophil count weekly", "Electroencephalogram"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "baseline metabolic monitoring before starting a second-generation antipsychotic", "keyTakeaway": "Before an antipsychotic: weight/BMI, waist, BP, glucose or A1c, lipids; repeat BMI each visit for 6 months, glucose and lipids at 4 months then yearly.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Weight and BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, and lipid panel
before.explanation: Baseline metabolic assessment is correct. The 2020 APA schizophrenia guideline recommends baseline weight and BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, and a lipid panel before starting an antipsychotic, then BMI at every visit for 6 months and quarterly after, and glucose or A1c and lipids at 4 months and then at least annually, because second-generation agents, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. A family history of diabetes adds risk. Weekly neutrophil counts apply to clozapine. TSH and creatinine are baseline tests for lithium. Routine olanzapine levels are not needed. An EEG is not indicated without seizures.

references.label: Keepers GA et al. The APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 3rd ed. Am J Psychiatry 2020

before.scenario: A 45-year-old woman comes for an annual physical examination. She has hypertension controlled with lisinopril. She does not mention alcohol use and has no signs of liver disease. Liver enzymes last year were normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the recommended approach to identifying unhealthy alcohol use in this patient?
before.options: {"options": ["Screen only if she develops signs of liver disease", "Order GGT and MCV as screening tests", "Refer to specialty addiction treatment if she reports any alcohol use", "Screen with a brief validated instrument such as the AUDIT-C, and give brief behavioral counseling if positive", "Perform a breath alcohol test at each visit"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "brief validated screening for unhealthy alcohol use in adults", "keyTakeaway": "Adults (including pregnant): screen for unhealthy alcohol use with AUDIT-C or single-question screen, then brief counseling for risky use.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Screen with a brief validated instrument such as the AUDIT-C, and give brief behavioral counseling if positive
before.explanation: Screening with a brief validated instrument is correct. The 2018 USPSTF recommendation (grade B) is to screen adults 18 and older, including pregnant women, for unhealthy alcohol use in primary care with brief validated tools such as the AUDIT-C or a single-question screen (for example, how many times in the past year did you have 4 or more drinks in a day, for women), and to provide brief behavioral counseling to those with risky drinking. Biomarkers such as GGT and MCV are insensitive screening tests. Waiting for liver disease misses the window for prevention. Breath tests detect recent intake, not patterns of use. Any drinking is not an indication for specialty referral; that is for alcohol use disorder.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions to Reduce Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults. JAMA 2018

before.scenario: A 32-year-old man is brought by his brother after 6 days of sleeping 2 hours a night without fatigue, talking rapidly, spending $15,000 on a new business, and stating that he will soon be a billionaire. He has no psychotic symptoms. He has had two prior depressive episodes and takes no medications. Urine drug screen, TSH, CBC, metabolic panel, and ECG are normal. He agrees to inpatient treatment.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Lamotrigine", "Gabapentin", "Topiramate", "Sertraline", "Quetiapine"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "quetiapine monotherapy for acute mania", "keyTakeaway": "Acute mania: first-line lithium, quetiapine, divalproex, or other listed SGAs; stop antidepressants; lamotrigine does not treat acute mania.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Quetiapine
before.explanation: Quetiapine is correct. The CANMAT/ISBD 2018 bipolar disorder guidelines list lithium, quetiapine, divalproex, asenapine, aripiprazole, paliperidone, risperidone, and cariprazine as first-line monotherapies for acute mania, with combination of an antipsychotic plus lithium or divalproex for more severe cases. He meets criteria for a manic episode, establishing bipolar I disorder. Sertraline, like other antidepressants, should be stopped in mania and can worsen or prolong it. Lamotrigine is effective for maintenance and bipolar depression but not for acute mania. Gabapentin and topiramate are not effective for mania and are not recommended. Valproate should be avoided in women who could become pregnant because of teratogenicity.

references.label: Yatham LN et al. CANMAT and ISBD 2018 Guidelines for the Management of Patients With Bipolar Disorder. Bipolar Disord 2018

before.scenario: A 9-year-old boy is brought by his parents because of severe temper outbursts about 4 times a week for the past 18 months, at home and at school, with screaming and throwing objects in response to minor frustrations. Between outbursts he is irritable and angry most of the day, nearly every day. He has never had a period of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, or grandiosity. He does not use substances and has no medical illness.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder", "Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder", "Oppositional defiant disorder", "Intermittent explosive disorder", "Bipolar I disorder"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "disruptive mood dysregulation disorder in a school-age child", "keyTakeaway": "Chronic irritability between frequent severe outbursts, >=12 months, >=2 settings, onset <10, no manic episodes: DMDD (takes precedence over ODD).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
before.explanation: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is correct. DSM-5-TR criteria require severe recurrent temper outbursts out of proportion to the situation, on average 3 or more times weekly, with persistently irritable or angry mood most of the day nearly every day between outbursts, for 12 months or more, in at least 2 settings, with onset before age 10 and diagnosis between ages 6 and 18. Bipolar I disorder requires distinct episodes of mania, which he has not had. Oppositional defiant disorder may share irritability, but when DMDD criteria are met, DMDD is diagnosed instead. Intermittent explosive disorder lacks persistent irritability between outbursts. ADHD involves inattention and hyperactivity rather than chronic severe irritability.

references.label: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), 2022

before.scenario: A 28-year-old man is found unresponsive in a public restroom with a syringe nearby. Emergency medical services arrive and assess him before giving any medication.
before.question: Which of the following findings is most consistent with opioid poisoning?
before.options: {"options": ["Pinpoint pupils with profuse salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, and diarrhea", "Dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, and absent bowel sounds", "Inducible ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, and agitation", "Pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate of 6/min, and hypoactive bowel sounds", "Dilated pupils, diaphoresis, temperature of 39.5 C (103.1 F), and pulse of 140/min"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "physical findings of the opioid toxidrome", "keyTakeaway": "Opioid toxidrome: CNS depression, respiratory depression, miosis, decreased bowel sounds; support ventilation and give naloxone.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate of 6/min, and hypoactive bowel sounds
before.explanation: Pinpoint pupils, bradypnea, and hypoactive bowel sounds are correct. The 2023 AHA focused update on cardiac arrest or life-threatening toxicity due to poisoning describes opioid poisoning as depressed consciousness with respiratory depression and miosis, and recommends supporting ventilation and giving naloxone for respiratory arrest or depression with a pulse. Dilated pupils, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, and tachycardia indicate a sympathomimetic toxidrome such as cocaine or methamphetamine. Dilated pupils with dry skin and urinary retention indicate an anticholinergic toxidrome. Miosis with secretions and diarrhea indicates a cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphates. Clonus, hyperreflexia, and agitation suggest serotonin syndrome.

references.label: Lavonas EJ et al. 2023 AHA Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning. Circulation 2023

before.scenario: A 70-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2), not on dialysis, has new focal seizures. Noncontrast head CT is unremarkable. Her neurologist requests contrast-enhanced brain MRI to evaluate for a mass lesion. She has no prior contrast reactions.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to contrast for her MRI?
before.options: {"options": ["Arrange hemodialysis immediately after gadolinium administration", "Give a group I gadolinium agent at half dose", "Give IV fluids and N-acetylcysteine before gadolinium", "Avoid all gadolinium contrast because eGFR is below 30", "Give a group II gadolinium-based contrast agent at the standard dose without delaying the study"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "group II gadolinium-based contrast without delay in advanced CKD", "keyTakeaway": "eGFR <30 or AKI: a group II gadolinium agent at standard dose is acceptable when needed; avoid group I agents; no dialysis just to clear gadolinium.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Give a group II gadolinium-based contrast agent at the standard dose without delaying the study
before.explanation: A group II gadolinium agent at standard dose is correct. The 2021 ACR/NKF consensus statements conclude that the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with group II agents (for example, gadobutrol, gadoterate, gadoteridol) is so low that diagnostic MRI should not be withheld or delayed in patients with eGFR below 30, AKI, or dialysis when contrast is clinically indicated. Avoiding contrast can impair diagnosis of a possible brain tumor. Group I agents carry the highest NSF risk and are contraindicated in this population. Starting dialysis solely to remove gadolinium is not recommended in patients not already on dialysis. IV fluids and N-acetylcysteine are not used to prevent gadolinium toxicity.

references.label: Weinreb JC et al. Use of Intravenous Gadolinium-based Contrast Media in Patients with Kidney Disease: ACR/NKF Consensus Statements. Radiology 2021

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m2) and diabetes is admitted with vertebral osteomyelitis and needs 6 weeks of IV antibiotics. He is being evaluated for future hemodialysis and has not yet had vascular access surgery. The team plans venous access for home antibiotic therapy.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate venous access?
before.options: {"options": ["Midline catheter in the nondominant upper arm", "Peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in the dominant arm", "Nontunneled subclavian central venous catheter", "Small-bore tunneled central venous catheter placed through the internal jugular vein", "Peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in the nondominant arm"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "avoiding PICC lines to preserve veins for future dialysis access in advanced CKD", "keyTakeaway": "CKD that may need dialysis: preserve arm veins; avoid PICCs and subclavian lines; use a small-bore tunneled internal jugular catheter if central access is needed.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Small-bore tunneled central venous catheter placed through the internal jugular vein
before.explanation: A small-bore tunneled internal jugular catheter is correct. The KDOQI 2019 vascular access guideline recommends preserving peripheral and central veins in patients with CKD who may need hemodialysis, and suggests avoiding PICCs, which are associated with upper extremity vein thrombosis and central venous stenosis that can prevent creation of a future arteriovenous fistula. When central access is needed, a small-bore tunneled internal jugular catheter is preferred. PICCs in either arm threaten fistula sites. Subclavian catheters carry a high risk of central venous stenosis. Midline catheters also occupy and damage upper arm veins. Referral for timely arteriovenous fistula planning should continue.

references.label: Lok CE et al. KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access: 2019 Update. Am J Kidney Dis 2020

before.scenario: A 74-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2) from diabetic nephropathy has worsening bilateral knee osteoarthritis pain. She takes lisinopril, furosemide, insulin glargine, and atorvastatin. Potassium is 4.9 mEq/L. She has no liver disease and drinks no alcohol. She asks for something stronger than heat and exercise for pain.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate oral analgesic?
before.options: {"options": ["Meloxicam 15 mg daily", "Naproxen 500 mg twice daily", "Acetaminophen up to 3 g daily", "Celecoxib 200 mg daily", "Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily"], "blueprintSystem": "renal", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "acetaminophen instead of NSAIDs for osteoarthritis pain in stage 4 CKD", "keyTakeaway": "Advanced CKD, especially on ACE inhibitor/ARB plus diuretic: avoid oral NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors); use acetaminophen.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Acetaminophen up to 3 g daily
before.explanation: Acetaminophen is correct. The KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline advises avoiding prolonged or regular use of NSAIDs in people with CKD, particularly at low eGFR and in combination with RAS inhibitors and diuretics (the so-called triple whammy), because they reduce renal blood flow and can cause AKI, hyperkalemia, sodium retention, and worsening hypertension. Acetaminophen at a conservative dose is the safest oral option. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and meloxicam are nonselective or preferential NSAIDs that carry these renal risks. Celecoxib is COX-2 selective, which lowers GI bleeding risk but does not protect the kidney. Her potassium is already near the upper limit, increasing the danger of an NSAID.

references.label: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease. Kidney Int 2024

before.scenario: A 31-year-old woman with chronic hypertension takes lisinopril 20 mg daily, and her blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. She stopped contraception last month because she wants to become pregnant. Creatinine and potassium are normal and urine albumin is normal. She is not currently pregnant.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive therapy?
before.options: {"options": ["Switch lisinopril to aliskiren", "Switch lisinopril to losartan", "Switch lisinopril to extended-release nifedipine", "Switch lisinopril to spironolactone", "Continue lisinopril throughout pregnancy"], "blueprintSystem": "cardiovascular", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "switching an ACE inhibitor to nifedipine before conception in chronic hypertension", "keyTakeaway": "Planning pregnancy with hypertension: stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin inhibitors; use nifedipine or labetalol (methyldopa alternative).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Switch lisinopril to extended-release nifedipine
before.explanation: Switching to extended-release nifedipine is correct. The 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety hypertension guideline recommends that women with hypertension who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant should not take ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or direct renin inhibitors because of fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia), and should be transitioned to nifedipine or labetalol, with methyldopa as an alternative. Losartan is an ARB with the same fetal risk. Continuing lisinopril into pregnancy is contraindicated. Spironolactone has antiandrogenic effects on a male fetus and is avoided. Aliskiren, a direct renin inhibitor, is also contraindicated. Switching before conception avoids inadvertent first-trimester exposure.

references.label: 2025 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults. Hypertension 2025

before.scenario: A 79-year-old man taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation falls at home and develops headache and vomiting. His last dose was 4 hours ago. Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. CT shows a 25-mL intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Blood pressure is 162/88 mm Hg. Platelet count is 210,000/mm3 and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to reverse anticoagulation?
before.options: {"options": ["Fresh frozen plasma 2 units", "Vitamin K 10 mg IV", "Idarucizumab 5 g IV", "Protamine sulfate 50 mg IV", "4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 2,000 units IV"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for intracranial hemorrhage on apixaban", "keyTakeaway": "Life-threatening bleed on apixaban or rivaroxaban: 4F-PCC (about 2,000 units or 25 to 50 units/kg); idarucizumab is only for dabigatran; vitamin K is for warfarin.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 2,000 units IV
before.explanation: Four-factor PCC is correct. The 2020 ACC expert consensus decision pathway advises reversal for life-threatening bleeding such as intracranial hemorrhage on a recently taken factor Xa inhibitor and finds a fixed 4F-PCC dose of 2,000 units reasonable; weight-based 25 to 50 units/kg is also used, and the 2022 AHA/ASA ICH guideline supports 4F-PCC. Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 after FDA review of thrombotic risk. Vitamin K is incorrect because it reverses warfarin, not factor Xa inhibitors. Fresh frozen plasma is incorrect because it is ineffective at practical volumes for DOAC reversal. Protamine is incorrect because it reverses heparin. Idarucizumab is incorrect because it is specific for dabigatran.

before.scenario: A 2-month-old boy is seen after newborn screening and confirmatory testing showed hemoglobin SS disease. He is healthy, feeding well, and has received his 2-month vaccines, including pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. He has no drug allergies.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent invasive pneumococcal infection?
before.options: {"options": ["Begin lifelong penicillin prophylaxis at age 5", "Oral penicillin V 125 mg twice daily until age 3, then 250 mg twice daily until age 5", "Begin penicillin prophylaxis at age 2 after the pneumococcal conjugate series is complete", "Amoxicillin only during febrile illnesses", "No antibiotic prophylaxis because he is receiving pneumococcal vaccines"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "oral penicillin prophylaxis from infancy to age 5 in sickle cell anemia", "keyTakeaway": "HbSS: penicillin V 125 mg BID from by 2 months to age 3, then 250 mg BID to age 5, plus full pneumococcal vaccination.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Oral penicillin V 125 mg twice daily until age 3, then 250 mg twice daily until age 5
before.explanation: Penicillin V 125 mg twice daily to age 3, then 250 mg twice daily to age 5, is correct. The 2014 NHLBI expert panel report on sickle cell disease recommends oral penicillin prophylaxis for all children with HbSS starting by 2 months of age and continuing until age 5, because functional asplenia makes invasive pneumococcal disease a leading cause of early death, along with complete pneumococcal vaccination. Delaying until age 2 leaves the highest-risk period unprotected. Antibiotics only during fever do not prevent fulminant sepsis, and every fever of 38.5 C or higher needs urgent evaluation. Vaccination alone is not enough in infancy. Routine prophylaxis can usually stop at age 5 in children without prior invasive infection or splenectomy.

references.label: Yawn BP et al. Management of Sickle Cell Disease: Summary of the 2014 Evidence-Based Report by Expert Panel Members (NHLBI). JAMA 2014

before.scenario: A 70-year-old man has a serum IgG kappa monoclonal protein of 0.8 g/dL found during evaluation of an elevated total protein. Serum free light chain ratio is normal. Hemoglobin, calcium, and creatinine are normal. He has no bone pain, weight loss, neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly, and urine protein is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Multiple myeloma", "Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia", "Light-chain (AL) amyloidosis", "Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance", "Smoldering multiple myeloma"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "low-risk IgG MGUS without end-organ damage", "keyTakeaway": "Low-risk MGUS (IgG, M protein <1.5 g/dL, normal FLC ratio, no CRAB): no marrow or imaging; SPEP at 6 months, then every 2-3 years.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
before.explanation: MGUS is correct. IMWG consensus guidelines define MGUS as a serum M protein below 3 g/dL with fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining end-organ damage (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). IgG type, M protein below 1.5 g/dL, and a normal free light chain ratio make this low-risk MGUS, so bone marrow biopsy and skeletal imaging are not routinely needed; follow-up is SPEP at 6 months, then every 2 to 3 years if stable. Smoldering myeloma requires M protein of 3 g/dL or more or 10% to 60% marrow plasma cells. Multiple myeloma requires end-organ damage or other defining events. Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia involves an IgM protein. AL amyloidosis causes organ involvement such as nephrotic-range proteinuria or cardiomyopathy.

references.label: Kyle RA et al. MGUS and Smoldering Multiple Myeloma: IMWG Consensus Perspectives on Risk Factors for Progression and Guidelines for Monitoring and Management. Leukemia 2010

before.scenario: A 72-year-old woman with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) takes warfarin with a stable INR. She is scheduled for elective total hip arthroplasty in 2 weeks. She has no mechanical heart valve, no stroke or TIA in the past year, and no recent VTE. Creatinine is normal.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate perioperative anticoagulation plan?
before.options: {"options": ["Continue warfarin through surgery", "Stop warfarin 1 day before surgery", "Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin", "Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery without heparin bridging, and resume it 12 to 24 hours after surgery when hemostasis is secure", "Stop warfarin and switch permanently to aspirin 81 mg daily"], "blueprintSystem": "hematologic", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "no heparin bridging when interrupting warfarin for elective surgery in atrial fibrillation", "keyTakeaway": "AF on warfarin for elective surgery: stop 5 days before, no bridging, resume 12-24 hours after; bridge only very high-risk (e.g., mechanical mitral valve).", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery without heparin bridging, and resume it 12 to 24 hours after surgery when hemostasis is secure
before.explanation: Stopping warfarin 5 days before surgery without bridging is correct. The 2022 ACCP perioperative antithrombotic guideline recommends interrupting warfarin about 5 days before elective surgery and suggests against heparin bridging in patients with atrial fibrillation, because bridging increases major bleeding without reducing thromboembolism; warfarin is resumed 12 to 24 hours after surgery. Bridging is generally reserved for very high-risk patients such as those with mechanical mitral valves. Continuing warfarin is unsafe for major orthopedic surgery. Stopping 1 day before leaves the INR elevated. Aspirin does not provide adequate stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Postoperative VTE prophylaxis should also be addressed.

references.label: Douketis JD et al. Perioperative Management of Antithrombotic Therapy: ACCP Clinical Practice Guideline. Chest 2022

before.scenario: A 26-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV infection after routine testing. He feels well. CD4 count is 410/mm3 and HIV RNA is 85,000 copies/mL. Genotype resistance testing, HLA-B*57:01, and hepatitis B serologies have been sent and are pending. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. He is not taking other medications and wants to start treatment as soon as possible.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
before.options: {"options": ["Start bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide today", "Wait until the CD4 count falls below 350/mm3", "Start abacavir-lamivudine-dolutegravir today", "Start raltegravir monotherapy today", "Wait for the genotype resistance result before starting any therapy"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "same-day antiretroviral therapy start after a new HIV diagnosis", "keyTakeaway": "New HIV: start ART for all, ideally same day; do not wait for genotype; avoid abacavir until HLA-B*57:01 negative; use regimens covering HBV if status unknown.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Start bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide today
before.explanation: Starting bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide today is correct. The HHS adult and adolescent antiretroviral guidelines recommend ART for everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, started immediately or as soon as possible after diagnosis, including the same day, when the patient is ready; resistance testing is sent but treatment need not wait for results. Bictegravir-FTC-TAF is a recommended initial regimen with a high barrier to resistance and activity against hepatitis B. Waiting for a lower CD4 count increases illness and transmission. Abacavir must not be started before HLA-B*57:01 is known to be negative, and abacavir-lamivudine does not fully treat possible hepatitis B. Monotherapy rapidly selects resistance.

references.label: HHS Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents: Initiation of Antiretroviral Therapy (clinicalinfo.hiv.gov, current)

before.scenario: A 34-year-old woman in Connecticut removed an engorged deer tick from her thigh yesterday after a weekend camping trip; she estimates it had been attached for about 48 hours. She feels well and has no rash or fever. She is not pregnant and has no drug allergies.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 10 days", "No treatment unless erythema migrans develops", "Doxycycline 200 mg orally as a single dose", "Lyme serology now and treatment if positive", "Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "single-dose doxycycline prophylaxis after a high-risk Ixodes tick bite", "keyTakeaway": "High-risk Ixodes bite (endemic area, attached >=36 h, within 72 h of removal): single-dose doxycycline 200 mg (4.4 mg/kg in children); no serology at time of bite.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Doxycycline 200 mg orally as a single dose
before.explanation: A single 200-mg dose of doxycycline is correct. The 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme disease guideline recommends single-dose doxycycline (200 mg for adults, 4.4 mg/kg up to 200 mg for children of any age) within 72 hours of tick removal for a high-risk bite: an identified Ixodes tick, in a highly endemic area, attached for 36 hours or longer. All three criteria are met here. A 21-day course is treatment for established Lyme disease, not prophylaxis. Serology immediately after a bite is not recommended because antibodies take weeks to develop. Amoxicillin courses are not recommended as prophylaxis. Watchful waiting is an acceptable option for low-risk bites but forgoes effective prevention for this high-risk exposure.

references.label: Lantos PM et al. IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Lyme Disease. Clin Infect Dis 2021

before.scenario: A 25-year-old man has a 4-cm painful, fluctuant swelling on his posterior thigh with 3 cm of surrounding erythema. He has had chills. Temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F) and pulse is 98/min. Blood pressure is normal. He is otherwise healthy, has normal kidney function, and has no drug allergies. Local rates of community-associated MRSA are high.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
before.options: {"options": ["Warm compresses and oral dicloxacillin", "Oral cephalexin without drainage", "Incision and drainage alone", "Admission for IV vancomycin without drainage", "Incision and drainage with wound culture plus oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "incision and drainage plus TMP-SMX for a skin abscess with systemic signs", "keyTakeaway": "Abscess: I&D for all; add MRSA-active oral antibiotic (TMP-SMX or doxycycline) if SIRS signs; IV vancomycin for severe infection.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Incision and drainage with wound culture plus oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
before.explanation: Incision and drainage with culture plus TMP-SMX is correct. The 2014 IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline recommends incision and drainage for all purulent abscesses, and adds an antibiotic active against MRSA, such as TMP-SMX or doxycycline, for moderate purulent infection with signs of systemic inflammation, such as temperature above 38 C or heart rate above 90/min. Culture guides therapy. Drainage alone suffices for simple abscesses without systemic signs, but this patient has fever and tachycardia. Cephalexin lacks MRSA activity and does not replace drainage. IV vancomycin is reserved for severe infection such as hypotension or failed oral therapy, and drainage is still required. Warm compresses with dicloxacillin will not treat a fluctuant MRSA abscess.

references.label: Stevens DL et al. Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections: 2014 Update by IDSA. Clin Infect Dis 2014

before.scenario: A 48-year-old landscaper has a painless ulcerated nodule on his right index finger that appeared 3 weeks after he was pricked by a rose thorn. Over the past 2 weeks, new nontender nodules have appeared in a line up the dorsal forearm. He has no fever and is otherwise healthy. He takes no medications. Culture of aspirated material grows Sporothrix schenckii complex.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["Liposomal amphotericin B IV", "Fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose", "Cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 10 days", "Itraconazole 200 mg orally daily, continued 2 to 4 weeks after lesions resolve", "Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double-strength orally twice daily"], "blueprintSystem": "infectious-diseases", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "itraconazole for lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis", "keyTakeaway": "Rose-thorn or soil inoculation with nodules ascending the lymphatics: sporotrichosis; treat lymphocutaneous disease with itraconazole 200 mg daily until 2-4 weeks after resolution.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Itraconazole 200 mg orally daily, continued 2 to 4 weeks after lesions resolve
before.explanation: Itraconazole is correct. The 2007 IDSA sporotrichosis guideline recommends itraconazole 200 mg orally daily for lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, continued for 2 to 4 weeks after all lesions have resolved, usually 3 to 6 months total; drug interactions and liver tests should be reviewed. Nodular lymphangitic spread from a thorn or soil inoculation site is classic. Cephalexin treats streptococcal and staphylococcal cellulitis, which does not produce chronic ascending nodules with a fungal culture. A single 150-mg fluconazole dose treats vaginal candidiasis; fluconazole is only a less effective high-dose alternative for sporotrichosis. Amphotericin B is reserved for severe, disseminated, or pulmonary disease. TMP-SMX treats nocardiosis, another cause of nodular lymphangitis.

references.label: Kauffman CA et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the management of sporotrichosis: 2007 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis 2007

before.scenario: A 66-year-old man has 1 year of weak urinary stream, hesitancy, a sensation of incomplete emptying, and nocturia twice nightly. He has no hematuria, dysuria, back pain, or neurologic symptoms. He takes no medications. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, nontender prostate without nodules. Urinalysis is normal.
before.question: Which of the following should be included in his initial evaluation to quantify symptom severity and guide treatment?
before.options: {"options": ["CT urography", "Cystoscopy", "Transrectal ultrasonography of the prostate", "Urodynamic pressure-flow studies", "International Prostate Symptom Score (AUA Symptom Index)"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "International Prostate Symptom Score in the initial evaluation of LUTS", "keyTakeaway": "LUTS/BPH initial workup: history, IPSS/AUA-SI, DRE, urinalysis (PSA if appropriate); urodynamics and cystoscopy are not routine.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: International Prostate Symptom Score (AUA Symptom Index)
before.explanation: The International Prostate Symptom Score is correct. The AUA guideline on LUTS attributed to BPH recommends, at initial evaluation, a medical history, a validated symptom score (IPSS or AUA Symptom Index), physical examination including digital rectal examination, and urinalysis, with PSA in selected patients; the score grades severity (mild 0 to 7, moderate 8 to 19, severe 20 to 35) and tracks response to therapy. Urodynamic studies are optional before surgical therapy, not routine at first evaluation. Cystoscopy is for hematuria, suspected stricture or cancer, or before some procedures. Transrectal ultrasound is used to size the prostate before procedures. CT urography evaluates hematuria.

references.label: Sandhu JS et al. Management of LUTS Attributed to BPH: AUA Guideline Amendment 2023. J Urol 2024

before.scenario: A 19-year-old college student comes for a preparticipation sports physical. He has no testicular symptoms and no history of cryptorchidism or family history of testicular cancer. He asks whether he should be doing testicular self-examinations or having yearly testicular exams.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response regarding testicular cancer screening?
before.options: {"options": ["Routine screening by clinician examination or self-examination is not recommended for asymptomatic males", "Have annual serum AFP and beta-hCG testing", "Have an annual clinician testicular examination", "Perform monthly testicular self-examination", "Have annual scrotal ultrasonography"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "no routine testicular cancer screening in asymptomatic young men", "keyTakeaway": "USPSTF: do not screen asymptomatic males for testicular cancer (no routine exam or self-exam); evaluate any mass promptly.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Routine screening by clinician examination or self-examination is not recommended for asymptomatic males
before.explanation: Not routinely screening is correct. The USPSTF reaffirmation statement recommends against screening for testicular cancer in asymptomatic adolescent and adult males (grade D), by clinician examination or self-examination, because the disease is rare, highly curable even when found because of symptoms, and screening leads to false positives and unnecessary procedures without evidence of benefit. He should be told to seek care promptly for a testicular mass, swelling, or pain. Monthly self-examination and annual clinician examination are screening and are not recommended. Scrotal ultrasound and tumor markers are diagnostic tests for a palpable mass, not screens. Higher-risk men, such as those with cryptorchidism, may be counseled individually.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Testicular Cancer: Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement. Ann Intern Med 2011

before.scenario: A 70-year-old woman has 1 year of urinary urgency, frequency of 11 times daily, nocturia twice nightly, and occasional urge leakage. She drinks 4 cups of coffee daily. She has no dysuria or hematuria. Urinalysis is normal and postvoid residual is 40 mL. She has mild hypertension and normal cognition.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
before.options: {"options": ["Indwelling urethral catheter", "Bladder training, pelvic floor muscle training, and caffeine and fluid modification", "Sacral neuromodulation", "Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injection", "Oxybutynin 5 mg three times daily"], "blueprintSystem": "genitourinary", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "behavioral therapy as first-line treatment for overactive bladder in an older woman", "keyTakeaway": "OAB: behavioral therapy for all first (bladder training, pelvic floor training, caffeine/fluid changes); be cautious with antimuscarinics in older adults.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Bladder training, pelvic floor muscle training, and caffeine and fluid modification
before.explanation: Behavioral therapy is correct. The 2024 AUA/SUFU overactive bladder guideline recommends offering behavioral therapies (bladder training, urgency suppression, pelvic floor muscle training, and fluid and caffeine management) to all patients with OAB, alone or with medication. When medication is added, clinicians should discuss the risk of dementia and cognitive impairment with antimuscarinics; oxybutynin has a high anticholinergic burden and beta-3 agonists are often preferred in older adults. OnabotulinumtoxinA and sacral neuromodulation are reserved for patients whose symptoms do not respond to behavioral and pharmacologic therapy. Indwelling catheters are a last resort and are not treatment for OAB with a normal postvoid residual.

references.label: Cameron AP et al. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder. J Urol 2024

before.scenario: A 15-year-old girl with fair skin, red hair, and freckles comes for a routine adolescent visit. She burns easily and plans to work as a lifeguard this summer. She has no unusual moles and no family history of melanoma. Her friends use indoor tanning beds.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive intervention?
before.options: {"options": ["Counsel her to minimize UV exposure with broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, shade, and avoidance of indoor tanning", "Counsel about sun protection only after she has a blistering sunburn", "Perform an annual total-body skin examination by a clinician", "Recommend vitamin D supplementation in place of sun protection", "Recommend gradual tanning bed use to build a protective base tan"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "counseling fair-skinned adolescents to minimize UV exposure", "keyTakeaway": "Fair skin ages 6 months-24 years: counsel on UV avoidance (sunscreen SPF >=15, clothing, shade, no tanning beds); routine skin exam screening is an I statement.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Counsel her to minimize UV exposure with broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, shade, and avoidance of indoor tanning
before.explanation: Counseling to minimize UV exposure is correct. The 2018 USPSTF recommendation (grade B) is to counsel young adults, adolescents, children, and parents of young children aged 6 months to 24 years who have fair skin about minimizing exposure to ultraviolet radiation, including broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher, protective clothing, seeking shade, and avoiding indoor tanning, to reduce skin cancer risk. The USPSTF found insufficient evidence (I statement) for routine clinician total-body skin examination in adults without symptoms. Waiting for a sunburn misses the purpose of prevention. Vitamin D supplements are not a substitute for sun protection. Tanning beds increase melanoma risk and no base tan is protective.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Behavioral Counseling to Prevent Skin Cancer: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2018

before.scenario: A 19-year-old woman has severe nodulocystic acne with scarring that has not responded to 3 months of oral doxycycline plus a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide. She is sexually active and uses condoms. She is otherwise healthy. Isotretinoin is planned.
before.question: Which of the following testing is required for this patient in connection with isotretinoin?
before.options: {"options": ["Complete blood count every month during treatment", "Two negative pregnancy tests before starting, and a pregnancy test each month during treatment", "No pregnancy testing if she agrees to use two forms of contraception", "Serum vitamin A level before each prescription", "Serum creatinine every month during treatment"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "labs", "blueprintTopic": "pregnancy testing before and during isotretinoin therapy", "keyTakeaway": "Isotretinoin in patients who can become pregnant: 2 negative pregnancy tests before, monthly tests during, 2 contraceptive methods; check LFTs and lipids; no routine CBC.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Two negative pregnancy tests before starting, and a pregnancy test each month during treatment
before.explanation: Pregnancy tests before and monthly during treatment are correct. The 2024 AAD acne guideline supports isotretinoin for severe, scarring, or treatment-resistant acne and notes the federally mandated iPLEDGE program, which for patients who can become pregnant requires two negative pregnancy tests before the first prescription, monthly pregnancy tests during treatment and after the last dose, and two forms of contraception (or abstinence), because isotretinoin is highly teratogenic. The guideline recommends checking liver function and lipids, and recommends against routine monitoring of the CBC. Serum creatinine is not affected by isotretinoin. Contraception does not replace pregnancy testing. Vitamin A levels are not monitored, although patients should avoid vitamin A supplements.

references.label: Reynolds RV et al. Guidelines of Care for the Management of Acne Vulgaris (AAD). J Am Acad Dermatol 2024

before.scenario: A 52-year-old woman has 2 months of painful mouth sores that make eating difficult. Over the past 2 weeks she has developed fragile, flaccid blisters on her chest and back that break easily and leave raw, painful erosions. She takes no new medications and has no fever. Oral examination shows multiple erosions of the buccal mucosa and gingiva. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin next to a blister causes the epidermis to separate.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Stevens-Johnson syndrome", "Dermatitis herpetiformis", "Pemphigus vulgaris", "Erythema multiforme major", "Bullous pemphigoid"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "pemphigus vulgaris with oral erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign", "keyTakeaway": "Pemphigus vulgaris: oral erosions first, flaccid fragile blisters, positive Nikolsky; DIF intercellular IgG; bullous pemphigoid has tense blisters, Nikolsky negative.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Pemphigus vulgaris
before.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is correct. The EADV S2K pemphigus guideline describes painful mucosal erosions, usually oral and often first, followed by flaccid blisters and erosions on the skin, with a positive Nikolsky sign due to loss of keratinocyte adhesion from anti-desmoglein antibodies; diagnosis is confirmed by perilesional biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing intercellular IgG, and first-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids with rituximab. Bullous pemphigoid affects older adults with tense blisters, often pruritic, rare mucosal involvement, and a negative Nikolsky sign. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is acute, febrile, and usually follows a new drug. Erythema multiforme major shows target lesions, often after herpes simplex. Dermatitis herpetiformis causes intensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces with celiac disease.

references.label: Joly P et al. Updated S2K Guidelines on the Management of Pemphigus Vulgaris and Foliaceus (EADV). J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2020

before.scenario: A 40-year-old man who slept outdoors overnight in subfreezing temperatures is brought to the emergency department. His fingers on both hands are white, hard, cold, and numb. Core temperature is 36.4 C (97.5 F), and he is alert. There is no risk of refreezing now that he is in the hospital.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of his hands?
before.options: {"options": ["Immerse the hands in water at 44 to 46 C (111 to 115 F)", "Immerse the hands in circulating water at 37 to 39 C (98.6 to 102.2 F) until the tissue is soft and pliable", "Rub the fingers with snow to restore circulation", "Warm the hands in front of a space heater", "Perform early surgical debridement of the affected fingers"], "blueprintSystem": "dermatologic", "taskCategory": "intervention", "blueprintTopic": "rapid rewarming in 37 to 39 C water for frostbite", "keyTakeaway": "Frostbite: rapid rewarming in 37-39 C circulating water (~30 min) when no refreeze risk; no rubbing or dry heat; delay amputation; consider tPA for severe cases.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Immerse the hands in circulating water at 37 to 39 C (98.6 to 102.2 F) until the tissue is soft and pliable
before.explanation: Rapid rewarming in 37 to 39 C water is correct. The 2024 Wilderness Medical Society frostbite guideline recommends rapid rewarming by immersion in circulating water at 37 to 39 C, usually for about 30 minutes, until the tissue is red or purple and soft, once there is no risk of refreezing, along with ibuprofen and analgesia; thrombolysis may be considered for severe injury within 24 hours. Rubbing the tissue, with or without snow, causes further mechanical damage. Dry heat sources such as space heaters or fires heat unevenly and can burn insensate skin. Water hotter than about 40 C risks burns. Surgical debridement or amputation is generally delayed for weeks until the line between viable and dead tissue is clear.

references.label: McIntosh SE et al. Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Frostbite: 2024 Update. Wilderness Environ Med 2024

before.scenario: A 28-year-old woman comes for her annual examination accompanied by her partner, who answers several questions for her. She has no injuries on examination. She has no chronic medical problems.
before.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to screening for intimate partner violence?
before.options: {"options": ["Screen only if physical injuries are found", "Notify law enforcement of any positive screen without her consent", "Screen her with the partner present so that both perspectives are heard", "Screen her privately, without the partner present, using a brief validated tool, and connect her to support services if positive", "Do not screen because evidence is insufficient for women of reproductive age"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "screening women of reproductive age for intimate partner violence", "keyTakeaway": "Screen all women of reproductive age for IPV, privately, with a brief validated tool; refer positives to support services; I statement for older/vulnerable adults.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Screen her privately, without the partner present, using a brief validated tool, and connect her to support services if positive
before.explanation: Private screening with a validated tool and referral to support is correct. The 2025 USPSTF recommendation (grade B) is to screen women of reproductive age for intimate partner violence and to provide or refer those who screen positive to ongoing support services; screening should occur privately, away from partners or family. Partner domination of the visit is a possible warning sign. Restricting screening to visible injuries misses most abuse. Screening in front of the partner is unsafe and unlikely to produce disclosure. In most states, reporting IPV in competent adults is not mandatory, and reporting without consent can increase danger; clinicians should know their state laws. The insufficient-evidence statement applies to screening older or vulnerable adults for abuse.

references.label: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse of Older or Vulnerable Adults: Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2025

before.scenario: Investigators study a new drug for chronic stable angina. Each of 60 participants is randomly assigned to receive either the new drug or placebo for 6 weeks, followed by a 2-week washout period with no study drug, and then the other treatment for 6 weeks. Weekly angina episodes are compared within each participant between the two treatment periods.
before.question: Which of the following best describes this study design?
before.options: {"options": ["Case series", "Prospective cohort study", "Parallel-group randomized controlled trial", "Randomized crossover trial", "Factorial randomized trial"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "foundational", "blueprintTopic": "identifying a randomized crossover trial design", "keyTakeaway": "Crossover trial: every participant gets each treatment in random order with washout; own control, smaller sample; watch for carryover and period effects.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Randomized crossover trial
before.explanation: A randomized crossover trial is correct. The CONSORT extension for randomised crossover trials describes designs in which each participant receives each intervention in a randomized sequence, separated by a washout period, so that each participant serves as his or her own control; this reduces between-subject variability and the required sample size, and is suited to stable chronic conditions with reversible treatment effects. Key threats are carryover and period effects. In a parallel-group trial, each participant receives only one intervention. A factorial trial tests two or more interventions simultaneously in combinations, such as drug A, drug B, both, or neither. A cohort study observes rather than assigns exposures. A case series describes outcomes in a group without a comparison.

references.label: Dwan K et al. CONSORT 2010 Statement: Extension to Randomised Crossover Trials. BMJ 2019

before.scenario: A 40-year-old woman has a nondisplaced distal fibula fracture after a fall. She is placed in a walking boot. She has a history of a bleeding duodenal ulcer, so NSAIDs are avoided, and her pain is not controlled with scheduled acetaminophen. She has no history of substance use disorder and the state prescription drug monitoring program shows no other controlled substance prescriptions. You decide that an opioid is warranted.
before.question: Which of the following prescriptions best follows current guidance?
before.options: {"options": ["Transdermal fentanyl 25 mcg/h patch for 1 week", "Methadone 5 mg every 8 hours for 1 week", "Immediate-release oxycodone at the lowest effective dose for 30 days with 2 refills", "Extended-release oxycodone 10 mg every 12 hours for 2 weeks", "Immediate-release oxycodone at the lowest effective dose for a few days, continuing scheduled acetaminophen"], "blueprintSystem": "professional-practice", "taskCategory": "professional", "blueprintTopic": "immediate-release opioid for no longer than the expected duration of severe acute pain", "keyTakeaway": "Acute pain needing opioids: immediate-release, lowest effective dose, only the quantity needed (often a few days); no ER/LA opioids or methadone in opioid-naive patients.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Immediate-release oxycodone at the lowest effective dose for a few days, continuing scheduled acetaminophen
before.explanation: Immediate-release oxycodone at the lowest effective dose for a few days with acetaminophen is correct. The CDC 2022 opioid prescribing guideline recommends maximizing nonopioid therapies, and when opioids are needed for acute pain, prescribing immediate-release opioids at the lowest effective dose and no greater quantity than needed for the expected duration of pain severe enough to require them, which is often a few days or less, with checking of the PDMP. Extended-release or long-acting opioids, including fentanyl patches, should not be used for acute pain in opioid-naive patients because of overdose risk. A 30-day supply with refills exceeds the expected duration of severe pain. Methadone has a long, variable half-life and QT effects and is not used for acute pain.

references.label: Dowell D et al. CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022. MMWR Recomm Rep 2022

before.scenario: A 52-year-old man, a lifelong nonsmoker, has a painless lump on the left side of his neck for 6 weeks. He had no recent upper respiratory infection, and a course of antibiotics from an urgent care clinic did not shrink it. Examination shows a 3-cm, mobile, nontender, fluctuant mass deep to the sternocleidomastoid at level II. The left palatine tonsil is mildly enlarged and firm. Ultrasonography shows a cystic node.
before.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
before.options: {"options": ["Thyroglossal duct cyst", "Reactive lymphadenitis", "Second branchial cleft cyst", "Lipoma", "Metastatic HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "diagnosis", "blueprintTopic": "cystic lateral neck mass in an adult as metastatic HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma", "keyTakeaway": "A persistent cystic level II neck mass in an adult is metastatic HPV-related oropharyngeal SCC until proven otherwise.", "kind": "vignette"}
before.correctAnswer: Metastatic HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
before.explanation: Metastatic HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC is correct. The 2017 AAO-HNS guideline on the adult neck mass warns that a neck mass persisting 2 weeks or more without clear infection is at increased risk of malignancy, that cystic neck masses in adults should not be presumed benign, and that empiric antibiotics should not delay workup; it recommends fine-needle aspiration rather than open biopsy and a targeted examination of the upper aerodigestive tract. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer often affects middle-aged nonsmokers and presents as a cystic level II node from a small tonsil or tongue-base primary. A branchial cleft cyst is a diagnosis of exclusion in an adult older than 40. Reactive nodes follow infection and shrink. A thyroglossal duct cyst is midline and moves with swallowing. A lipoma is soft and subcutaneous. Takeaway: cystic lateral neck mass in an adult over 40 = metastatic oropharyngeal cancer until proven otherwise; FNA, not antibiotics.

references.label: Pynnonen MA et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation of the Neck Mass in Adults. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017
